refuted.title: Cut the ~64-85 ms processing delay with a low-delay filter-bank equalizer or asymmetric windows while keeping fine frequency resolution
refuted.why:
The description of the current code is mostly right. RXA.c:323-337 creates EMNR with fsize=4096 and ovrlp=4 at ch[channel].dsp_rate. No exported setter changes fsize or ovrlp; the SetRXAEMNR* functions cover only run, gain/NPE method, AE, position, psi, train and post2. calc_window builds a normalised sqrt-Hamming window over fsize samples. I traced xemnr and calc_emnr with a typical bsize of 64. oainidx = (4096-64-1024) % 1024 = 960, and an output sample leaves roughly fsize-bsize ≈ 4032 samples after it came in, about 84 ms at 48 kHz. The upper end of the 64-85 ms claim is the accurate one. The pipeline adds two more linear-phase 2048-tap bandpass filters by default (nbp0 and bp1, mp=0), about 21 ms each, so EMNR is the largest single source of delay but not the only one. ae.psi=20 is fixed in bins, as claimed. The proposal is wrong on npl, though: delta_LF and delta_MF are computed as 1000 Hz and 3000 Hz over (rate/2) times msize (emnr.c:547-548), so they track the sample rate correctly. The claim about monitoring your own audio while transmitting is also wrong: EMNR is created only in RXA, and the TX monitor path never goes through it. WDSP has no low-delay EMNR variant. NNR is a separate neural NR with its own 512-point STFT at 16 kHz.

The headline benefit cannot be achieved. "5-15 ms delay with the same 11.7 Hz analysis resolution" conflates the resolution of the gain estimate with the resolution of the filter actually applied. In a filter-bank equalizer the applied filter is an L-tap FIR. A 5-15 ms FIR resolves roughly 70-200 Hz, not 11.7 Hz, so the 2049-bin gain vector is smoothed down to a few tens of effective bands. The same limit applies to Mauler-Martin asymmetric windows, where the short synthesis window sets both the delay and the effective resolution. This is the basic trade-off between time and frequency resolution, and no implementation trick removes it. Minimum-phase conversion lowers the average delay, but sharp spectral detail still means long ringing and large group delay near those features. The proposal's own risk section concedes that sharp gain detail is lost.

For amateur use, that fine resolution is most of why EMNR works on weak SSB and CW signals: it separates voice harmonics and single carriers from noise between them. A 5-15 ms filter turns it into a coarse short-window suppressor. There is a second problem. The gains still come from an 85 ms sqrt-Hamming frame in which the newest samples carry almost no weight, so gain decisions trail the audio by tens of milliseconds. The filter-bank equalizer would apply late gains to current audio and clip syllable and CW element onsets. A dit at 30 WPM lasts 40 ms, so CW, the mode the proposal is meant to help, would suffer most. Going to 8x overlap shortens the hop but not the window's centre-of-mass lag.

The cited papers are real: Löllmann & Vary in Speech Communication 49(7-8), 2007, and Mauler & Martin at EUSIPCO 2007. Both are designed around 8-16 kHz speech with roughly 256-512-point DFTs, not 4096-point narrowband analysis. The Apple Silicon point does not matter, because WDSP is cross-platform C.

A cheaper and more honest low-latency option exists. Expose fsize, ideally specified in milliseconds, through a setter, accepting coarser bins in exchange for less delay. Separately, enable the existing minimum-phase option (RXASetMP) on the bandpass filters. That was not the proposal, and the proposal's claimed benefit as stated is refuted.

refuted.title: Hybrid neural a-priori SNR / speech-presence estimation feeding the existing MMSE-LSA gain (Deep Xi-style), run on Core ML/ANE
refuted.why:
Inside emnr.c the description is roughly right. calc_gain (emnr.c ~1100-1240) gets xi from the decision-directed recursion in all four gain methods, with alpha derived from tau = -128/8000/ln(0.985). Noise comes from LambdaD (Martin minimum statistics, the default npe_method 0 set in RXA.c:323), LambdaDs (SPP) or LambdaDl (an MCRA-2-style estimator with delta_LF/delta_MF thresholds). Several of the specifics are wrong or overstated, though:
(1) The DD one-frame onset bias is already addressed in method 3. After the DD estimate it computes a two-step refinement, xi_ts = mask^2 * gamma (the TSNR of Plapous et al.), and recomputes the gain from it.
(2) An OM-LSA-style speech-presence floor already exists. Method 0 multiplies the gain by the speech-presence term witchHat/(1+witchHat) with q=0.2. The default method 2 uses GG(gamma, xi) * GGS(gamma, xi/(1-q)), which is the LSA gain combined with a speech-presence gain. So "add an OM-LSA-style floor" is not new.
(3) The zeta table is trained, not hand-crafted. readZetaHat/zetaHat.c is a learned 60x60 table, and train setters (SetRXAEMNRtrainZetaThresh/T2) exist.

The decisive point is that WDSP 2.11 already ships neural noise reduction as its own RXA block. nnr.c and nnet.c (about 2,650 lines, NR0V 2026) are created in RXA.c:339 next to EMNR, with an nnrbypass partner. They implement GRU, Conv2d/ConvTranspose2d, PReLU, a DPRNN (dual-path RNN) block, a DeepFilterNet-style deep-filtering head (dfhead with order, gain limits and attack/release smoothing), a conditioning stage, loadable model slots (NNET_NSLOTS=4) with per-model sample-rate, hop and lookahead checks, and a per-model training band used to configure the bypass filter for USB/LSB. In other words, a causal recurrent network trained on band-limited speech is already in this library. It uses a more modern architecture than Deep Xi (DPRNN plus a deep filter rather than a ResLSTM a-priori SNR estimator). So "the largest available gain is a neural estimator" has already been taken in this DSP block, just as a separate module rather than grafted onto EMNR. Feeding a second network's xi into EMNR's GG/GGS back end would duplicate NNR's training-data and maintenance burden, and in the literature since 2019 hybrid Deep Xi/MMSE generally scores below end-to-end mask or deep-filter models of similar size. The main remaining argument is interpretability: a bounded, closed-form gain fed by the network. NNR already bounds its output with a mask floor and a maximum gain (setFloor/setMaxGain).

The citations are real: Nicolson & Paliwal, Speech Communication 111 (2019) 44-55, and Valin, MMSP 2018. But the cited PESQ/segSNR gains are measured against a DD/MS baseline on general noise corpora, not against an existing neural NR on HF audio. Nothing here shows a benefit over what WDSP 2.11 already provides. For CW and digital modes, EMNR and spectral-gain NR are usually bypassed anyway, and a speech-trained xi estimator would likely damage carriers and tones. On the stated criteria (already done in another module of the same library, and parts of the current-behaviour claim inaccurate), the proposal is refuted.

summary: ANR and ANF (anr.c / anf.c xanr/xanf lines 82-134) share one engine: a real-valued adaptive line enhancer on the I channel of the post-demod audio. A 64-tap normalised LMS predictor (RXA.c defaults: delay 16, two_mu 1e-4, gamma 0.1) predicts d[n] from d[n-delay-j]. Both regularise the NLMS step with 1/(sigma+1e-10) (line 103). Both apply Kamenetsky-Widrow variable leakage: they compare a-posteriori errors with and without leak (nel/nev, lines 109-110), step lidx up or down, and map it through a 4th power, ngamma = gamma*lidx^4*den_mult (line 119). ANR outputs the prediction y (line 106). ANF outputs the error, the same filter used as a notch. They run pre-AGC at position 0 or post-AGC at position 1 (RXA.c lines 674-684). SNBA (snb.c) is a Vaseghi/Rayner-Janssen style AR impulse restorer. It resamples to 12 kHz, takes 256-sample frames with 4x overlap (hop 64), fits an order-64 AR model by autocorrelation and Levinson (lmath.c asolve), and inverse-filters to a two-sided residual (invf). It thresholds residual power against k2 times a median-anchored robust mean (det), bridges gaps, extends pre and post, and zeroes the hits. It then repairs each burst in merit order by least-squares AR interpolation (xHat via the Trench Toeplitz inverse trI), refitting the AR model per gap, over npasses=2.

kept.title: SNBA: SetRXASNBAasize can overflow the Levinson work buffers (heap overrun)
kept.current: create_snba allocates wrk.asolve_r and wrk.asolve_z as (exec.asize + 1) doubles, using the creation-time asize (64). SetRXASNBAasize only writes rxa[channel].snba.p->exec.asize = size and reallocates nothing. asolve(xsize, asize, ...) then memsets and writes r[0..asize] and z[0..asize] (lines 97-117), and execFrame calls it with exec.asize (line 505). Any asize above the creation value writes past both heap blocks. A second, minor issue is in execFrame (lines 514-535). On pass >= 1 the k==0 iteration does not call scanFrame, so it repairs whatever bimp/limp/p_opt/next the last scan of the previous pass left behind. It is not the best-merit burst of the reset 'unfixed' map.
kept.proposed: In LyraDSP, size the asolve and xHat work arrays for the maximum legal asize (asize <= xsize/2 is a sensible hard limit because invf needs asize samples on each side). Make the setter clamp to that maximum. If not, decalc and re-allocate the work arrays under the lock. For the minor issue, call scanFrame unconditionally at the top of each k iteration, or at least at k==0 of every pass after the first.
kept.benefit: Removes heap corruption, which shows up as random crashes or audio garbage, whenever a UI or API exposes the AR order. The scanFrame fix gives a marginal quality gain: the second pass starts on the best-conditioned gap.
kept.risk: None for default settings (asize stays 64). Clamping changes nothing an operator can currently use safely.
kept.evidence: Line-level: snb.c:115-116 allocate (d->exec.asize + 1) * sizeof(double). snb.c:608 changes asize with no reallocation. lmath.c:97-98 and 99-117 index r[] and z[] up to asize. snb.c:519-520 guard scanFrame with 'if (k > 0)' inside the pass loop, while unfixed is reset at line 516.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code and the description is accurate.

- **Allocation size is fixed at creation.** snb.c:115-116 allocate asolve_r and asolve_z as (exec.asize + 1) doubles, using the creation-time asize. RXA.c:241-259 passes 64. snb.c:104-105 also size the xHat work arrays (xHat_a1rows_max = xsize + asize, xHat_a2cols_max = xsize + 2*asize) from that same creation-time asize.
- **The setter reallocates nothing.** SetRXASNBAasize (snb.c:605-610) only assigns exec.asize under the lock.
- **The overrun path is real.** asolve (lmath.c:93-125) memsets and writes r[0..asize] and z[0..asize], and execFrame calls it with exec.asize (snb.c:505). So any asize above 64 overruns both blocks on every frame.
- **The xHat arrays overflow too.** scanFrame clamps p_opt to pval, which tracks asize, and xHat builds A1/A2 with a1rows = xusize + asize and a2cols = xusize + 2*asize. A larger asize therefore also overruns xHat_A1, xHat_A2 and xHat_P1. That supports the proposal's call to size the xHat arrays as well as the asolve arrays.
- **There is no hidden guard.** WDSP has no clamp or reallocation for asize anywhere else.

Mitigating factors:
- With the default asize of 64 the bug never fires.
- I found no call to SetRXASNBAasize anywhere in the Lyra tree. So it is a latent memory-safety bug in an exported PORT API, and it only becomes live if a UI or API exposes the AR order.

The suggested xsize/2 cap is reasonable. invf filters from asize to xsize - asize, and the autocorrelation reads x[j-i] back into xbase, so asize must stay well below xsize.

The minor scanFrame claim is also accurate:
- At snb.c:516-520, unfixed is reset at the top of each pass, but at k==0 scanFrame is skipped.
- So pass 1 starts on the impulse that the last scan of pass 0 picked: the best of the few still unfixed, with indices and p_opt computed when its neighbours were already marked fixed.
- The sample positions are still valid, so nothing breaks. The effect is only a different repair order and a possibly larger AR order for the first repair of pass 1. That fits the proposal's own 'marginal' label.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This is a real but latent heap overrun. If anything calls SetRXASNBAasize with a size above the creation value of 64, it writes past asolve_r and asolve_z on every frame, and past the xHat work arrays (A1, A2, P1) whenever a repair uses p > 64. Nothing in Lyra calls the setter today, so the fix is defensive hardening that only matters if the AR order is ever exposed. Two acceptable fixes: clamp asize to the allocated maximum (keeping it at or below about xsize/2), or reallocate the work arrays under csDSP when asize changes. The scanFrame-at-k==0 change only alters the order in which gaps are repaired on passes after the first. Any audible effect would be marginal at best.

kept.title: NLMS regulariser 1e-10 is absolute, so ANR/ANF behaviour depends on signal level pre-AGC
kept.file_function: anr.c:xanr line 103 (and lines 109-110, 121-122); anf.c:xanf same lines
kept.current: inv_sigp = 1.0 / (sigma + 1e-10), where sigma = sum over the 64 reference samples of d^2. At position 0 (pre-AGC, RXA.c line 674-675) audio is in ADC full-scale units. sigma equals 1e-10 at an RMS of about 1.25e-6 (about -118 dBFS), which is a realistic level for weak HF signals on a quiet band. Below that, the effective step two_mu*sigma/(sigma+1e-10) shrinks in proportion to power. The leak factor c0 = 1 - two_mu*ngamma (line 121) is level-independent, so leakage outweighs the update for weak signals. The ANR weights shrink, its output y loses gain, and adaptation slows by 10x per 10 dB. The nel/nev leak decision (lines 109-110) also changes, through the sigma*inv_sigp term.
kept.proposed: Use a relative regulariser. Track a slow running estimate of input power P (one-pole, about 1 s) and set delta = kappa * L * P with kappa about 1e-2 to 1e-1. Alternatively use Benesty's SNR-based delta = L*sigma_v^2*(1+sqrt(1+SNR))/SNR, with sigma_v^2 from a minimum-statistics floor. Keep a tiny absolute floor (about 1e-30, or 1e-20 in float32) only to avoid 0/0 during digital silence.
kept.benefit: Makes ANR and ANF pre-AGC behaviour level-invariant: the same convergence time and output gain for an S1 signal as for S9. The benefit is audible on weak signals when ANR runs pre-AGC, and there is none post-AGC (position 1), where levels are near unity.
kept.risk: Effective step on weak signals rises to the nominal NLMS value. Operators who tuned gain or leak around the current pre-AGC behaviour may hear faster adaptation. Post-AGC behaviour does not change.
kept.evidence: Benesty, Paleologu & Ciochina, 'On Regularization in Adaptive Filtering', IEEE Trans. ASLP 19(6), 2011. Haykin, Adaptive Filter Theory (NLMS with regularisation). The line-level arithmetic is above: sigma = 64*a^2 = 1e-10 at a = 1.25e-6.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description is accurate. In anr.c and anf.c, xanr and xanf compute sigma = sum over the 64 taps of d^2 and set inv_sigp = 1.0/(sigma + 1e-10). The nel/nev leak decision uses two_mu*sigma*inv_sigp, c0 = 1 - two_mu*ngamma does not depend on level, and c1 = two_mu*error*inv_sigp. In RXA.c, xanf/xanr(...,0) run before xwcpagc, and the default position in create_anf/create_anr is 0. No other mode or option in WDSP makes the regulariser relative to signal level.

Are these levels realistic? Lyra's HardwareCatalog uses rxMeterOffset values of about 1 dB, and its meter maps dBm as raw meter dB + trim - LNA gain. So on an ANAN-class radio at 0 dB attenuation, dBFS is roughly dBm. Position 0 comes after nbp0 and takes only the real channel, which carries half the complex power. sigma = 1e-10 therefore corresponds to about -115 dBm of in-passband power. A quiet 10 m or 6 m band in a 2.4 kHz filter (about -125 to -130 dBm), or a 250-500 Hz CW filter (about -135 dBm), puts sigma at 1e-11 to 1e-12. That cuts the effective normalised step by 10 to 100 times. The ANR leak lidx is clamped at a minimum of 120, so ngamma is at least about 0.013 and the adaptive leak cannot compensate. The level dependence is real. On an HL2 with +20 dB or more of LNA gain the threshold moves to about -135 dBm or lower, so it rarely matters there.

The benefit is overstated or mis-characterised in several ways:
(1) "Output loses gain": at position 0, AGC runs immediately afterwards and restores the level. Lost gain is not an audible defect pre-AGC.
(2) The weights settle at a Wiener solution with diagonal loading of about ngamma/r, where r = sigma/(sigma+1e-10). The extra relative leak on weak inputs therefore acts as heavier loading. That suppresses weak noise eigenmodes more than the dominant narrowband mode. A rough calculation suggests the current behaviour gives more aggressive noise reduction, plus slower tracking, on weak input. That is a trade-off rather than plain degradation, so making it level-invariant may make weak-signal ANR sound noisier.
(3) The cited paper is real (Benesty, Paleologu and Ciochina, IEEE TASLP 19(6), 2011), and the formula is quoted correctly. But that SNR-based delta grows as SNR falls, which slows adaptation on weak signals, the opposite of what the proposal wants. It was derived for system identification, not for a line enhancer, so it is a poor fit as the alternative.
(4) The 10x slower adaptation is real but starts from a nominal two_mu of 1e-4, which already takes hundreds of ms. The extra slowness mainly hurts tracking of QSB and of changes in pitch or notch frequency.

The primary fix, delta = kappa*L*P with a slow power tracker, is cheap and principled, and adds no latency. However, it means patching vendored WDSP, and it changes the noise-reduction character on weak signals in ways that were not shown to be better. Simply lowering the constant (for example to 1e-20) gives most of the level invariance more simply. Real, but low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The 1e-10 absolute regulariser makes pre-AGC (position 0) ANR and ANF adapt more slowly and leak relatively harder when in-passband input power is below about -115 dBFS. That level is about -115 dBm on ANAN-class radios at 0 dB attenuation, and is reached on quiet high bands or with narrow CW filters. On an HL2 with LNA gain it is rarely reached. A relative regulariser (or just a much smaller absolute floor) would make tracking speed independent of level, so weak signals would track QSB and changing tones as fast as strong ones. The output level loss is not a real problem pre-AGC, because AGC restores it. The heavier relative leak on weak input also gives somewhat stronger noise suppression, so a level-invariant version may sound noisier on weak signals. The audible net benefit is unproven and needs A/B listening. Post-AGC (position 1) is unaffected.

kept.title: SNBA: make the AR fit unconditionally stable (windowed autocorrelation, white-noise correction, bandwidth expansion, reflection guard)
kept.current: asolve forms r[i] = sum_{j=0}^{xsize-1} x[j]*x[j-i], an unwindowed lagged product reaching into the previous frame through negative indices into xbase. This is not the biased autocorrelation of one finite sequence, so the Toeplitz matrix is not guaranteed positive definite. With order 64 on only 256 samples, Levinson can produce |alpha| >= 1, beta <= 0 and an unstable inverse filter. The only guard is 'if (a[i] != a[i]) a[i] = 0.0' (line 123), which catches NaN but not +/-inf or an unstable but finite model. Digital silence (r[0]=0) takes the 0/0 path every frame. The second fit (line 524) runs on x with the detected samples zeroed (line 511), which biases the model towards white. A finite but wild model can push large values from xHat into x, and from there into xbase history and the output resampler.
kept.proposed: (1) Compute r from a Hann- or Hamming-windowed copy of the analysis span (the biased estimator gives a PSD Toeplitz). (2) Apply white-noise correction r[0] *= 1 + 1e-4 (or about 1e-5 if double). (3) Apply a Gaussian lag window or bandwidth expansion, a_i *= gamma^i with gamma about 0.995, as in G.729/AMR. (4) In Levinson, stop the recursion and keep the lower-order model if |k| >= 0.9999 or beta < 1e-9*r[0]. Also check isfinite on the result. (5) For the per-gap refit, use the covariance method on undamaged samples only, which excludes equations that touch zeroed samples (Janssen et al.). Keep asolve, trI and xHat in Float64 in LyraDSP. They run only per frame and per gap, and the Toeplitz system of the error filter is ill-conditioned for narrowband (CW, carrier) audio, whose inverse spectrum has deep notches.
kept.benefit: Mainly robustness: it removes the rare frames that produce clicks or NaN poisoning, and it is required if any of this moves to float32. There may be a small quality gain from the unbiased gap refit (fewer 'dull' interpolations on long bursts). Expect marginal change on typical static crashes.
kept.risk: The lag window slightly broadens the AR spectral peaks. That marginally lowers detection sensitivity for impulses buried in strong tonal content. gamma close to 1 keeps this negligible.
kept.evidence: Makhoul, 'Linear prediction: a tutorial review', Proc. IEEE 63(4), 1975 (autocorrelation vs covariance methods, PSD guarantee). Kabal, 'Ill-conditioning and bandwidth expansion in linear prediction of speech', ICASSP 2003. Janssen, Veldhuis & Vries, 'Adaptive interpolation of discrete-time signals that can be modeled as autoregressive processes', IEEE Trans. ASSP 34(2), 1986. Line-level: lmath.c:101-102 unwindowed lagged sum, line 111 divides by beta unguarded, line 123 NaN-only guard.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description is right. lmath.c:93-125 asolve computes r[i] += x[j]*x[j-i] for j = 0..xsize-1. snb.c calls it with x = xaux = xbase + xsize, so the negative indices read the previous frame's samples from xbase. That makes r a lagged cross-product, not the biased autocorrelation of one finite sequence, so the Toeplitz matrix is not guaranteed PSD. Levinson divides by beta with no guard, and the only check is the NaN test on a[i]. The defaults in RXA.c:241-259 are xsize 256 and asize 64 at 12 kHz. snb.c:511 zeroes the detected samples before the per-gap refit at snb.c:524. WDSP has no windowed or guarded LPC path that already does this.

I tested it with a C harness in the scratchpad: the asolve code unchanged except for counters, a least-squares gap interpolator equivalent to xHat, and band-limited input like the bpsnba/12 kHz path delivers.

The problem is not rare; it happens most of the time.
- Band-limited noise (0 to 2.9 kHz): 13,000 of 20,000 frames had some |k| >= 1 and beta <= 0. The largest |k| was 6.8e5 and the largest |a_i| was 3e5.
- Narrowband CW-like signal: 13,300 of 20,000 frames.
- Carrier plus weak noise: all 20,000 frames.
- The biased (rectangular, zero-outside) autocorrelation of the same samples gave 0 unstable frames in every case.

The overstated parts:
- NaN and Inf poisoning is not demonstrated. Digital silence gives 0/0, which becomes NaN, which the guard turns into a = 0. Detection then finds nothing, which is harmless. Inf would need beta to be exactly 0.
- "Unstable inverse filter" is the wrong framing. WDSP only ever applies the FIR error filter A(z), in invf and as the least-squares matrix in xHat, never 1/A(z), so nothing recursively blows up. In xHat, A1 has a unit diagonal, so A1^T A1 is always invertible.
- The real harm is a garbage whitening model in many frames. That weakens detection, which I did not test, and causes occasional large interpolation errors. With 2-sample gaps on band-limited noise, the worst frame's error was 10.8x the signal power with WDSP and 0.5x with the stable estimator. That is an audible click.

Interpolation SNR, current code versus the plain biased-autocorrelation method:
- Gap of 2: noise 18.1 to 22.7 dB, CW 36.3 to 47.0 dB, carrier 36.4 to 42.9 dB.
- Gap of 16: carrier 24.9 to 36.7 dB.
- Gap of 6 on broadband noise: 3.8 dB versus 4.25 dB for WDSP, about the same.

The specific recipe in the proposal, a Hann window plus white-noise correction of 1e-4 plus gamma = 0.995 lag expansion, was mixed. Its worst-case error was always much better than WDSP's. Its average SNR was sometimes worse than WDSP's: 17.2 vs 18.1 dB on noise with a gap of 2, and 20.2 vs 22.5 dB on CW with a gap of 16. Over 64 lags, gamma = 0.995 shrinks the last coefficient to 0.995^64 = 0.73, which is far stronger than in G.729's order-10 use. Gentler settings (1e-6 and 0.9995) did not fix it, which points at the Hann window itself.

So the core claims hold: the estimator is not PSD, there is no reflection or beta guard, and the refit runs on zeroed samples. The fix works, and the simplest form, a biased autocorrelation restricted to the frame plus a |k|/beta stop, performed best. Item (5), the covariance-method refit that excludes zeroed samples, I did not test. It is plausible per Janssen et al. 1986, which is a real and relevant reference, as are Makhoul 1975 and Kabal 2003.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This is a quality fix, not a fix for rare crashes or NaN values. In WDSP 2.11, asolve builds its autocorrelation from a product that reaches back into the previous frame, so the Toeplitz matrix is often not positive definite. On band-limited audio with SNB's defaults (order 64, 256 samples, 12 kHz), Levinson goes unstable (|k| >= 1, beta <= 0) in roughly 65 to 100% of frames, with coefficients up to 1e5. The result is a garbage whitening filter. It weakens detection and sometimes produces wild gap interpolations: in the worst test frame the error was 10x the signal power, which is a click. NaN and Inf do not occur in practice. Silence is already caught by the NaN guard, and only the FIR error filter is ever applied, so nothing blows up recursively. The fix that tested best is the standard biased autocorrelation: zero outside the frame, no taper needed. Add a Levinson stop when |k| >= 1 - eps or beta <= tiny*r[0], keeping the lower-order model, plus an isfinite check. In tests this raised mean interpolation SNR by about 4 to 12 dB on narrowband and carrier signals and by about 4.6 dB on 2-sample gaps in band-limited noise. On broadband noise with a 6-sample gap it was about the same, slightly worse. Worst-case error dropped 10 to 600x. Use the proposed Hann window, 1e-4 white-noise correction and gamma = 0.995 with care. At order 64 they cost average quality in some cases (up to about 2 dB below the current code), so if bandwidth expansion is used, gamma should be much closer to 1. The covariance-method gap refit was not tested. Keeping the code in Float64 is sensible.

kept.title: SNBA latency: emit each hop one frame earlier, with bit-identical output
kept.current: Output is copied from xaux[0..incr) after execFrame (line 557), so a sample waits a full xsize = 256 samples (21.3 ms at 12 kHz) in the frame, on top of the two resamplers. But execFrame never modifies xaux[0..asize). det() only writes detout[i] for i >= asize: loops at 337/345/355 start at asize, and the pre and post extensions keep j >= asize. Samples in [0,asize) are therefore never zeroed. scanFrame finds bursts only where detout == 1, so bimp >= asize, and xHat (line 528) and the restore (line 533) write only at bimp >= asize. With the defaults incr = 256/4 = 64 = asize, the final frame a sample takes part in, at positions [0,64), cannot change it.
kept.proposed: Let k = floor(asize / incr), which is 1 by default. After execFrame, copy xaux[k*incr .. (k+1)*incr) to outaccum instead of xaux[0..incr), and shorten the initial output-accumulator offset to match. Those samples are final, because the next k frames see them only inside [0, asize). Recompute k whenever asize or ovrlp changes. If k = 0 (asize < incr), fall back to current behaviour.
kept.benefit: Cuts k*incr = 64 samples, 5.33 ms at the 12 kHz internal rate, from SNBA latency with bit-identical audio. That is roughly 25% of SNBA's frame delay. It is verifiable with a sample-exact A/B test against WDSP.
kept.risk: None to output quality if the invariant (no writes below asize) is kept. A future change to det or xHat that writes below asize would silently break it, so add a debug assertion.
kept.evidence: Line-level invariant: snb.c:329/337/345/355 start at asize. Lines 390-391 guard j >= asize. Line 398 only increases j. scanFrame bimp comes from detout. Line 528 writes at &x[bimp[next]]. RXA.c:248-250 sets ovrlp 4, xsize 256, asize 64, so incr = 64.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the invariant against the source, and it holds. WDSP does not already do this.

How the frame moves: xsnba copies each new block of incr samples into xaux[xsize-incr..xsize), which is position 192 with the defaults. It runs execFrame in place, copies xaux[0..incr) to outaccum (line 557), then shifts all of xbase left by incr (line 559). So a sample sits at positions 192, 128, 64 and 0 in four consecutive frames and is output at the frame where it is at 0.

Nothing in execFrame writes x[0..asize):
- det() writes detout only for i >= asize (lines 337, 345, 355). The bridge fill starts at bsamp >= asize. The pre-extension is guarded by j >= asize (line 391). The post-extension only moves forward.
- detout is malloc0'd and zeroed in flush, so detout[0..asize) stays 0, and the zeroing loop at line 508 cannot touch those samples.
- scanFrame's bimp values come from detout, so bimp >= asize. xHat output (line 528) and the savex restore (line 533) are written at &x[bimp].
- asolve (lmath.c:93) only reads x. It does read below index 0, into the history half of xbase, which is unchanged by the proposal. invf only reads x.

With the RXA.c defaults (xsize 256, ovrlp 4, asize 64, so incr 64), a sample's last chance to change is the frame where it sits at position 64. Copying xaux[64..128) after execFrame therefore emits the same values 64 samples sooner. The output is the old stream advanced by exactly 64 samples. In the usual case isize >= incr (oaoutidx = 0), so the 64 samples are a real cut in end-to-end latency, not a buffering artefact.

Corrections to the proposal:
1. The frame delay today is 3*incr = 192 samples, not xsize = 256. The change takes it from 192 to 128 samples, about 33% of the frame delay.
2. Do not change the output-accumulator offset. init_oaoutidx is only block re-buffering for the isize < incr case. Changing the source slice alone gives the whole saving; shortening the offset as well would cause underflow or misalignment.
3. Changing k at runtime shifts the output by k*incr samples once, a small glitch. SetRXASNBAovrlp already re-inits through decalc/calc, so it is not a real concern there.

Related existing problem, separate from this proposal: SetRXASNBAasize changes asize without reallocating or flushing. The asolve_r/z and xHat work buffers are sized from asize at create, so a larger runtime asize already overruns them, and stale detout entries in [old, new) could persist. The proposal does not depend on this and does not make it worse.

Practical value: 5.33 ms off an optional noise blanker that already adds two resamplers plus the RXA block latency. The change is real, bit-exact, nearly free and easy to verify with an A/B test, but the benefit is small for HF/VHF speech, CW or digital modes. Hence low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Copying xaux[k*incr..(k+1)*incr), with k = floor(asize/incr), instead of xaux[0..incr) cuts SNBA's frame delay from 3*incr = 192 to 128 samples with the defaults. That saves 64 samples, 5.33 ms at 12 kHz, and the audio is bit-identical, just shifted earlier. The output-accumulator offset (init_oaoutidx) must stay as it is; only the source slice changes. It is worth an assertion that det, xHat and the restore never write below asize. The benefit is real but small compared with the full RX chain latency.

refuted.title: ANR/ANF: no validation of delay and taps, so a degenerate predictor can see the current sample
refuted.why:
The code reading is right. In anr.c:99/126, idx = (in_idx + j + delay) & mask, with mask = dline_size - 1 = 2047 (anr.c:57, ANR_DLINE_SIZE 2048 at anr.h:30). d[] and w[] are fixed at 2048 entries (anr.h:45-46). SetRXAANRVals, SetRXAANRTaps and SetRXAANRDelay (anr.c:183-211) store the values with no bounds check, and anf.c does the same (lines 185-209). in_idx counts down (line 129), so offsets j+delay > 0 point at older samples. With delay == 0, tap 0 reads the sample being predicted, NLMS drives w[0] toward 1, ANR (output y) becomes a pass-through, and ANF (output error) goes near-silent. The analysis is also right that n_taps > 2048 writes past w[], and that n_taps + delay - 1 >= 2048 wraps back onto d[in_idx].

The claimed benefit does not hold up, though. The proposal says these settings are "easy to hit from a UI slider or a saved profile", and in this product they cannot be reached. Lyra calls only SetRXAANFVals(ch, 64, 16, 1e-3, 1e-7) and SetRXAANRVals(ch, taps, 16, gain, 1e-7) (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:4282, 4301). Delay is always 16, and taps are computed as 32 + round(96*s) with s clamped to [0,1], so 32 to 128. Lyra never calls SetRXAANRTaps, SetRXAANRDelay or the ANF equivalents. WDSP's own create defaults (RXA.c, 64 taps, delay 16) are also safe. No realistic parameter path in Lyra gives delay 0, taps over 2048, or taps + delay over 2048.

What remains is defensive API hardening for configurations nobody sends. It would cost little but would not fix any observed or reachable failure. The second part, taps and delay in milliseconds scaled by sample rate, is a separate feature and is not justified by this bug. ANR/ANF run at the fixed RXA DSP rate, and the current hardcoded values are sensible there.

refuted.title: Float32 hazards in the leaky NLMS: leak quantisation to exactly 1.0 and weight-update stalling
refuted.why:
The description of the code is correct. anr.c and anf.c (xanr/xanf, lines 83-130) keep d[], w[], sigma, c0, c1, lidx and ngamma in double. The leak is multiplicative: c0 = 1 - two_mu*ngamma and w = c0*w + c1*d. ngamma = gamma*lidx^4*den_mult. The RXA.c defaults (lines 281-317) match the proposal. Both blocks use two_mu 1e-4, gamma 0.1 and den_mult 6.25e-10. ANR has lidx in [120,200] and ANF has lidx in [0,200]. I checked the arithmetic and it holds. For ANR, two_mu*ngamma runs from 1.30e-6 to 1.0e-5, which gives about 22-168 float32 steps below 1.0. For ANF, two_mu*ngamma = 6.25e-15*lidx^4, which is below 2^-25 when lidx is under about 46.7. Caraiscos & Liu (IEEE Trans. ASSP 32(1), 1984) is a real paper on LMS roundoff and stalling, and it is relevant.

It still fails as an improvement to WDSP 2.11, for three reasons.
(1) WDSP already does what it proposes. Everything is double, and the proposal is to keep it double. It does not change WDSP's algorithm. It is a warning about a hypothetical float32 port. I searched the Lyra checkout for any ANR/ANF port (two_mu, ngamma, lidx) and found none, so there is no float32 code that it applies to.
(2) The 'ANF never forgets' hazard does not matter in practice. Even in double, two_mu*ngamma < 3e-8 means a leak time constant above about 3.4e7 samples, which is roughly 12 minutes at 48 kHz. That is effectively no leak already, so rounding it to exactly 1.0 makes no audible difference. lidx is also a control variable that moves by +1 or -3 every sample. It passes through that region rather than sitting in it.
(3) The stalling claim is overstated. With 64 taps, the normalised step two_mu*e*d/sigma is about 1e-4/64 of the input scale, about 1.5e-6 relative. That is still about 10 float32 ulps (eps 1.19e-7), not below one. The ANR leak term of 1.3e-6 to 1e-5 relative is also tens to hundreds of ulps. Precision would degrade a little but would not freeze.
Even for a port, the expected effect is small and unproven by any measurement. As a change to WDSP itself there is nothing to change.

refuted.title: ANR/ANF: run the line enhancer at a decimated rate, or scale taps and delay with sample rate
refuted.why:
The description of the code is mostly correct. ANR and ANF run per sample at ch[].dsp_rate. RXA.c:282-319 creates them with 64 taps, delay 16, two_mu 1e-4, and setSamplerate_anr/anf (anr.c:149-152, anf.c:149-152) only flush and never rescale. SNBA does resample to 12 kHz internally (RXA.c:246, snb.c calc_snba).

"Fixed 64 taps" overstates it, though. Those are only the create-time defaults. Taps, delay, gain and leakage can all be changed at runtime through SetRXAANRVals/Taps/Delay/Gain/Leakage and the matching SetRXAANF* calls (anr.c:184-230, anf.c:185-230), which is how Thetis's setup page drives them. The delay line is ANR_DLINE_SIZE = ANF_DLINE_SIZE = 2048, so taps plus delay can reach about 2000 samples, roughly 40 ms at 48 kHz.

The main benefit claimed is a longer predictor span, giving finer frequency resolution and a narrower ALE line or ANF notch. That is already available at the native rate by setting taps to 256-512 and delay to about 64. This adds no resampler group delay and no extra band-limiting. The cost is about 2 x 512 x 48000, roughly 50 M MAC/s, which is trivial on Apple Silicon. So the Accelerate polyphase resample, extra latency and AM band-limit tradeoff buy nothing the existing parameters can't already give.

The convergence argument doesn't hold for this setup. Oversampled, band-limited input does give a large eigenvalue spread, but the small eigenvalues belong to stopband directions that carry essentially no input energy. Their weights don't affect the output, and the leakage term (gamma/ngamma) pulls them toward zero. In-band modes converge on in-band eigenvalues, and NLMS normalises by the total power (sigma), so decimating does not meaningfully speed up convergence of the components that matter.

The suggestion of 10-20 ms spans at 12 kHz for CW also skips the tracking-versus-resolution tradeoff. A long, slow predictor smears keying transients and fading, and a dit at 30 WPM is only 40 ms, so "separate CW tones properly" is not established.

The citations are real. Widrow et al., Proc. IEEE 1975 covers the ALE, and Widrow & Stearns 1985 covers eigenvalue spread. They are just not evidence that decimation beats a longer predictor at full rate.

What survives is a minor point. Defining taps and delay in milliseconds and converting them in setSamplerate_anr/anf would make the behaviour independent of sample rate. That matters only if the host changes dsp_rate, and a host that pins dsp_rate at 48 kHz can do the same conversion itself when it calls SetRXAANRVals. Since decimation is the core of the proposal and it is not better than what the existing parameters already allow, I treat the proposal as refuted.

refuted.title: ANR/ANF: add variable step size (VSS-NLMS) for fast capture with low steady-state misadjustment
refuted.why:
The description of the current code is correct. In anr.c and anf.c, lines 109-122 of xanr/xanf are identical. They implement NLMS, w = c0*w + two_mu*e*x/(||x||^2+1e-10). The Kamenetsky-Widrow nel/nev comparison adapts only the leak, through lidx and ngamma. two_mu is fixed, and RXA.c:291 and RXA.c:311 set it to 1e-4 by default. No variable-step mode exists anywhere in the source. With NLMS, a mode's time constant is about 1/(two_mu * the fraction of input power in it). That gives about 1e4 samples (about 0.2 s at 48 kHz) for a dominant carrier, and seconds for a weak one. The five citations are real and correctly attributed.

The claimed benefit does not hold up, for these reasons:

1. **The Aboulnasr-Mayyas robustness does not apply here.** The rule is robust only when the measurement noise is close to white, so that E[e(n)e(n-1)] is about 0. ANF/ANR run after the receive passband filter (nbp0), on real audio at the DSP rate. That audio is roughly a 2.7 kHz band sampled at 48 kHz, about 8x oversampled. Its normalised lag-1 autocorrelation is around 0.95. Speech is also strongly correlated from sample to sample. So e(n)e(n-1) is close to e(n)^2, and the method collapses into a Kwong-Johnston power-driven step. That step rises at every speech onset and noise burst. In ANF that notches voiced harmonics; in ANR it gives watery artefacts. Those are the two failure modes the proposal says it avoids.

2. **NPVSS needs a noise-power estimate that is hard to get here.** For ANF, the "noise" is the wanted speech plus band noise, which is non-stationary. This is the double-talk problem from echo cancellation. Getting it right needs a detector or extra tracking machinery, not one or two tuning constants.

3. **A VSS statistic cannot speed up capture of weak tones.** A tone 10 dB below speech and noise leaves a residual in e(n) that is buried in the non-predictable part. Any statistic of e(n) that could reliably detect it is essentially the predictor itself. So the claim of capturing weak heterodynes faster while keeping the same steady state is not supported.

4. **The step size is already a user setting, and the tradeoff is the normal one.** two_mu is exposed through SetRXAANFVals and SetRXAANFGain, which clients use. This project's own engine (the Lyra worktree, src/wdsp_engine.cpp:3437) calls SetRXAANFVals with gain 1e-3. That captures a dominant carrier in about 1e3 samples, roughly 20 ms at 48 kHz, which is already the "tens of ms" the proposal promises. Glover's result (notch bandwidth proportional to mu) is the tradeoff users already choose by setting the gain.

5. **The benefit is unmeasured.** The proposal itself says it needs listening tests, and no simulation or measurement backs the claimed depth and speed.

A possible but unproven variant: a time-based step schedule (high mu for a short time after flush or retune, then decaying to two_mu), or a statistic taken at a long lag beyond the speech correlation time. Neither is what was proposed, and both are of marginal value given that the gain is already adjustable.

I am refuting because the specific methods proposed are ill-suited to oversampled, band-limited audio that contains speech, and the claimed gain cannot be confirmed.

summary: Both blankers run on the raw wideband IQ, before any channel filtering. They flag a sample as an impulse when |x| > threshold * avg, where avg is a one-pole IIR mean of |x| (time constant backtau). avg is updated with the current sample before the test, and that includes the impulse itself (nob.c:118-122, nobII.c:179-184). avg is initialised to 1.0 (nob.c:45, nobII.c:148). ANB (xanb, nob.c:108-187) runs a 5-state gate over a delay line of trans_count+adv_count samples. It multiplies the live delayed signal by a raised-cosine ramp down, zeroes for the advance and hang periods, then ramps the live signal back up. NOB-II (xnob, nobII.c:158-494) keeps a much longer look-ahead delay line: out->scan is adv_slew+adv+1 samples and scan->in is max_imp_seq+hang+hang_slew+filterlen samples, with max_imp_seq hard-coded to 25 ms in create_nobEXT (nobII.c:623). At each detection it scans forward to measure the whole impulse sequence and merges bursts that fall within hang+adv of each other. It then fills the gap with zero (mode 0, Lyra's mode), a held 10-tap exponentially weighted average of the samples before (mode 1) or after (mode 3) the gap, their mean (mode 2), or a straight line between them (mode 4). Sequences longer than max_imp_seq fall back to a zero-and-stay-down path (states 5-9). NOB-II's raised-cosine slews (states 1, 4, 5, 9) cross-fade between frozen sample values (Ilast, Inext) and the fill value; they do not window the live signal. slew.c (xuslew) applies a one-shot 0.5(1-cos) ramp to the TX signal on its first non-zero sample after an optional delay.

kept.title: Detect impulses on a linear-prediction residual instead of raw |x|, so strong signals neither hide impulses nor trigger the blanker
kept.current: Detection is mag = |x[n]| tested against avg*threshold, with avg = backmult*avg + (1-backmult)*mag over the whole wideband IQ (nobII.c:179-184, nob.c:118-123). The background estimate is therefore set by the strongest signal anywhere in the IQ span. Simulated at 48 kHz with backtau 20 ms and Gaussian noise: the false-alarm rate matches the Rayleigh prediction P_fa = exp(-pi*T^2/4) (7.2e-3 measured vs 7.4e-3 predicted at T=2.5). A CW carrier keyed with a 5 ms raised-cosine edge flags 123 samples on each key-down at T=12 when the carrier is 40 dB above the noise, and 46 samples at T=6 when it is 20 dB above. Each of those becomes a blank of several ms that gates every other signal in the passband. In the other direction, while a constant-envelope carrier dominates, an impulse must exceed T times the carrier's amplitude, not T times the noise, so the blanker goes deaf.
kept.proposed: Run a short complex adaptive linear predictor over the IQ: NLMS order 8-16, updated sample by sample, with the update frozen while a sample is flagged. Alternatively, run block Burg LPC every few ms. Detect on the prediction error e[n] = x[n] - sum a_k x[n-k], using |e[n]| > T * sigma_e, with sigma_e a robust running scale (see the background-estimator proposal). Carriers, CW key-down edges and steady SSB/AM are predictable and drop out of e[n]. Impulses, which are broadband, are not predictable and stand out. This is the detector WDSP already uses in SNBA at audio rate (snb.c: asolve/invf/det, lines 306-400, which threshold the inverse-filter residual against median power). The proposal moves that idea to the complex IQ-rate pre-filter blanker, where a strong out-of-passband signal currently controls the detection. Keep the existing magnitude detector as a fallback or option.
kept.benefit: Large wherever a strong signal sits inside the IQ span, which is the normal case on contest bands and near broadcasters. Key-down edges and other envelope changes on strong carriers stop triggering blanks, so the blanker stops causing gating clicks and splatter. Weak impulses are still detected under a strong carrier, because sensitivity becomes relative to the unpredictable floor and not to the carrier's level. On a quiet band with only noise the residual is roughly the input, so behaviour is unchanged.
kept.risk: The predictor adds a small group delay and must not adapt onto the impulses, so its update has to be frozen on flagged samples. Clusters of very wideband signals (e.g. strong FT8 or OFDM data) are less predictable, so the gain shrinks there. CPU at 384 kS/s with order 16 NLMS is about 12M complex MACs per second, trivial on Apple Silicon. Thresholds are not interchangeable with today's values, so the UI mapping needs recalibrating.
kept.evidence: Vaseghi & Rayner, 'Detection and suppression of impulsive noise in speech communication systems', IEE Proc. I, 1990. Godsill & Rayner, 'Digital Audio Restoration', Springer 1998, ch. 5 (AR-residual click detection). Oudre, 'Automatic detection and removal of impulsive noise in audio signals', IPOL 2015. WDSP's own snb.c det()/invf(). The key-down and P_fa numbers come from a pure-Python simulation of the exact avg/threshold recursion in nobII.c:179-184.

verdict.reasoning:
The code matches the description. nobII.c:177-184 and nob.c:118-123 compute mag = |x| on the raw wideband IQ, update avg = backmult*avg + ombackmult*mag (backmult = exp(-1/(fs*backtau)), set at nob.c:47 and nobII.c:45), and flag when mag > avg*threshold. Neither file has another detector; the modes in nobII only choose how the gap is filled. SNBA's AR-residual detector (snb.c) runs at audio rate after demodulation, so WDSP does not already do this at IQ rate.

I re-simulated the exact recursion at 48 kHz with backtau 20 ms:
- Gaussian noise at T=2.5 gave P_fa 7.8e-3, against 7.4e-3 predicted.
- A carrier 40 dB up with a 5 ms raised-cosine key-down flagged 127 samples at T=12. At 20 dB and T=6 it flagged 41. The proposal's 123 and 46 are within noise of these.
- With a steady carrier 40 dB up, 15 impulses at 30 sigma were all missed (0/15) at T=4.

So the false triggers on strong signals and the deafness under a strong carrier are both real.

Next I tried the proposed fix: order-8 complex NLMS, mu=0.05, with detection on |e| > 6*sigma_e. The shaped key-down produced 0 flags, with or without freezing, and all 15 impulses under the 40 dB carrier were detected. The core idea holds.

However, the rule as written ("freeze the update while a sample is flagged") has a lock-in failure. A hard step, such as a carrier switching on abruptly, a retune, or start-up while a strong signal is already present, makes the residual exceed the threshold. Adaptation then freezes, so the predictor never learns the new signal and every later sample stays flagged. In my runs that was 10000/10000 samples after a hard key and 19985/20000 at start-up. A cap on freeze length fixes it (for example, keep adapting once a flagged run exceeds 20 samples, or reuse max_imp_seq). With the cap, the hard key-down left a 58-sample transient and the impulse test had about 56 false flags, mostly that start-up transient and impulse tails.

Further caveats:
- The inverse filter smears each impulse over p extra samples, so blanks get longer.
- An order of 8-16 can only null about that many strong carriers. On a crowded contest band or the broadcast-heavy parts of 40 m at night, many strong signals stay in the residual, so "large benefit in the normal case" is overstated. Block Burg at a higher order would help.
- Thresholds need recalibrating, as the proposal says.
- CPU and latency are fine: the predictor is causal and the existing delay line stays.

The cited literature is real and relevant: Vaseghi & Rayner, IEE Proc. I, vol. 137, 1990; Godsill & Rayner, Digital Audio Restoration, Springer 1998, chapter on clicks; Oudre, IPOL 2015. Those works mostly treat audio-rate AR models. Applying the method to oversampled IQ is a reasonable extension: at 192-384 kS/s, narrowband signals are very predictable. My checks were simulations only, not measurements on real band recordings.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
Detecting on a linear-prediction residual of the IQ, instead of on raw |x|, stops smoothly-keyed CW, the envelope swings of SSB/AM and steady carriers from triggering the blanker. It also restores sensitivity to impulses buried under a strong carrier. In simulation it caught 15/15 impulses 40 dB below a carrier that the current detector missed entirely, and it produced 0 flags on a 40 dB keyed-carrier edge, where the current detector flagged about 127 samples. Three conditions apply:
- The update freeze must be capped, or the predictor locks up permanently after any abrupt signal step or a start-up with a strong signal present.
- The gain is limited to the few strongest signals that an order-8-16 predictor can null, so it is smaller on very crowded bands.
- Thresholds need recalibrating, and blanks get slightly longer because the inverse filter smears each impulse.

kept.title: NOB-II slews cross-fade frozen samples instead of windowing the live signal, so the taper does nothing for signals away from IQ DC
kept.current: State 1 outputs Ilast*scale + (1-scale)*I. Ilast is the last state-0 output, latched at lines 199-200, and is constant from then on; I is the constant or linear fill value. State 4 outputs Inext*scale + (1-scale)*I, where Inext is one sample latched at detection (lines 245-246). States 5 and 9 output Ilast*scale and Inext*scale. During every slew, then, the live signal has already gone: a component at frequency f != 0 in the IQ stops rotating at the first slew sample and is replaced by a constant. For every off-DC signal the effective gate has rectangular edges, and the slew only shapes a DC blob at the hardware centre frequency. ANB (nob.c:138-140, 166-168) does it correctly: it multiplies the live delayed sample dline[out_idx] by the ramp.
kept.proposed: Write each slew as a proper cross-fade between the delayed live signal and the fill: out = w[n]*dline[out_idx] + (1-w[n])*fill[n], with w following the awave/hwave tables. In mode 0 (Lyra's mode) this reduces exactly to ANB-style raised-cosine gating. In the hold and interpolate modes it gives a smooth hand-over from the real signal into the fill and back. Ilast and Inext are then no longer needed for slewing. The samples under the slews are the advance and hang regions, which by construction contain no flagged samples, so windowing the live signal there is safe.
kept.benefit: Moderate. For every signal not at IQ DC, the blanker's gating spectrum changes from rectangular edges (first sidelobe -13 dB, 6 dB/octave roll-off) to raised-cosine edges (-31 dB, 18 dB/octave beyond about 1/t_slew). Strong signals elsewhere in the span then throw less splatter into the receive passband each time the blanker fires. It also removes a spurious DC click of size |Ilast| at the hardware centre frequency, which is audible when tuned near centre. With Lyra's 0.1 ms slews the improvement is concentrated at offsets above roughly 10 kHz from the strong signal; close in it is small.
kept.risk: Very low. The output is identical at the gap edges, and in mode 0 it matches long-standing ANB behaviour. Users who tuned slew times by ear may hear slightly more of the signal during the slews, which is the intent.
kept.evidence: Line-level reading of nobII.c:199-200, 245-246, 337-339, 385-387, 395-396 and 475-476 against nob.c:138-140 and 166-168. Window sidelobe figures from Harris, 'On the use of windows for harmonic analysis with the DFT', Proc. IEEE 1978.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is correct. In nobII.c, state 0 copies dline[out_idx] into Ilast/Qlast on every sample (lines 199-200), so they hold the last pass-through sample and never change after the state machine leaves state 0. State 1 outputs Ilast*scale + (1-scale)*I (lines 337-338). State 4 uses Inext, a single sample read at detection (lines 245-246). States 5 and 9 output Ilast*scale and Inext*scale (lines 395-396, 475-476; Inext is re-read in states 7 and 8). No slew state reads dline[out_idx], so the live signal stops at the first slew sample. ANB in nob.c (lines 138-140 and 166-168) multiplies the live delayed sample by the ramp. NOB-II has no mode or option that does this, and WDSP only "already does it" in the sense that ANB is a separate blanker without NOB-II's impulse merging, max-sequence/overflow handling or fill modes.

Lyra creates the blanker with create_nobEXT(ch, run 0, mode 0, ..., 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.020, 20.0) in src/wdsp_engine.cpp:1377. I did not open create_nobEXT to map each of those values to its parameter, so "mode 0" and "0.1 ms slews" are a reading of the call, not a checked fact.

One caveat on the claim that the edges are "rectangular". The output waveform is continuous, because the frozen ramp starts at Ilast, the last live sample. Split the output into two parts: the live tone cut off with a hard edge, and a smooth ramp at DC. The two step terms cancel only at frequencies far from both the tone and DC. When the receive passband is close to a strong signal that is itself well away from IQ DC (the usual case in a 96-192 kHz span), the tone part dominates and behaves like a rectangular edge, as claimed. The ramp term is a real slewed DC click at the hardware centre whenever |Ilast| is large.

The proposed cross-fade is sound. Both slew regions are free of flagged samples by construction. The advance slew lies before scan_idx, and earlier impulses are merged by the look-ahead loop. The hang slew sits inside the hcount = hang_count + hang_slew_count guard. In mode 0 the change reduces to ANB-style raised-cosine gating. In the hold and interpolate modes the fill is constant (or linear), so the real signal is cut off either way, and a smooth fade of the real signal is strictly better.

The Harris 1978 reference is real. Its -13/-31 dB first-sidelobe figures describe whole windows, not the edges of a gate, so they fit only loosely here. The asymptotic roll-off (6 dB/oct for a hard edge, 18 dB/oct for a raised-cosine edge with continuous slope) is the part that applies.

Rough size of the effect: blanker firing at 100 Hz, gap about 0.3 ms, receiver 20 kHz from a strong carrier, 2.4 kHz passband. The splatter is about -42 dBc now and might fall another ~20 dB with 0.1 ms raised-cosine edges. For an S9+40 signal that is audible, so the gain is real for impulse noise next to strong stations. Within about 10 kHz of the strong signal the gap length dominates and the gain is small.

The change adds no latency. The risk is low, but only if each slew is indexed so that w goes exactly from 1 to 0 and back, matching the existing awave/hwave conventions. The awave table uses (i+1)*PI/(n+1) and hwave uses i*PI/n, and these are asymmetric.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This only gains anything when the receiver is well away from IQ DC and more than roughly 1/t_slew (about 10 kHz with 0.1 ms slews) from the strong signal. There, replacing the frozen-sample slews with a raised-cosine cross-fade of the live delayed signal changes how the strong signal's splatter falls off as the blanker fires. It currently falls off about as fast as a hard edge (6 dB/oct) and would fall off at about 18 dB/oct. For a strong neighbour 20 kHz away with the blanker firing at 100 Hz, splatter in the passband could drop by roughly 20 dB. The change also removes the slewed DC click of size |Ilast|, which is audible when tuned near the hardware centre. Within about 1/t_slew of the strong signal the gap length dominates and there is little gain. Latency does not change. In mode 0 the result equals ANB gating, and in the fill modes it gives a smooth hand-over into and out of the fill. The Harris figures are only loosely relevant, because they describe whole windows rather than gate edges.

kept.title: Add complex AR (LSAR) gap interpolation; the hold and linear modes only work for content near IQ DC
kept.current: Modes 1-4 fill the gap with a constant or a straight line built from 10-tap exponentially weighted averages before (I1/Q1) and after (I2/Q2) the gap (fcoefs sum to 1.0, lines 108-117). In complex IQ, a signal at offset f is a rotating phasor, so a constant or straight line deletes it. The 10-tap average also attenuates it before holding: |H| is -3.0 dB at 3 kHz/48 kS/s, -6.2 dB at 20 kHz/192 kS/s and -11.7 dB at 48 kHz/192 kS/s (computed from fcoefs). For anything but a signal at the hardware centre, the 'interpolating' modes behave much like zeroing plus a DC step. WDSP already has least-squares AR interpolation, but only in SNBA (snb.c: xHat lines 265-305, execFrame 492-537), which runs on real audio after the RX filter.
kept.proposed: Add mode 5: complex-valued AR interpolation over the gap. Fit an order p=16-32 complex AR model by Burg's method on about 256-1024 clean samples around the gap; NOB-II already buffers samples after the gap in its look-ahead. Then either (a) solve the least-squares AR interpolation for the missing samples (Janssen et al. 1986, the same maths as SNBA's xHat, made complex), or (b) the cheaper option: extrapolate forward from the left and backward from the right with the AR filter and cross-fade the two with a raised-cosine weight (Etter 1996). Fall back to zero when the gap exceeds a limit (e.g. 2-4 ms) or the context is itself mostly flagged. Option (b) costs O(p*gap) per event.
kept.benefit: Large for short gaps (tens to a few hundred samples) containing strong narrowband signals. A sum of K sinusoids is exactly predictable by an order-2K AR model, so a strong carrier crosses the blank with an interpolation error typically 20-40 dB below its level. It is then no longer gated, which removes the main source of blanker-induced splatter. Noise-like content gets a statistically plausible continuation instead of a hole, which reduces the 'NB pumping' of the noise floor. Gains shrink for gaps above about 1 ms on fast-changing modulation, and for dense impulse trains where the context is corrupted.
kept.risk: CPU per event is bursty: a Burg fit of order 32 over 512 samples is about 65k complex MACs, roughly 6.5M per second at 100 events/s, still trivial. Poorly conditioned fits on very strong signals need care (see the numerical proposal). Interpolation needs samples after the gap, so latency equals the maximum gap you choose to interpolate (which pairs with the latency proposal).
kept.evidence: Janssen, Veldhuis & Vries, 'Adaptive interpolation of discrete-time signals that can be modeled as autoregressive processes', IEEE TASSP 34(2), 1986. Etter, 'Restoration of a discrete-time signal segment by interpolation based on the left-sided and right-sided autoregressive parameters', IEEE TSP 44(5), 1996. Godsill & Rayner 1998, ch. 5. Burg 1975 (PhD thesis, Stanford). WDSP snb.c xHat/asolve for the real-valued precedent.

verdict.reasoning:
Code check (nobII.c): fcoefs (lines 108-117) are a 10-tap exponentially weighted average that sums to 1.0. I1/Q1 comes from bfbuff (the samples before the gap) and I2/Q2 from the first 10 unflagged samples after the gap in the dline look-ahead. Modes 0-4 (lines 286-318) are zero, sample-hold, mean-hold, hold-sample and linear. The output states 2 and 3 emit I += deltaI, so every fill is a constant or a straight line in IQ. I recomputed |H| of fcoefs: -2.97 dB at 3k/48k, -6.24 dB at 20k/192k and -11.70 dB at 48k/192k, which matches the claim. nob.c (ANB) only slews to zero. No other file does AR interpolation on IQ. Burg and LS interpolation appear only in snb.c, on real audio after the RX filter. So this is not already in WDSP. For a phasor away from IQ DC, a held or linear fill is a DC term with arbitrary phase. Its error energy is about the same as zeroing, or worse, so the description 'zeroing plus a DC step' is fair.

Algorithmic merit: the main practical harm of an IQ blanker is that it gates strong signals elsewhere in the 48k-1.5M span, and the gating splatter lands in the listening passband. That is the familiar 'NB makes IMD on a crowded band' complaint. LSAR interpolation, or Etter's two-sided AR extrapolation, directly reduces that error energy for strong narrowband or highly oversampled signals over gaps of tens to a few hundred samples. NOB-II already has the right structure: blank_count is known before output starts, it already reads post-gap samples from the look-ahead, and overflow already falls back to zero. The citations are real and correctly attributed: Janssen/Veldhuis/Vries IEEE TASSP 34(2) 1986, Etter IEEE TSP 44(5) 1996, Godsill and Rayner 1998, and Burg's 1975 thesis.

Overstatements and corrections:
(1) 'Noise-like content gets a statistically plausible continuation': wrong. The LSAR estimate is the conditional mean, and the AR extrapolations decay toward zero. Over a gap of broadband noise the fill tends to zero, so the hole remains. Filling it would require adding synthetic excitation, which the proposal does not include. The claim about reducing NB 'pumping' of the noise floor is therefore not supported.
(2) A sum of K complex exponentials needs complex AR order K, not 2K.
(3) A wideband span holds many signals. Order 16-32 models only the strongest spectral peaks. That is enough to suppress splatter from the strong signals, but a weak in-passband signal sitting 60-80 dB down will not be reconstructed well. It is still no worse off than with zeroing.
(4) Latency is the maximum interpolated gap plus the right-hand context (for example, 256 samples is about 1.3 ms at 192k), not the gap alone.
(5) Context contaminated by sub-threshold impulse tails or by dense impulse trains will degrade the fits, so the fallback is essential.
(6) The '20-40 dB' error figure depends on SNR and gap length and has not been demonstrated on RF.

CPU cost is trivial, as stated. Overall this is a real, literature-backed improvement for crowded bands with strong signals. It is not transformative for every user, and its noise-floor claim is wrong.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
Add a complex AR interpolation mode to NOB-II, either Etter-style two-sided extrapolation with a cross-fade or full LSAR. It would cut the gating splatter that strong carriers and SSB/CW signals anywhere in the IQ span currently produce when they are blanked. Modes 1-4 do not prevent this for any signal away from IQ DC, because they are attenuated (up to about -12 dB) and then held or ramped, so in effect they zero the signal. Expect a meaningful reduction of NB-induced IMD on crowded bands for gaps of tens to a few hundred samples. It will be smaller on dense impulse trains, where the context is contaminated, and on long gaps.

It gives no real benefit for noise-like content: the conditional-mean fill decays to zero, so the noise-floor hole stays. It also only weakly reconstructs a weak in-passband signal that sits under much stronger signals, though it is never worse than zeroing.

The cost is an extra 1-3 ms of look-ahead latency for the right-hand context and a modest amount of code. CPU use is negligible.

kept.title: NOB-II always adds about 25.6 ms of receive latency because of a fixed 25 ms look-ahead; zero mode needs almost none of it
kept.current: flush_nob places in_idx at scan_idx + max_imp_seq + hang_count + hang_slew_count + filterlen, and scan_idx at out_idx + adv_slew + adv + 1. create_nobEXT hard-codes max_imp_seq_time = 0.025 (line 623). With Lyra's parameters (0.1 ms slew, hang and advance) at 48 kS/s the delay is 4+4+1+1200+4+4+10 = 1227 samples = 25.6 ms; at 192 kS/s it is 4887 samples, still 25.5 ms. The look-ahead exists so the forward scan (lines 212-241) can see a whole impulse sequence and the post-gap anchor I2 (lines 261-285) before choosing between fill and overflow. In mode 0 (zero, which Lyra uses) neither I2 nor the full sequence length is needed. ANB gets by with only trans_count+adv_count of delay (nob.c:41).
kept.proposed: Make the look-ahead depend on the mode. In mode 0, run causally after the advance: start the gate at detection plus adv, and extend the zero/hang online while impulses keep arriving, as ANB's state 3 does with htime = -count (nob.c:153-164). That cuts the delay to about adv_slew+adv+1 samples (about 0.2 ms). In fill or interpolate modes, set the look-ahead to the longest gap you are willing to interpolate (1-4 ms is plenty: hold/linear fills longer than that are poor, and AR quality drops too). Longer sequences go straight to the existing zero path. Expose max_imp_seq_time; do not hard-code it.
kept.benefit: About 23-25 ms less receive latency whenever NB2 is on. That is audible in CW full break-in (QSK), in the sidetone-to-receive relationship and in general tuning 'feel'. It also shrinks the discontinuity when the blanker is toggled (see the run-toggle bug). No change in blanking quality for mode 0.
kept.risk: Changes the timing of the blanker's behaviour for long impulse sequences. Today a 3-25 ms sequence in fill mode is held or interpolated across; with a shorter look-ahead it would be zeroed, which is arguably no worse given how poor a 10 ms hold is. Fixed delay compensation elsewhere in Lyra, if any, has to follow the new delay.
kept.evidence: Delay computed from nobII.c:144-145 with counts from init_nob lines 40-44 and create_nobEXT line 623 using Lyra's create_nobEXT arguments (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:1377-1379: slew/hang/adv 0.0001 s, backtau 0.020). For comparison, ANB uses delay = trans_count + adv_count (nob.c:41).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description of current behaviour is correct. flush_nob (nobII.c:143-145) sets scan_idx = out_idx + adv_slew_count + adv_count + 1 and in_idx = scan_idx + max_imp_seq + hang_count + hang_slew_count + filterlen. Samples are written at in_idx and read at out_idx, so the delay is in_idx - out_idx. create_nobEXT hard-codes max_imp_seq_time = 0.025 (line 623). Nothing in nobII.c lets you change it: there is no SetEXTNOB*/pSetRCVRNOB* setter for max_imp_seq_time. Lyra calls create_nobEXT(ch, 0, 0 /*mode zero*/, inSize, inRate, 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.020, 20.0) at src/wdsp_engine.cpp:1377, in both RX1 and RX2. With those values the counts at 48 kS/s are 4/4/4/4, max_imp_seq 1200, filterlen 10, giving 1227 samples (25.6 ms). That matches the proposal. Lyra calls xnobEXT only when NB is enabled (wdsp_engine.cpp:6270). So the delay applies only with NB2 on, and then it also delays the panadapter, capture and zero-beat feed. ANB's delay is trans_count + adv_count (nob.c:41), and its state 3 extends the gate online with htime = -count, as the proposal says.

The mode-0 argument holds. In mode 0 the forward scan only determines blank_count and Inext. I1 and I2 are computed only for modes 1-4. NOB-II already contains a causal zero-with-online-extension path: overflow states 5-9 use staydown in state 7 to look back at recent imp flags. So the change mostly means taking the overflow path in mode 0 straight away instead of writing new logic. In mode 0 the current non-overflow hang slew (state 4) ramps toward a fixed sample, Inext. The overflow path (state 9) does the same with a sample read from the look-ahead window. Windowing the live signal instead, as ANB's state 4 does, is no worse and arguably better, so 'no loss of blanking quality' is plausible.

Corrections and caveats:
(1) The minimum delay is not about adv_slew+adv+1 (about 0.2 ms). State 7 reads imp at scan_idx + hang_slew + hang, and states 8/9 read Inext at offsets based on scan_idx, so the delay must stay at least about adv_slew+adv+1+hang+hang_slew. Keeping the filterlen margin adds 10 more. That is about 18-27 samples (0.4-0.6 ms) at 48k: still a cut of about 25 ms.
(2) A look-ahead that depends on mode means SetEXTNOBMode has to re-flush the delay line, which causes a glitch when the mode changes.
(3) create_nobEXT is a shared WDSP export that Thetis also uses, so this needs a new parameter or a new setter, not a changed default.
(4) The QSK/'feel' benefit is real but limited. Lyra's RXA chain (dspSize blocks plus FIR bandpass) already adds tens of ms, so 25 ms is a noticeable fraction of the total rather than the main cause. It matters most at high-speed full break-in, where delayed gap audio gets cut off by the next key-down.
(5) Shortening the look-ahead in fill modes does change behaviour for 1-25 ms sequences. That does not affect Lyra, which uses mode 0.

I found nothing that refutes the core claim.
verdict.corrected_benefit: With NB2 (NOB-II) enabled in zero mode, which is how Lyra uses it, about 25 ms of fixed delay can be removed from the IQ path. That path feeds both audio and the panadapter. The 25 ms comes from the hard-coded 25 ms max_imp_seq look-ahead in create_nobEXT. The blanker would then run on a look-ahead of only advance + hang (about 0.4-0.6 ms at 48 kS/s, not 0.2 ms), using the online gate extension that NOB-II's overflow path (states 5-9) already implements. Zero-mode blanking quality should be about the same; a hang slew that windows the live signal could even be slightly better. This needs a new exported parameter or setter so that Thetis is not affected, and a change of mode must re-flush the delay line. The benefit shows up mainly in high-speed QSK and in how the receiver feels to tune. It is a meaningful share of the total RX latency, not the main source of it.

kept.title: Robust, impulse-censored background estimate with a calibrated false-alarm rate; avg is inflated by impulses, starts at 1.0 and collapses during silence
kept.file_function: nob.c:initBlanker line 45, xanb line 119; nobII.c:flush_nob line 148, xnob line 180
kept.current: avg = backmult*avg + ombackmult*mag is updated with every sample, impulses included (nob.c:119, nobII.c:180). A train of impulses therefore raises its own threshold. Example: 100 impulses/s, 3 samples each at 100x the background, at 48 kS/s: the mean of |x| rises by about 62%, so the threshold rises about 4.2 dB and the blanker partly defeats itself on exactly the dense power-line or ignition noise it exists for. avg starts at 1.0 (nob.c:45, nobII.c:148). With typical IQ levels of 1e-4 to 1e-3, the blanker is blind for roughly 7-9 backtau (about 140-180 ms at 20 ms) after create, flush or a sample-rate change. After a stretch of silence or a big level drop, avg decays toward 0, and the first samples when signal returns are all flagged until avg reaches mag/T, which takes N*ln(T/(T-1)) samples: about 84 samples (1.7 ms) at T=12 and about 490 samples (10 ms) at T=2.5, at 48 kS/s with N=960. The threshold is a multiple of mean|x|, so in noise P_fa = exp(-pi*T^2/4) (confirmed by simulation). At Lyra's most aggressive setting (T=2.5, src/wdsp_engine.cpp:4538) that is 0.74% of samples, which with blanks of about 17 samples each means roughly 10% of pure-noise samples get blanked.
kept.proposed: (1) Censor the estimator: skip the update on flagged samples, or clip the input to min(mag, T*avg) (a clipped-mean CFAR), or use an order-statistic estimator, e.g. the median of |x| over the last few ms computed per block. (2) Seed avg from the first block's median, not from 1.0. Hold avg (do not decay) on exact-zero input, and add a level-step guard: if more than K consecutive samples are flagged (K well above any realistic impulse width), treat it as a level change and snap avg to the current median instead of blanking. (3) Give users a P_fa-based setting: T = sqrt(-4 ln(P_fa)/pi) on the magnitude detector, or the equivalent for the residual detector, so 'strength' has a predictable cost in blanked time.
kept.benefit: Moderate to large in dense impulse noise: the threshold stays put instead of rising several dB. It removes the start-up blind spot and the burst of blanking on signal onset after silence or tuning jumps. It makes the aggressive end of the strength control predictable; Lyra's T=2.5 floor should probably sit nearer T=3.5-4 (P_fa 6.6e-5 to 3.5e-6).
kept.risk: An order-statistic estimator costs more than one multiply-add; doing it per block with a median over about 256 samples keeps it cheap. A censoring estimator can latch high after a genuine upward level step, which the K-consecutive guard handles. Existing threshold presets shift slightly.
kept.evidence: Rohling, 'Radar CFAR thresholding in clutter and multiple target situations', IEEE TAES 19(4), 1983 (OS-CFAR). Rayleigh P_fa derivation: P(|x| > T*E|x|) = exp(-pi*T^2/4) for circular complex Gaussian x, matched by simulation of the nobII.c:179-184 recursion. Onset figures from the closed form for a one-pole IIR step response.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the code is accurate. In nob.c:45 and nobII.c:148, avg is set to 1.0. In nob.c:119 and nobII.c:180, avg = backmult*avg + ombackmult*mag runs on every sample, with no censoring. Detection is mag > avg*threshold, compared after the update. Neither file offers a censored or order-statistic background estimate, and no other WDSP blanker does: SNBA works on audio with a different detector. Lyra uses NOB-II only, through create_nobEXT(ch, 0, mode=0 (zero), inSize, inRate, slew=hang=adv=0.1 ms, backtau=20 ms, threshold=20). pushNbState maps strength to T = 12 - 9.5*strength, so T runs from 12 down to 2.5.

Checking the claims:
(a) Impulse inflation. The example's arithmetic is right: (47700 + 300*100)/48000 = 1.62x, about +4.2 dB. In that exact example the 100x impulses are still caught, because 12*1.62 = 19.4 < 100. Only impulses between 12x and 19x get missed. So the stated example understates where this really bites. At ignition or arcing rates near 1000/s the same arithmetic gives about 7.2x, so T*avg is about 87x the background and the 100x impulses start to slip through. The effect is real, it grows with impulse density, and that is exactly the situation a blanker exists for.
(b) Rayleigh false-alarm rate. P(|x| > T*E|x|) = exp(-pi*T^2/4) is correct, giving 0.74% at T=2.5. NOB-II blanks about 4+4+1+4+4 = 17 samples per detection at 48 kS/s in Lyra's setup, and Lyra uses mode 0, which zeroes them. So roughly 10% of pure-noise time gets zeroed at maximum strength. That is a real and avoidable cost, but it comes from Lyra's strength-to-T mapping, not a WDSP defect.
(c) Start-up blind spot. It is real (ln(1e3..1e4) is about 7-9 time constants, about 140-180 ms). But Lyra never calls flush_nob, so it happens only at channel creation. Negligible.
(d) Decay during silence or a level drop. This needs very long exact-zero or very low input, such as IQ muted during TX, and it costs at most a few ms of blanking. Minor.

The remedies are standard and sound. A clipped or censored mean, min(mag, T*avg), costs one compare per sample. OS-CFAR (Rohling, IEEE TAES 19(4), 1983) is a real and relevant reference. A one-pole estimator censored this way can latch after an upward step, which the proposed K-consecutive guard addresses. The main value is the censoring, plus a P_fa-based calibration of Lyra's T floor. The seeding and silence fixes are cosmetic. Nothing here affects latency, and the method applies directly to HF impulse noise. I am not refuting it, but I rate it medium rather than large: the stated example overstates the effect at 100 impulses/s, and parts (c) and (d) are minor for how Lyra uses the blanker.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Censoring the background estimate keeps the threshold from rising with impulse density. The 100/s example only lifts the threshold about 4 dB and loses only impulses in the 12-19x range, but at dense ignition or arcing rates (about 1000/s) the uncensored threshold rises about 17 dB and strong impulses get through. The clipped mean costs one compare per sample and adds no latency. Separately, the closed form exp(-pi*T^2/4) shows that Lyra's maximum-strength T=2.5, with zero-mode NOB-II, zeroes about 10% of pure-noise samples. Raising the floor to about T=3.5 (P_fa 6.6e-5) is a cheap Lyra-side fix. Seeding avg from data and holding it through silence are minor polish: Lyra never flushes the blanker, so the start-up blind spot only happens once, at creation.

kept.title: Run toggle leaves a stale delay line and changes latency, so 25 ms of old IQ is replayed or current IQ is dropped
kept.file_function: nobII.c:xnob lines 173/490-492 and pSetRCVRNOBRun/SetEXTNOBRun lines 521-526, 649-655; nob.c:xanb lines 113/185-186 and pSetRCVRANBRun/SetEXTANBRun lines 233-238, 348-354
kept.current: When run==0, xnob and xanb do a zero-delay memcpy and never touch or flush dline, imp or the indices. The run setters only assign a->run, with no flush. Turning the blanker on therefore outputs dline contents from whenever it last ran (about 1227 samples, 25.6 ms, for NOB-II with Lyra's settings, possibly from another frequency) before the current signal comes through 25.6 ms late. Turning it off drops 25.6 ms of signal with a hard splice. Lyra makes this worse by not calling xnobEXT at all while NB is off (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:6270-6272) and never calling flush_nobEXT. ANB has the same defect with a shorter delay. Separately, xanb reads a->run at line 113 before taking cs_update; this is a benign but formal data race.
kept.proposed: On a run 0->1 transition, flush (zero) the delay line and reset avg from the current block (see the estimator proposal). Better still, keep the delay line running while bypassed: output the delayed signal with no blanking, so latency stays constant and toggling is seamless; or cross-fade between the bypass and blanked paths over one slew time. In LyraDSP, read run inside the lock or make it atomic.
kept.benefit: Removes a 25 ms burst of stale or wrong-frequency audio (a click or garble) each time NB is enabled, and a 25 ms dropout/splice each time it is disabled. Small in duration but clearly audible and reproducible.
kept.risk: Running the delay line while bypassed costs a ring-buffer copy (negligible) and adds a constant 25 ms latency even with NB off, unless the latency proposal is adopted too. Flush-on-enable instead gives about 25 ms of silence on enable, which is better than stale audio but not seamless.
