kept.evidence: nobII.c:173 'if (a->run)' / 491 'else if (a->in != a->out) memcpy'; pSetRCVRNOBRun (521-526) and SetEXTNOBRun (649-655) only set a->run. Same pattern in nob.c:113, 185-186, 233-238, 348-354. Lyra: no flush_nobEXT call; xnobEXT is guarded by nbEnabled_ at src/wdsp_engine.cpp:6270.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code and the core claim holds.

WDSP side, nobII.c:
- xnob (line 173 `if (a->run)`, lines 490-492 `else if (a->in != a->out) memcpy`) passes the input straight through with no delay when run==0. On that path it never touches dline, imp, avg, state, bfbuff/ffbuff or the in/scan/out indices.
- pSetRCVRNOBRun (521-526) and SetEXTNOBRun (649-655) only assign a->run under cs_update. Neither calls flush_nob.

The delay line is in_idx - out_idx = adv_slew + adv + 1 + max_imp_seq + hang + hang_slew + filterlen. create_nobEXT hardcodes max_imp_seq_time = 0.025, so the delay is always about 25 ms. Lyra calls create_nobEXT(ch, 0, 0, inSize, inRate, 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.020, 20.0) with inRate defaulting to 192 kHz. That gives about 19+19+1+4800+19+19+10 = 4887 samples, or 25.45 ms. The proposal's "1227 samples" is the 48 kHz figure, but the 25 ms latency it states is right.

nob.c (ANB) has the same pattern:
- xanb reads a->run at line 113 before taking cs_update, which is a formal but harmless data race.
- The bypass is a memcpy at 185-186.
- The run setters at 233-238 and 348-354 only set run.

Behaviour that follows: when run goes 0->1, the first ~25 ms sent on to the RXA chain is stale IQ from whenever the blanker last ran. That can be another frequency, gain or band. The stale avg and state values also carry over, but backtau is 20 ms so the threshold re-adapts quickly. The current signal then arrives 25 ms late, joined with a hard discontinuity. When run goes 1->0, the ~25 ms still in the delay line is never output and the output jumps straight to undelayed input. That skips 25 ms of signal with a hard splice. Both effects follow directly from the code and are realistic: NB is a commonly toggled control and Lyra's settings are normal.

Lyra side: there is no flush_nobEXT call anywhere in src, and xnobEXT is guarded by nbEnabled_ at wdsp_engine.cpp:6270. One overstatement: the claim that Lyra's guard "makes this worse" is wrong. Because xnob does nothing to its state when run==0, skipping the call gives the same result. The guard does not make it worse. Also, on the very first enable after create, init_nob has already called flush_nob, so the dline is zeros. The stale-audio case only appears on the second and later enables.

Severity: a single ~25 ms glitch and a click per toggle. It is reproducible, and if the stale IQ is strong (for example from a different band) it can briefly pump AGC. It does not affect steady-state reception. The fixes are cheap and low-risk:
- Simplest: flush on a 0->1 transition (in the setter, or by having Lyra call flush_nobEXT when enabling), which costs ~25 ms of silence or a ramp.
- Better: keep the delay line running in bypass so latency stays constant. That adds a permanent 25 ms of latency while NB is off.
The proposed cross-fade is also reasonable. It is a real bug with modest impact, so the priority is low.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Each time NB is turned on (after the first time), about 25 ms of stale IQ from the last time the blanker ran is no longer replayed, so no brief burst of old or wrong-frequency signal and no click. Each time NB is turned off, about 25 ms of signal is no longer skipped with a hard splice. The delay is about 25 ms at any sample rate (4887 samples at Lyra's 192 kHz default), because create_nobEXT fixes max_imp_seq_time at 25 ms. The same fix pattern applies to ANB, which has a shorter delay. The simplest fix is flush-on-enable (in the WDSP run setter, or Lyra calling flush_nobEXT when NB is enabled), which turns the stale burst into ~25 ms of silence. Running the delay line while bypassed makes toggling seamless but costs a constant 25 ms of latency. Lyra's nbEnabled_ guard does not make this worse, because WDSP's run==0 path never touches the blanker state anyway. The xanb run read outside the lock is a formal data race with no practical effect. The impact is limited to a glitch on each toggle; steady-state reception is unaffected.

kept.title: Small timing off-by-ones: ANB's effective advance is one sample short (lets impulses through when advtime=0), and NOB-II over-counts one sample per merged burst
kept.file_function: nob.c:initBlanker line 41 and xanb lines 127-146; nobII.c:xnob lines 212-241
kept.current: ANB: the delay line holds D = trans_count + adv_count (line 41). At detection, state 0 still outputs one unscaled sample (128-135). The ramp then starts with wave[0] = 0.5, scale 1.0 (138), so the output reaches zero only trans_count+1 samples after detection, and the k-th sample after detection is scaled by 0.5+0.5cos((k-1)pi/trans). The detected sample leaves at k = D. With adv_count = 0 it is passed at sin^2(pi/(2*trans_count)): -6 dB for trans=2, -16.7 dB for trans=4, nowhere near the 40-60 dB an impulse needs. In general the zero region covers only adv_count-1 samples before the impulse. NOB-II: when the look-ahead (225-234) finds a further impulse at offset j-1 from tidx, it adds len = j, which already includes that impulse, and then the next pass of the while loop (215-221) counts the same impulse again. With m merges, blank_count is m too large: the blank runs m samples long, and Inext = dline[tidx] (245-246) is latched m samples before the point where state 0 actually resumes. That is a phase step of m*omega for every off-DC signal at the end of the slew, and the mode-4 slope is slightly off.
kept.proposed: ANB: set in_idx = trans_count + adv_count + 1 (or start the ramp on the detection sample and index wave from 1), so the full advtime is honoured and the detected sample is always at zero gain. NOB-II: add len-1 instead of len at line 235, or start the next while loop at tidx+1 after counting the impulse once. Write unit tests that place a single-sample impulse and assert exact zero-gain coverage, for adv_count in {0, 1, 4}.
kept.benefit: Small but measurable. Removes an impulse leak of up to -6 dB on ANB when advtime is set to zero, and a one-sample timing error per merged burst on NOB-II, which shows up as a tiny phase discontinuity on strong off-DC signals. Easy to lock down with tests during the port.
kept.risk: Effectively none. ANB's latency grows by one sample.
kept.evidence: Trace of nob.c:128-146 with in_idx initial offset D (line 41) and wave[i] = 0.5cos(i*pi/trans) (line 50). Trace of nobII.c:212-241 for an impulse at offset H then another at H+1+d, d < adv+adv_slew: blank_count ends at H+d+3 for a true span of H+d+2 samples.

verdict.reasoning:
I traced both code paths and both off-by-ones are real. The practical impact is smaller than the proposal suggests.

ANB (nob.c): in_idx starts at D = trans_count + adv_count (line 41), so a sample written at time n leaves at time n+D. When sample n is detected, state 0 still outputs one unscaled sample and switches to state 1. From n+1, state 1 applies scale 0.5+wave[dtime] with dtime = 0..trans, so the first ramp sample has gain 1.0 and gain reaches 0 only at n+1+trans. State 2 then outputs zeros for adv_count+1 samples. The detected sample leaves at n+trans+adv. With adv_count=0 that falls at dtime = trans-1, with gain 0.5-0.5cos(pi/trans) = sin^2(pi/2T): -6 dB for T=2 and -16.7 dB for T=4, as claimed. With adv_count >= 1 the detected sample lands at zero gain, and the zero region starts adv-1 samples before the impulse instead of adv. So this is a real one-sample shortfall. It only leaks the impulse when advtime*fs < 1. That is not the usual setting: an advtime around 0.1 ms gives about 19 samples at 192 kHz. It can happen at low sample rates or with very small advtime. The leaked sample is the first one over threshold, on the rising edge; the peak samples that follow fall inside the zero region.

NOB-II (nobII.c): I confirmed the double count. The while loop leaves tidx on a non-impulse sample. The look-ahead finds the next impulse at lidx = tidx+j-1, adds len=j, and sets tidx to that impulse; the next while pass then counts it again. So blank_count is m too large after m merges. With no merge, Inext = dline[tidx] is exactly the first sample state 0 resumes with. After m merges it is latched m samples early, and ff_idx (scan_idx+blank_count) and the mode-4 slope denominator are shifted by m as well.

The practical effect is negligible, though. The hold, interpolate and slew modes freeze a constant (DC) phasor during the blank and the hang slew. For an off-DC signal the blanked region is already a gap with a discontinuity at resume, so the extra |1-e^{jm omega}| step is hidden by that artifact. Near DC, where hold modes do useful work, m*omega is tiny. It also needs merged bursts. Calling it an audible improvement is overstated; as a correctness fix with tests for a port it is fine.

The risk statement "effectively none" is wrong for the first ANB option. dline_size = (int)((MAX_TAU+MAX_ADVTIME)*MAX_SAMPLERATE)+1 = 6145. At maximum tau and advtime at 1.536 MHz, D = 6144, so in_idx = D+1 = 6145 = dline_size. The first write would be out of bounds, and the wrap test (++in_idx == dline_size) would never fire after that. That fix therefore also needs dline_size increased by 1. The other option, starting the ramp on the detection sample or indexing wave from 1, avoids both the latency change and this overflow. For NOB-II the len-1 fix is correct.

Nothing in WDSP already fixes these: no other mode or option covers them. Lyra currently creates only NOB-II (create_nobEXT), not ANB.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Two real off-by-one timing bugs; fixing them is a correctness cleanup, not an audible gain at normal settings. ANB: the zero-gain region starts one sample late, so the first above-threshold sample passes at sin^2(pi/2T) gain (-6 dB for T=2), but only when advtime*fs < 1 (adv_count=0); at typical advtime (about 19 samples at 192 kHz) nothing leaks. Prefer indexing the ramp from the detection sample. Setting in_idx = D+1 instead needs dline_size increased by 1, or it overflows at max tau/advtime at 1.536 MHz. NOB-II: blank_count is one sample too long per merged impulse, so Inext, the ff-buffer start and the mode-4 slope are latched m samples early. The resulting phase step is masked by the hold and slew discontinuities already present on off-DC signals and is tiny near DC. Worth fixing with exact-coverage unit tests during the port, low user-visible impact.

kept.title: Memory safety and float32 hazards when porting: unclamped time parameters overrun fixed buffers, the IIR average and AR fits need care in float32
kept.file_function: nob.c:initBlanker lines 36-50, create_anb 80-82; nobII.c:init_nob lines 40-57, create_nob 94-102, flush_nob 144-145
kept.current: Buffers are sized from MAX_TAU/MAX_ADVTIME = 2 ms and MAX_SAMPLERATE = 1.536 MHz (nob.c:29-31, 80-82; nobII.c:29-34, 94-102). No setter clamps tau, advtime, hangtime, hang/adv slew times or samplerate (pSetRCVR*/SetEXT* in both files). init writes wave[0..trans_count] and awave/hwave[0..count-1] directly, and flush_nob puts in_idx at an offset that can exceed dline_size. After that, '++in_idx == dline_size' never wraps and xnob writes past the heap block. This is reachable at high rates (more than 2 ms at 1.536 MS/s) or with large UI values. The forward-filter scan (nobII.c:265-275) has no bound and can read past in_idx into data about one ring-length old when the region after the gap contains flagged samples (only when adv+adv_slew+hang_slew < filterlen). In float32: (a) the one-pole average with long backtau at high fs, e.g. 1 s at 1.536 MS/s, has 1-b = 6.5e-7, about 11 ulp of 1.0, so the time constant quantises by about 5% and each update is only a few ulp of avg. (b) On exact-zero input avg decays into subnormals within about 80 time constants (about 1.6 s at 20 ms) and then to 0. (c) Any AR fit added for interpolation or detection: with a strong carrier 70-90 dB above the noise, the autocorrelation matrix has an eigenvalue spread of 1e7-1e9, beyond float32's roughly 1e7, so float32 Levinson-Durbin can produce reflection coefficients of 1 or more, an unstable predictor and garbage fill.
kept.proposed: In LyraDSP, derive all buffer sizes from the actual configured parameters (re-allocate on change outside the audio thread) or clamp every time parameter to its MAX in the setters. Bound the forward-filter scan to in_idx. Keep the background average in double, or compute it per block (vDSP mean or median of |x| over the block, then a one-pole across blocks), which is cheaper and avoids accumulating rounding error. Flush the average to a floor on zero input. For any AR stage, estimate in double precision with Burg (which guarantees |k| < 1), or regularise (white-noise loading of about 1e-9 of R[0]). The signal path itself (gain multiply, ring buffer, linear-fill accumulation over at most about 1200 samples, error about 7e-5 relative) is safe in float32.
kept.benefit: Prevents a heap overflow class that the current code only avoids because callers pass small values. Keeps detector timing accurate at high IQ rates and long time constants. Makes the AR proposals stable in exactly the strong-signal cases they are meant for. Apart from the overflow, the impact on today's Lyra settings (20 ms backtau, rates up to 384k) is small.
kept.risk: Negligible. Clamping changes nothing for in-range values. Double precision for one scalar per sample or one small fit per event costs essentially nothing.
kept.evidence: nob.c:80-82 vs 36-41 and 49-50; nobII.c:94-102 vs 40-57 and 144-145; nobII.c:265-275 (unbounded while). Float32 eps 1.19e-7; Burg-vs-autocorrelation conditioning: Kay & Marple, 'Spectrum analysis - a modern perspective', Proc. IEEE 1981, and Marple, 'Digital Spectral Analysis', 1987, ch. 8.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description of current behaviour is accurate. In nob.c, wave is allocated as (int)(1.536e6*0.002)+1 and dline from MAX_TAU+MAX_ADVTIME (lines 80-82). initBlanker writes wave[0..trans_count] (lines 48-49), using counts taken directly from tau, hangtime and advtime. In nobII.c, dline and imp are sized from the MAX_* constants (lines 94-100), while init_nob and flush_nob use the configured times as they are. None of the pSetRCVR* or SetEXT* setters in either file clamps anything, so the claim that nothing clamps is correct.

xnob's ring index uses '++in_idx == dline_size' to wrap. If flush_nob starts in_idx at or past dline_size, that test never fires and xnob writes past the heap block. This is a real latent overflow.

It is worse than the proposal says. I compiled the size arithmetic. At 1.536 MS/s with every parameter at its own MAX (2 ms each, 25 ms seq), dline_size is 50690 but flush_nob sets in_idx to 50699. So nobII overflows even with in-range maxima, because the +1 and +filterlen terms are not in the allocation. Clamping to MAX alone would not fix nobII. The fix has to derive the size from the parameters, or add filterlen+slack to the allocation.

The unbounded forward-filter scan (nobII.c, the while ffcount < filterlen loop) is real. It skips flagged samples with no bound relative to in_idx, so it can read ring data from the previous cycle. It cannot go out of bounds because the index wraps, and it needs adv+adv_slew to be short relative to filterlen. That makes it a minor correctness issue.

The practical reach in Lyra today is nil. Lyra calls create_nobEXT with fixed 0.1 ms slew/hang/adv, 20 ms backtau and 20 threshold (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:1376-1379), and only ever sets threshold and run. WDSP itself runs in double.

The float32 points apply only to a hypothetical float32 port:
- (a) The quantisation example needs a 1 s backtau at 1.536 MS/s, which nobody uses. At 20 ms and 384k, 1-b is about 1.3e-4, which is fine in float32.
- (b) avg decaying to zero on exact-zero input is not specific to float32. Double does the same thing, only later. Flooring the average is still a sensible fix because avg=0 flags every nonzero sample as an impulse after silence. On Apple Silicon, subnormals do not carry the x86 performance penalty.
- (c) There is no AR stage in these files, so this point is advice for future work. It is technically sound: Burg's reflection coefficients satisfy |k|<=1 by construction, and Levinson on an ill-conditioned autocorrelation matrix in float32 can lose stability. The Kay & Marple 1981 Proc. IEEE paper and Marple's 1987 book are real and relevant.

Nothing contradicts the proposal's statements. Its value is defensive hardening for a port, not a fix to current behaviour, so the priority is low.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
This is defensive hardening for a reimplementation, not a fix to anything Lyra does today. Lyra passes fixed 0.1 ms times to the double-precision WDSP blanker and only changes threshold and run, so nothing reaches the overflow now.

In any port, size the NOB/ANB rings and windows from the configured parameters, including the +1 and +filterlen terms, and reallocate outside the audio thread. Clamping to the MAX_* constants is not enough for nobII. At 1.536 MS/s with every time parameter at its maximum, WDSP's own flush_nob puts in_idx at 50699 when dline_size is 50690, so the write overflows.

Also bound the forward-filter scan to in_idx (a minor stale-data read). Put a floor under the background average so a stretch of digital silence does not leave avg at 0 and blank everything afterwards. This happens in double as well.

The float32 timing concern only matters for extreme time constants. The Burg / double-precision / diagonal-loading advice applies only if an AR interpolation stage is added later.

summary: The NNR block takes the real channel at dsp_rate and decimates it by an integer factor to the model rate (16 kHz in every built-in model). The decimator is a Kaiser-windowed sinc, beta 7.857 (about 80 dB stopband), cutoff 0.45*nrate, 51 taps per phase (nnr_design_proto, nnr_push_input). It then runs a sqrt-Hann WOLA STFT: N=512, hop 256 (hop 128 for slot 3), 257 bins (nnr_frame). Each frame is compressed to |X|^0.3 with phase kept and scaled by one broadband EMA power normaliser with tau 2 s and bias correction (run_cond). It then goes through a causal DPCRN-style U-net with 4 Conv2d encoders (kt=2, kf=5, frequency stride 2, 257->129->65->33->17), 2 DPRNN blocks (a bidirectional GRU across the 17 bands, then a per-band GRU across time) and 4 ConvTranspose2d decoders with skips. The output is 2*order channels of complex deep-filter coefficients (DeepFilterNet-style), applied to the raw, un-normalised STFT over the last `order` frames (5/5/12/24 for slots 0-3) in run_dfhead. After that come per-bin post-processing steps: an optional expander knee, optional attack/release smoothing, a gmax clamp (+12 dB) and a gmin floor (the mask_floor, -25 dB in RXA.c). The output is inverse-FFT'd, overlap-added, polyphase-interpolated back to the original rate and buffered in a FIFO pre-filled with `prime = decim*hop` zeros. The models carry `lookahead`=1 (I parsed it from the built-in blobs), but no runtime code consumes it except the delay formula (nnr.c:216). The lookahead is therefore implicit in training: the frame-t output estimates frame t-1. The total is about 51 ms at 48 kHz for slots 0-2 and about 43 ms for slot 3. For models that declare a training band (slots 2 and 3, 200-3000 Hz), setNNRbypassRun moves NNR before the AGC (position 0). It feeds NNR from a 2048-tap minimum-phase bandpass and skips bpsnba/snba/eqp/anf/anr/emnr. Inference is hand-written scalar double C. Model 0 costs about 6.3 MMAC per frame (about 0.39 GMAC/s), and model 1 about 2.2 times that. Weights are stored as f64.

kept.title: Deep-filter gain clamp/floor/smoothing is referenced to the wrong frame when lookahead=1
kept.file_function: nnet.c:run_dfhead (lines 601-605 set cur_re/cur_im to the newest ring slot; lines 629-683 compute g=|y|/|x_cur|, the gmax/gmin clamps, the knee and the smoothing; lines 679-680 set the floor fallback y=gmin*x_cur); nnet.c:nnet_build 1193-1196 and create_nnet_slot 1277 (lookahead is stored and then never used)
kept.current: run_dfhead writes the newest STFT frame x[t] into ring slot `head` (cur_re/cur_im). It forms y = sum_i C_i * x[t-i] over the last P frames. Every post-processing decision then uses g = |y_k| / |x_t,k|: the alpha/knee expander, the attack/release smoother, the `g > gmax` clamp (+12 dB by default, NNET_GMAX_DB) and the `g < gmin` floor. When |y| is tiny, the floor substitutes y = gmin * x_t. All four built-in models declare lookahead=1 (parsed from the embedded blobs), and nnr_build_stft (nnr.c:216) adds `lookahead*hop` to the reported delay. Nothing at runtime shifts anything, so the lookahead lives in training: the frame-t output is an estimate of clean frame t-1. The clamp, the floor and the smoother therefore compare a frame t-1 estimate against frame t input.
kept.proposed: Pass the lookahead L (n->lookahead is already parsed) into create_dfhead. Use ref = ring[(head - L + P) % P] (requires P > L, which holds for P=5/12/24) as the reference for g. Use the same ref for the floor fallback `yre = gmin*ref_re`, and key gprev on the same alignment. Confirm against the training/export code that lookahead is a target delay. If it turns out lookahead is NOT actually used in training, the bug moves instead: getDelay_nnr then over-reports by one hop, and that term should be dropped.
kept.benefit: This removes a systematic trailing-edge clamp. At a CW key-up or the end of a syllable, x_t is already noise while y still estimates the tone/voiced frame t-1. With a per-bin SNR above about 12 dB (common for CW in a 31 Hz bin), g exceeds gmax and the last frame of every element is pulled down by (SNR - 12) dB. That audibly softens or truncates keying tails and word endings exactly on strong signals, where NR should be transparent. At onsets the mirror case puts a -25 dB copy of the onset frame one hop early. Expected to be clearly audible on high-SNR CW (slots 2/3). It is subtler on SSB voice, where per-bin SNRs are lower.
kept.risk: Very low if the training semantics are confirmed. If the models were trained with a post-clamp in the loop that used x_t (unlikely, since the clamp is inference-only), the networks may have partly compensated. A/B on keyed CW at high SNR.
kept.evidence: Line-level. nnet.c:601-605 make cur = newest slot; 631-636 compute g against cur; 663-681 clamp against it; n->lookahead (nnet.c:1196) is never read by run_nnet/run_dfhead; nnr.c:216 counts `lookahead*hop` in the latency. Built-in blobs: `lookahead`=(1.0) in all four. DeepFilterNet's DF op with lookahead l is y_t = sum_i C_{t,i} x_{t-i+l}, i.e. it targets the frame l hops before the newest (Schröter, Escalante-B., Rosenkranz, Maier, 'DeepFilterNet', ICASSP 2022; DeepFilterNet2, IWAENC 2022).

verdict.reasoning:
The code matches the description. In nnet.c run_dfhead, lines 601-605 write the newest frame into ring slot `head`, and cur_re/cur_im point there. y is formed as sum_i C_i * ring[head-i]. g = |y|/|cur| (lines 631-636) feeds the knee expander, the smoother, the gmax clamp and the gmin floor. The ay<=tiny fallback is y = gmin*x_cur. n->lookahead is set in create_nnet_slot (line 1277) and overwritten in nnet_build (1193-1196). Its only reader is getLookahead_nnet (line 1731), which just returns it. Nothing in run_nnet/run_dfhead uses it. All four embedded blobs carry `lookahead 1`. nnr.c:216 adds lookahead*hop to the reported delay, and no runtime buffer creates that extra hop.

The repo has no training or export code, so I cannot check whether lookahead is a target delay. I cannot refute the inconsistency, though. Either the network output is late by one frame (as the delay accounting asserts) and the gain reference is misaligned, or it is not and getDelay_nnr over-reports by one hop. Both are bugs, and the proposal names both. The delay formula strongly suggests the author meant target-delay semantics, which matches DeepFilterNet's DF lookahead. The citations are real and relevant.

What runs by default: alpha=1, so the knee is off. sm_att/sm_rel=0, so the smoother is off. That leaves only the +12 dB gmax clamp and the floor. Most of the time the misalignment does nothing: in steady state |s[t-1]| is about |s[t]|, so g stays near or below 1. It only bites at sharp offsets. With 50%-overlap sqrt-Hann frames, a key-up near a frame boundary leaves frame t-1 with a partial tone while x_t is noise only. If the per-bin SNR of that partial frame is above about 12 dB (easy for a strong CW signal in a 31 Hz bin), the clamp pulls that last output frame down by (SNR-12) dB. That trims up to about one hop (~16 ms) of each element's tail and can sharpen the key-up. The onset mirror case (a floor-level early copy) is negligible.

The effect is real but small. 'Clearly audible' is unverified and probably overstated: it changes one partial frame per element, and the default smoother is off, so there is no compounding. The fix branch also depends on training semantics that cannot be checked here. If lookahead is not a target delay, the proposed reference shift would introduce the misalignment it is meant to remove. So I am not refuting it, but I rate it low until the training alignment is confirmed and an A/B on strong keyed CW shows an audible difference.
verdict.corrected_benefit: There is a real code inconsistency. n->lookahead (1 in every built-in model) is counted in the reported latency, but run_dfhead never uses it. Either the gain reference is one frame off or the latency report is one hop too high. If the models were trained with a one-frame target delay, which the delay accounting implies but no training code in the repo confirms, the default +12 dB gmax clamp compares the frame t-1 estimate against frame t input. On strong signals with sharp offsets (high-SNR CW key-up), that attenuates the last partial frame of each element by roughly (per-bin SNR - 12) dB, trimming up to ~16 ms of the tail. Referencing the clamp and floor to ring[head-L] removes this. With the knee and smoother off by default, the steady-state effect is nil. The audible gain is probably subtle, limited to tails and onsets of strong keyed signals, and needs an A/B to confirm. If training turns out not to delay the target, the correct fix is instead dropping lookahead*hop from the reported delay, and the reference shift must not be applied.

kept.title: Use the minimum safe FIFO prime H - gcd(size, H) instead of a full hop
kept.file_function: nnr.c:nnr_build_stft line 215 (t->prime = a->decim * hop); nnr.c:nnr_reset_state line 396; delay formula line 216
kept.current: The output FIFO is always pre-filled with prime = decim*hop zeros (768 samples = 16 ms at 48 kHz for hop 256). Frames complete exactly every H = decim*hop input samples, counted from reset, because dcount and nacc start at 0. xnnr pushes `size` inputs and then pops `size` outputs. The worst-case deficit between consumed and produced samples is therefore max_k (k*size mod H) = H - gcd(size, H), not H.
kept.proposed: Set t->prime = H - gcd(a->size, H) and keep the delay formula consistent with it: delay = decim*(fftsize - hop + lookahead*hop) + nproto - 1 + prime. orsize needs no change. setSize_nnr already rebuilds via calc_nnr, so the prime tracks buffer-size changes. For WDSP's power-of-two dsp_size with H = 3*2^8 (48 kHz) or 3*2^9 (96 kHz), gcd = min(size, 256 or 512).
kept.benefit: About 5.3 ms less latency at 48 kHz and 96 kHz with dsp_size >= 256 (2.7 ms for the hop-128 slot), out of about 51 ms total. If LyraDSP ever uses a block size that is a multiple of H, the full 16 ms disappears. Marginal-to-modest, but free.
kept.risk: Exact only while frame boundaries stay phase-locked to block boundaries, which holds because every reset (nnr_reset_state) zeros dcount/nacc and refills the FIFO. A variable block size would break the bound, so fall back to H if the host does that. Keep the nunder counter as a guard.
kept.evidence: Line-level. A frame fires when nacc reaches hop (nnr.c:364), i.e. every H inputs from reset (nnr.c:384-387). The output deficit after k blocks is k*size mod H, whose maximum over k is H - gcd(size, H) by elementary number theory.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code in /Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source/nnr.c and the description of the current behaviour is accurate.

- nnr_build_stft sets t->prime = a->decim * hop (line 215), and that value is added into t->delay (lines 216-218).
- nnr_reset_state zeros dpos_dec, dcount, nacc and the FIFO, then pushes `prime` zeros (line 396).
- nnr_push_input: dcount reaches decim on every decim-th input, and nacc reaches hop after hop decimated samples, so a frame fires on exactly every H = decim*hop inputs counted from reset.
- Each frame calls nnr_push_output hop times, and each call puts decim samples, so a frame produces exactly H outputs.
- xnnr pushes all `size` inputs before it pops `size` outputs, so the lowest FIFO level in a block is reached at the end of that block's pops. After k blocks the count is prime - (k*size mod H). Its worst case over k is H - gcd(size, H), not H.

The phase lock holds wherever the state could change:
- SetRXANNRRun calls flush_nnr, which runs nnr_reset_state.
- setModel_nnr resets the state.
- setSize_nnr and setSamplerate_nnr rebuild everything through calc_nnr, so a prime computed from a->size follows buffer-size changes.
- RXA creates NNR with a fixed ch[channel].dsp_size and always calls xnnr with whole blocks.
- orsize is computed from prime, so a smaller prime only shrinks the FIFO, which is safe.
- getDelay_nnr has no consumer in WDSP besides debug prints, and keeping prime inside the delay formula keeps the reported delay correct.

I simulated it for H in {384, 768, 1536, 3072} and power-of-two sizes from 64 to 4096, over 5000 blocks each. With prime = H - gcd(size, H), the lowest FIFO level is exactly 0: no underrun, with no slack. WDSP does not already do this anywhere.

Corrections to the claim:
- The saving is gcd(size, H) samples. At 96 kHz (H = 1536) it is 5.3 ms only when dsp_size >= 512. With dsp_size = 256 it is 256 samples, about 2.7 ms, not 5.3 ms.
- With small dsp_size (64 or 128) the saving is only 1.3-2.7 ms at 48 kHz.
- WDSP block sizes are powers of two and H always carries a factor of 3, so the "full 16 ms disappears" case never happens.

The benefit is real but modest: about 5 ms out of about 51 ms, at no cost. Because the margin is exactly zero, any future change that processes partial blocks would cause underruns. The nunder counter would catch them, but keep that guard.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The NNR output delay drops by gcd(dsp_size, H) samples with no change in sound and no FIFO underrun, as long as whole fixed-size blocks are processed. That is 256 samples (5.3 ms) at 48 kHz with the hop-256 slot when dsp_size >= 256. At 96 kHz it is 5.3 ms only when dsp_size >= 512, and 2.7 ms at dsp_size 256. The hop-128 slot saves 2.7 ms at 48 kHz. Smaller block sizes save less. With power-of-two block sizes the full prime never goes away.

kept.title: Cut algorithmic latency with hop 128 and an asymmetric analysis/synthesis window pair (retrain)
kept.file_function: nnr.c:nnr_design_windows (lines 167-178, symmetric sqrt-Hann), nnr_build_stft delay (line 216); model geometry from nnet_probe_slot
kept.current: Symmetric sqrt-Hann analysis and synthesis windows of length N=512 (32 ms at 16 kHz). Latency is N + lookahead*hop + resampler = about 48 + 3.2 ms for hop 256 (slots 0-2) and about 40 + 3.2 ms for hop 128 (slot 3). The 32 ms synthesis window is the dominant term, and it exists only to get 31.25 Hz resolution on the analysis side.
kept.proposed: (a) Move voice models to hop 128 (overlap 4), as slot 3 already does. The code supports it unchanged and it halves both the lookahead and the FIFO-prime terms. (b) Retrain with an asymmetric window pair: keep a long analysis window (N=512, for 31.25 Hz CW/pitch resolution) and use a short synthesis window of 2*hop at the end of the frame, designed for perfect reconstruction. Algorithmic latency then becomes synthesis length + lookahead rather than N. nnr_design_windows and olascale need generalising, because the current olascale assumes Hann-squared COLA.
kept.benefit: (a) alone: about 51 -> 43 ms. (a)+(b): roughly 51 -> 20-25 ms with the same frequency resolution, which is significant for CW break-in and for operators who notice the NR-on/off timing shift. Wang et al. report almost no quality loss down to 4-8 ms latency with this technique.
kept.risk: Requires retraining every model, because the existing weights are tied to the sqrt-Hann pair. Hop 128 doubles inference cost (about 0.8 GMAC/s for model 0). That is trivial on Apple Silicon via Core ML or BNNS but was presumably the reason WDSP chose hop 256 for scalar double C. Short synthesis windows slightly increase frame-boundary artefacts if the network is not trained with them.
kept.evidence: Mauler & Martin, 'A low delay, variable resolution, perfect reconstruction spectral analysis-synthesis system for speech enhancement', EUSIPCO 2007; Wang, Wichern, Watanabe, Le Roux, 'STFT-domain neural speech enhancement with very low algorithmic latency', IEEE/ACM TASLP 2023. DeepFilterNet uses a 20 ms window, a 10 ms hop and about 40 ms total; RNNoise uses a 20 ms window and a 10 ms hop (Valin, MMSP 2018).

verdict.reasoning:
Code check (nnr.c). nnr_design_windows (lines 167-178) sets both awin and swin to sqrt of a periodic Hann of length fftsize. olascale = (2/overlap)/N is correct only for Hann-squared COLA, as the proposal says. In nnr_build_stft, delay = decim*(N - hop + lookahead*hop) + nproto - 1 + prime, where prime = decim*hop. That reduces to decim*(N + lookahead*hop) + nproto - 1. I decoded the geom and lookahead metadata from the four model blobs:
- Slots 0 and 1 (voice: nnr_la1_sw1, big48_la1) carry no geom tensor, so they fall back to 16000/512/256. Lookahead is 1.
- Slot 2 is 16000/512/256 with DF order 12.
- Slot 3 (cwf_ovl4) is 16000/512/128 with DF order 24.
All four use lookahead 1. At 48 kHz (decim 3, nproto 153) that gives 2456 samples = 51.2 ms for hop 256 and 2072 samples = 43.2 ms for hop 128, which matches the proposal. No asymmetric window or low-delay synthesis path exists anywhere in nnr.c, nnet.c, nnio.c or nnrbypass.c. Only slot 3 already uses hop 128, so the proposal is not already implemented.

Literature. Mauler & Martin (EUSIPCO 2007) and Wang, Wichern, Watanabe, Le Roux (IEEE/ACM TASLP 2023, 'STFT-Domain Neural Speech Enhancement With Very Low Algorithmic Latency') are real and directly relevant. The DeepFilterNet and RNNoise framing figures quoted are roughly right.

Weaknesses that cut the claimed benefit:
1. The latency arithmetic for (a)+(b) is optimistic. With hop 128, a synthesis window of 2*hop = 256 and lookahead 1, the formula gives 256 + 128 samples at 16 kHz (24 ms) plus 3.2 ms resampler, about 27 ms, not 20-25 ms. Getting near 20 ms would also mean dropping lookahead.
2. (a) is not 'code unchanged, free'. The voice models would also need retraining at hop 128. The GRU time dynamics and the deep-filter span are tied to frame rate, which is why slot 3 doubled the DF order from 12 to 24 relative to slot 2. At hop 128 the voice models' order 5 would need to become about 10 to keep the same time span. That doubles inference in WDSP's scalar double C on Windows, and that cost applies to upstream WDSP, not only to a Core ML port.
3. Short synthesis windows plus a multi-frame complex deep filter increase circular time-aliasing in the output region. The 'same frequency resolution' claim holds on the analysis side only, and the network must be trained end to end with the new window pair. Quality parity for this DPCRN plus DF architecture on HF noise is unverified. Wang et al. still show some degradation as latency shrinks.
4. Retraining needs the 'NR Master Tool' training pipeline and dataset. Neither is in the WDSP source tree, so this is a research project, not a patch.
5. The significance is overstated. WDSP's classic NR2 (EMNR, created in RXA.c with FFT 4096 at the DSP rate) already adds about 85 ms at 48 kHz and is widely accepted. RX NR latency does not affect QSK T/R switching or sidetone. The NR-on/off timing shift against the min-phase nnrbypass filter is real, but it also exists with NR2.

Net: the description of current behaviour is accurate, and the technique is sound and published. The gain is a real but moderate cut of about 24 ms, and it costs a full retrain, double compute and some quality risk. It is a plausible improvement rather than a refuted one, but low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Moving the voice models to hop 128 (with retraining, and roughly doubling the deep-filter order to keep the same time span) cuts NNR algorithmic latency from about 51 ms to about 43 ms at the cost of about 2x inference. Adding a retrained asymmetric pair (long analysis window N=512, short synthesis window of 256 samples, with olascale/COLA generalised) brings it to about 27 ms with lookahead 1, or about 19 ms with lookahead 0. Analysis-side resolution stays at 31.25 Hz, but there is a risk of time-aliasing and quality loss with the multi-frame deep filter. It needs the external training pipeline. The benefit is a smaller NR-on/off timing shift and snappier RX audio. It is not decisive for CW QSK, and NNR is already lower-latency than WDSP's NR2 (about 85 ms).

kept.title: Pre-AGC level normaliser adapts too slowly to level steps (tau = 2 s, symmetric)
kept.file_function: nnet.c:run_cond lines 815-823; NNET_TAU_DEFAULT line 46; calc_cond line 752
kept.current: Features are normalised by one broadband EMA of mean |X|^0.6 with tau = 2 s (alpha = exp(-1/(2*62.5)) = 0.992 per frame), with bias correction only at start-up. When the bypass is on, NNR runs at position 0, before the AGC (nnr.c:748), so its input level follows fading, retuning and strong stations appearing. A 40 dB step changes pw by 10^(4*0.6), about 24 dB, so the features run 12 dB hot (or cold) and take about 1.4 s (around 87 frames) to come within 3 dB.
kept.proposed: Use an asymmetric normaliser, fast attack (about 100-200 ms) with slow release (about 2 s), or re-seed the EMA on a detected step (e.g. |10*log10(pw/phat)| > 15 dB), and flush it on retune or mode change from the host. Ideally train with the same normaliser and include level steps and QSB in the training augmentation. Per-band normalisation as in DeepFilterNet (exponential unit-norm per bin, tau about 1 s) is an alternative but changes the input contract and needs retraining.
kept.benefit: Fewer seconds of out-of-distribution input after band changes, strong-signal onsets or deep fades, and therefore fewer bursts of over- or under-suppression and noise pumping after a strong station drops. The effect size is uncertain and could be marginal, because the 0.3 compression already shrinks the step. A/B it on recorded band changes before committing.
kept.risk: Any normaliser change at inference only is a train/test mismatch for the existing weights. A fast attack can make the noise floor pump with QRN impulses unless pw is computed robustly (e.g. median, or clipping outlier frames).
kept.evidence: Line-level: nnet.c:752, 815-823; position switching in nnr.c:747-754. DeepFilterNet feature normalisation: Schröter et al., ICASSP 2022 (exponential mean/unit normalisation with alpha set by tau = 1 s).

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the code is mostly accurate. calc_cond (nnet.c:752) sets alpha = exp(-1/(tau*frame_rate)). tau is NNET_TAU_DEFAULT = 2.0 (line 46, commented "leave at default"). The frame rate passed in is nrate/hop, which is 16000/256 = 62.5 at the defaults (nnr.c:35-37, 466-468). So alpha is about 0.992. run_cond (nnet.c:795-830) compresses each bin to |X|^0.3 (cexp 0.3, pexp -0.7), takes the broadband mean of |X|^0.6 (pw) and smooths it with one symmetric EMA. The wstate term is a bias correction that only matters at start-up. Features are then scaled by 1/sqrt(phat). The network's mask and deep filter (run_dfhead) are applied to the uncompressed X, so the normaliser only changes what the network sees as input. When the bypass is on, the demod and noise chain is skipped, and xnnr(...,0) runs before xwcpagc (RXA.c:656-681). The position switch at nnr.c:747-754 is as described. There is no asymmetric attack/release and no step re-seed anywhere. The only related control is SetRXANNRTau (nnr.c:863), clamped to 0.05-30 s and marked test-only. It changes the symmetric tau, so it is not the proposal.

Errors in the proposal:
(1) The arithmetic is off. pw is proportional to power^0.3, so a 40 dB step moves pw by 10^1.2, about 12 dB, not 24 dB. The final "features 12 dB hot" happens to be right, since feature amplitude moves by 10^0.6, which is 12 dB in 20log terms.
(2) It understates the case that matters most. For an upward step, getting within 3 dB takes about 79 frames (1.26 s). For a downward step, such as a strong station dropping out, it takes ln(14.85) x 125, about 337 frames or 5.4 s. The normaliser does not reset itself after a step; it only re-converges at the EMA rate.

Problems with the proposed fixes:
(a) A 100-200 ms fast attack with a 2 s release turns the mean-level normaliser into a peak follower. It tracks speech syllables and QRN, which shifts the operating point several dB away from what the weights were trained on. It also erodes the absolute speech-vs-noise level cue the network relies on. Without retraining this is likely harmful.
(b) The detector threshold as written (|10log10(pw/phat)| > 15 dB) is in compressed-pw units, which is about a 50 dB signal step, so it would almost never fire. Read in signal dB instead, it is about 4.5 dB in pw units, and single speech-onset frames cross that routinely. Either way a persistence gate (N consecutive frames) is needed.
(c) The DeepFilterNet citation (Schröter et al., ICASSP 2022) is real, but DeepFilterNet itself uses a symmetric, slow (tau about 1 s) exponential normaliser. It supports slow symmetric normalisation, matched in training, more than a fast attack.
(d) The benefit at inference only is unproven. It depends on how level-sensitive weights we cannot inspect are. The proposer already concedes it may be marginal.

What survives: the core observation is real and confirmed in code. Pre-AGC, there are seconds of mis-scaled input after large level steps, about 5 s after a strong-signal drop. A persistence-gated re-seed of pstate/wstate, plus a host-side flush on retune or mode change, is a cheap, low-risk way to shorten that. It changes nothing in steady state, so it adds little train/test mismatch. Whether listeners notice the difference has to be A/B tested.
verdict.corrected_benefit: When the bypass is on, NNR runs before the AGC. Its symmetric 2 s EMA normaliser then takes about 1.3 s to settle after a 40 dB upward step and about 5.4 s after a 40 dB downward step (strong station gone). During that time the network sees inputs up to 12 dB too hot or too cold. A cheap, low-mismatch fix is to re-seed pstate/wstate when the broadband level stays shifted for several consecutive frames, and to flush the normaliser on retune or mode change. Steady-state behaviour stays the same, so the existing weights stay in distribution. Do not add a 100-200 ms fast attack without retraining, because it would track syllables and impulses and bias the features. The audible benefit is unproven and needs an A/B test on recorded band changes and QSB.

kept.title: Rate mismatch permanently latches run=0; rebuild also resets test/tuning parameters
kept.current: If dsp_rate is not an integer multiple of nrate (e.g. 24 kHz or 44.1 kHz), calc_nnr sets a->run = 0. A later setSamplerate_nnr to a valid rate does not restore it, so the user's 'NNR on' is silently lost. SetRXANNRRun only acts when run != setit (nnr.c:772), so the UI shows the block as on while it is not running. Every decalc/calc also recreates all nets with the defaults tau=2, gmax=12, alpha=1, smoothing off and network mode, discarding values set via SetRXANNRTau/MaxGain/Alpha/Knee/Smooth/TestMode. It also reparses all four model blobs, twice per slot (probe and build).
kept.proposed: Keep a separate `user_run` flag and compute the effective run as user_run && rate_ok in calc_nnr. Cache the tunables in the NNR struct and re-apply them to every slot after calc_nnr. In LyraDSP, also support non-integer ratios with a rational polyphase resampler (e.g. 44.1 kHz -> 16 kHz as L/M = 160/441) instead of disabling the block.
kept.benefit: Correct behaviour across sample-rate and buffer changes. No direct audio-quality change.
kept.risk: None meaningful.
kept.evidence: Line-level: nnr.c:418-424 write a->run = 0 with no restore path; nnet.c:1278-1281 hard-set the defaults on every create_nnet_slot.

verdict.reasoning:
The code does what the proposal says. In nnr.c:416-424, calc_nnr sets decim = rate/nrate. With the default nrate of 16000 (nnr.c:35), or whatever the first loadable slot reports, a rate that is not an integer multiple makes it set decim=1 and a->run=0. Nothing ever sets run back to 1. setSamplerate_nnr and setSize_nnr (nnr.c:624-640) do decalc then calc and keep only a->model; the mask floor survives because create_nnet_slot receives a->mask_floor. SetRXANNRRun (nnr.c:772) only acts when run != setit. So a host that still shows "on" and never re-sends 1 is silently off after a bad-then-good rate change. create_nnet_slot (nnet.c:1271-1281) hard-sets tau=NNET_TAU_DEFAULT, gmax=NNET_GMAX_DB and sm_att=sm_rel=0, and Alpha, Knee and TestMode also live only in the per-slot nets. Every setSize/setSamplerate therefore discards values set through SetRXANNRTau, MaxGain, Smooth, Alpha, Knee and TestMode.

There is one more hazard the proposal misses. If the user re-sends run=1 while the rate is still invalid, SetRXANNRRun accepts it, and the network runs with decim forced to 1 on audio at the wrong rate.

Practical reach is very small, though:
(a) Valid rates are 48k, 96k, 192k and 384k, which covers every RX dsp_rate Thetis-style hosts use. 24 kHz and 44.1 kHz are not realistic WDSP RXA dsp_rates. Lyra fixes dspRate=48000 (src/wdsp_engine.h:98) and, by its own comment (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:5390), never calls SetDSPBuffsize or the rate setters on RX. So the latch is unreachable in Lyra and very unlikely in Thetis.
(b) The parameters that get reset are explicitly labelled in the source as "Used in testing; not intended as a user control". Lyra resolves only SetRXANNRRun, SetRXANNRMaskFloor and SetRXANNRModel, and those settings already survive a rebuild.
(c) Parsing the models twice per slot costs a little on the non-real-time rebuild path only; it does not affect audio.
(d) The rational polyphase resampler part (L/M=160/441) is not justified. It adds a new resampler and new latency or filter design to the NNR block to support dsp_rates nobody runs. WDSP already has resample.c, and the clean fix is to keep the block bypassed at an invalid rate.

So the bugs are real but latent and defensive, not a realistic misbehaviour.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This is a defensive fix only, and it does not change audio. It separates the user's requested run state from an effective run = user_run && rate_ok in calc_nnr. That stops a bad-then-good dsp_rate change from silently latching NNR off, and stops the block from running at a mismatched rate if run=1 is re-sent while the rate is invalid. Optionally, it caches the test-only tunables (tau, gmax, alpha, knee, smoothing, test mode) in the NNR struct and re-applies them after rebuilds. Neither bug can be reached at the 48k/96k/192k/384k dsp rates real hosts use, and not at all in Lyra, which fixes RX dsp_rate at 48 kHz and never changes it. Drop the rational-resampler part; it adds complexity and latency to support rates nobody uses.

refuted.title: Implement the attenuation floor as a noisy-signal mix, not a per-bin magnitude clamp of the DF output
refuted.why:
Checked against nnet.c:584-684 (run_dfhead), nnet.c:686 (setGains_dfhead), nnet.c:1708 (setFloor_nnet) and nnr.c:792.

What the proposal gets right: the floor is a per-bin, per-frame magnitude clamp. When g < gmin, y is rescaled to magnitude gmin*|x_cur| and keeps y's own phase. Only when |y| <= 1e-30 is it replaced by gmin*x. The reference is also misaligned. cur_re/cur_im is the newest frame x_t, while every shipped model has lookahead 1 (nnr_model_*.c headers; nnr.c:216 adds lookahead*hop to the delay). So the output describes frame t-1 but the floor magnitude comes from x_t. That one-frame misalignment is a real, minor defect. It belongs to the earlier proposal, though.

Where the description of current behaviour is wrong:
1. There is no switch between "network output" and "residual with arbitrary phase". The phase always comes from y, above the floor and below it. The magnitude is continuous at the threshold: max(g, gmin) times |x|. The x-phase branch needs |y| <= 1e-30, which essentially never happens with real band noise. The claimed flip-flop is therefore not how the code behaves. At most there is a kink in the gain curve, not a jump.
2. The floor already has "the same spectral shape as the band noise", because its magnitude is exactly gmin*|x|. The proposal lists this as a gain of the mix, but the current code already has it.
3. The literature is misused. Berouti, Schwartz and Makhoul's 1979 spectral floor is exactly a per-bin max() clamp, max(|X|^2 - a|N|^2, b|N|^2). It was introduced to reduce musical noise. So Berouti supports the current design, not the mix. Cappé 1994 explains how decision-directed smoothing in Ephraim-Malah suppresses musical noise. It does not compare clamp floors with noisy-mix floors. The DeepFilterNet citation is real: enhance.py atten_lim_db does compute noisy*lim + enhanced*(1-lim). But it is offered there as a user-level limit, not as a fix for musical noise, and there is no published comparison of it against a gain clamp.

What actually changes with the mix:
- The floor component would carry the true noisy phase instead of y's phase.
- The floor would become a soft knee. With incoherent phases the magnitude is about sqrt(lim^2 + g^2), instead of a hard max().
Neither has shown an audible benefit. y is itself a linear combination of recent noisy frames, so its phase is noise-like, as is the noise's own phase.

The mix also has costs:
- It is not a guaranteed floor. If y is anti-phase with x, the two can cancel below lim*|x|, so the claim that its depth is "exactly the user's floor setting" is false.
- It would have to be reconciled with the existing alpha/knee shaping and attack/release gain smoothing (nnet.c:638-660), which already target frame-to-frame gain fluctuation.

The audible benefit claimed for HF speech and CW is speculative, and the mechanism given for it misdescribes the code. Hence refuted.

The one part worth keeping is to use the lookahead-aligned frame (x_{t-L}, already in the ring buffer) as the floor reference. That is a separate, small fix.

refuted.title: float32 / Core ML partition: put only the normalised core on the ANE; keep cond, DF head and post-processing in f32 on CPU, and rescale the tiny-value thresholds
refuted.why:
The cited code matches the description. nnet.c:43-44 define DF_TINY 1e-30 and COND_TINY 1e-20. run_dfhead (line 632-633) computes ax = sqrt(xr*xr+xi*xi) and does `continue` when ax <= DF_TINY, so the gmax/gmin clamp is skipped and gprev[k] is not updated. run_cond (line 801-802) gates on mag > COND_TINY. nnio.c reads f32 or f64 blobs and widens everything to double (lines 164-194). run_nnet (1562-1570) runs cond, then the core, then dfhead on the raw xre/xim. I did not re-count the 154,176 f32-inexact values, but nothing in the code contradicts that count.

It still fails as an improvement to WDSP, for four reasons.

(a) There is no bug in WDSP. The whole path runs in double, so the "level-dependent silent failure on weak pre-AGC signals" cannot happen there. The hazard only exists in a float32 or FP16 port. No such port exists in WDSP or in the Lyra tree: a grep found no Core ML, mlmodel or nnet code there, only an onnxruntime notices file.

(b) The float32 numerics are wrong for the levels the proposal itself gives. Pre-AGC bin magnitudes of 1e-6 to 1e-4 square to 1e-12 to 1e-8. That is about 26 orders of magnitude above the smallest f32 normal (1.2e-38). In f32, xr*xr only underflows when |xr| is below about 1e-19, roughly -380 dBFS. A real receiver never gets there: the ADC/FFT noise floor is somewhere near 1e-7 to 1e-9. Only exact digital zeros reach it, and those are treated the same way in f32 and f64. The cond path also stays well inside f32 range: s = mag^-0.7 stays within roughly 1e13 even at mag = 1e-19, and pfloor = 1e-9 (create_cond at line 1288) bounds the gain. So point (3), hypotf or a relative threshold, fixes nothing real. "Float32 on CPU is safe" (point 1) is true, but it is ordinary porting hygiene, not an improvement.

(c) The gprev/clamp `continue` only fires for bins at or below 1e-30 in double, which in practice means exactly-zero input, such as start-up or no-signal zeros. Holding gprev through digital silence is arguably intended. Leaving the DF prediction unclamped there is negligible, because it is a small sum of coefficients times the last few frames. This has no audible effect on real HF/VHF signals.

(d) Points (2) and (4) are generic design advice for a hypothetical Core ML/ANE port. Keep FP16 away from raw spectra, partition at the normalised cond output, and validate GRU drift. They are sensible if such a port is ever built, but they change nothing for speech, CW or digital-mode reception in WDSP. The "near-zero CPU" benefit depends on other proposals and was not measured here.

Net: the description of the current code is accurate, but the claimed defect does not happen in WDSP, and the float32 underflow argument is off by many orders of magnitude for realistic signal levels.

refuted.title: Spend Apple Silicon headroom on capacity: default to the larger model and consider an 8 kHz geometry for 200-3000 Hz modes
refuted.why:
Parts of the description check out. In the nnr_model_0.c and nnr_model_1.c headers, slot 0 is chans 16/32/48/64, hid 32, order 5, val_si_sdr 7.674. Slot 1 is chans 24/48/72/96, hid 48, val_si_sdr 8.244. Both use 257 bins. nnet_probe_slot does read `geom` and `band`. The nnr prototype cutoff is 0.45*nrate (nnr.c:149). The load-bearing claims fail, though.

(1) "Default to the larger model" is effectively already there. SetRXANNRModel chooses the slot at runtime (nnr.c:649, 802). Lyra already offers it as a user setting: Lyra/src/wdsp_engine.cpp:3906-3909 nnrSlotFor uses nnrModel_ 0=Standard / 1=Premium, saved as dsp/nnrModel. Changing the default is a one-line host preference, not a WDSP algorithm improvement. The +0.57 dB is also not a clean capacity measurement. The two checkpoints come from different runs (nnr_la1_sw1 at step 64000, nnr_big48_la1 at step 96000), so training length and recipe are confounded with model size. The "well under 1% of a core on the ANE" argument does not apply to this code. nnet.c is portable scalar C in double precision, with no Accelerate/BNNS/CoreML path, so the ANE is never used. A port would be a separate, large project.

(2) The claim that "nnet_probe_slot already reads geom, so no framework change is needed" is false. In calc_nnr (nnr.c:400-416), the first loadable slot sets a single channel-wide nrate, decimation factor and resampler prototype. Any later slot with a different rate is rejected: "model slot %d rejected - it wants %d Hz and the channel resamples to %d" (nnr.c:452-457). A mixed setup, with an 8 kHz SSB/CW model next to 16 kHz models in other slots, cannot coexist in a channel as WDSP stands. The proposal names exactly that setup ("needs separate slots, as the band mechanism already allows"). Supporting it would need per-slot resamplers, or a rebuild of the decimator on every model switch. Lyra switches models automatically on CW and voice mode changes (wdsp_engine.cpp:2652, 3934), so that rebuild would land in a hot path.

(3) Separate CW models already exist. Slots 2 and 3 are CW models with deep-filter order 12 and 24, reaching val SI-SDR 10.8 and 12.0 dB. The DFN-style split proposes extra deep filtering for the CW tone, which the current design already covers with dedicated, higher-order CW models.

The literature cited (DPCRN Interspeech 2021, DeepFilterNet, GTCRN ICASSP 2024) is real. The proposal itself concedes that the gains are a few tenths of a dB and that training data matters more. What is left is a default flip that Lyra users can already make themselves, an 8 kHz geometry that the current framework would reject in mixed-slot use, and a speculative architecture change with no measured benefit.

summary: AM (amd.c xamd mode 0, lines 133-145) is a plain envelope detector, sqrt(I^2+Q^2), with an optional "fade leveler" that swaps the fast-tracked carrier DC (tauR 20 ms) for a slow one (tauI 1.4 s). SAM (mode 1, lines 150-232) is a second-order type-2 PLL. Its NCO counter-rotates the input, an atan2 phase detector runs on the whole correlator output (lines 222-223) with gains g1/g2 from init_amd lines 77-78 (omegaN 250, zeta 1, about 99 Hz loop pole, lock clamped to ±2 kHz). Sideband selection comes from a 7+7-stage polyphase allpass Hilbert pair (lines 160-189); I measured it at roughly 60 dB opposite-sideband rejection from 20 Hz to 23.9 kHz at 48 kHz, in both double and float32. NFM (fmd.c xfmd, lines 206-250) uses the same PLL structure set very wide (omegaN 20000, pole about 7.9 kHz), then a one-pole DC block, then two cascaded 2048-tap linear-phase FIRs (fcimp -6 dB/oct de-emphasis, then a 240-3300 Hz bandpass), a CTCSS notch and an optional limiter. FMSQ uses the 5-20 kHz noise in the pre-de-emphasis audio with absolute thresholds; AMSQ uses a 10 ms average of the pre-demod IQ magnitude; SSQL is a zero-crossing-rate syllabic-modulation detector. WBFM (wbfm.c xwbfm, lines 744-766) is a quadricorrelator plus a fixed DC block. It splits the MPX into 0-15.2k, a 50 Hz-wide 19k pilot (8192 taps) and 22.8-53.2k bands, regenerates 38 kHz by squaring the AGC-normalised pilot, and hard-switches mono/stereo from pilot magnitude only. It then applies a bilinear one-pole de-emphasis and a 58-75 kHz noise-power squelch. The CW matched filter (matchedCW.c build_matched, lines 45-114) is a rectangular-envelope complex tone of length 1.2067*rate/FWHM, so its sinc response has a -6 dB width equal to FWHM. apfshadow.c only routes the APF controls to one of four filter blocks.

kept.title: WBFM: de-emphasis setter never reaches the filters, and the noise-squelch 'Butterworth' bandpass is really two identical resonators
kept.current: (a) SetRXAWBFMdmph only writes a->dmph and a->dmph_type. Each DMPH object gets its run flag and tau (75 or 50 us) once, in create_dmph called from calc_wbfm (627-628), and xdmph (189-205) checks only DMPH->run. calc_wbfm runs again only from setSamplerate_wbfm/setSize_wbfm. So turning de-emphasis off, or switching 75 us to 50 us (Europe), does nothing until a rate or size change. (b) calc_bqs is described as a 4th-order Butterworth 58-75 kHz bandpass. For the 2nd-order prototype, pole_im^2 == pole_re^2, so both sections get a1_a = 0.707*BW and a2_a = W0^2. Both biquads are therefore the same synchronously tuned resonator; the prototype poles are never mapped through the LP-to-BP transform. Evaluated at fs = 384 kHz: peak +6.0 dB at 66.2 kHz, -3 dB band 62.4-70.1 kHz (7.8 kHz instead of 17 kHz), RDS at 57 kHz only 11 dB down. The peak falls on the 67 kHz SCA subcarrier used in the US.
kept.proposed: (a) In the setter, under csDSP, set dmphL->run and dmphR->run, set tau from the type, and call calc_dmph on both (or set a recalc flag that the DSP thread acts on). (b) Do the real transform: each prototype pole p gives the roots of s^2 - p*BW*s + W0^2 = 0; pair conjugate roots into two stagger-tuned biquads, then apply the bilinear transform. A sturdier noise estimator is better still: measure noise power in bands that carry no signal by standard, namely the 15.5-18.5 kHz and 19.5-22.5 kHz guard bands around the pilot (ITU-R BS.450). Optionally add 60-64 kHz and 76-90 kHz when Nyquist allows. Scale each band by the f^2 triangular-noise law and take the minimum, so SCA or RDS energy can never pass for noise.
kept.benefit: (a) This one is clearly audible. The treble difference between 75 us and 50 us de-emphasis is about 3.3 dB at 10 kHz and about 3.6 dB at 15 kHz, so European listeners currently get dull audio and the toggle appears broken. (b) The squelch stops treating 67 kHz SCA or strong RDS as noise, which can close or gain-limit strong stations. Using the guard bands also lets the squelch work at fs < 150 kHz, which the 58-75 kHz band cannot.
kept.risk: The thresholds noise_high_thresh 0.50 and noise_low_thresh 0.15 were tuned by ear against the current filter (marked 'Tune this!', lines 372-373). A correct filter changes gain (-6 dB peak) and noise bandwidth (about 2x), so they must be rescaled. The dmph fix only makes the documented behaviour actually happen.
kept.evidence: Line-level: create_dmph is called only from calc_wbfm; SetRXAWBFMdmph touches no DMPH field. LP-to-BP pole mapping as in Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, sec. 7.1, or Parks & Burrus 1987. I computed the cascade response from the code's own coefficient formulas. FM stereo guard band per ITU-R BS.450-3.

verdict.reasoning:
(a) Confirmed. SetRXAWBFMdmph (wbfm.c:797-807) only writes a->dmph and a->dmph_type under csDSP. The DMPH objects get run and tau only in create_dmph (170-182), and create_dmph is called only from calc_wbfm (627-628). xdmph (189-205) reads only its own DMPH->run and coefficients. calc_wbfm runs again only through setSamplerate_wbfm and setSize_wbfm, which rxa.c calls on a DSP rate change (753) and a size change (817). Mode switches in rxa.c (885/908) only toggle wbfm.p->run. So switching de-emphasis on or off, or from 75 us to 50 us, has no effect until the next rate or size change. Defaults are dmph=1 and type=0 (75 us), so a European user who picks 50 us keeps 75 us. That is about 3.3 dB of extra treble cut at 10 kHz and roughly 3.4-3.6 dB at 15 kHz, which is audible. The fix is simple and low-risk: under csDSP, set run and tau on dmphL and dmphR, then call calc_dmph. Optionally flush the state as well.

(b) Confirmed by computing the response from the code's own formulas. The prototype poles have pole_im^2 == pole_re^2, so the BW^2 term cancels. Both sections get a1_a = 0.707*BW and a2_a = W0^2, so they are identical resonators and no LP-to-BP pole mapping is done. At fs = 384 kHz both sections come out as b = (0.1274, 0, -0.1274), a1 = -0.853, a2 = 0.820. The cascade peaks at +6.02 dB at 66.19 kHz. The -3 dB band is 62.38-70.13 kHz, about 7.75 kHz wide instead of 17 kHz. The response is -11.0 dB at 57 kHz (RDS) and -0.15 dB at 67 kHz (SCA). So this is not the advertised 4th-order Butterworth, and the noise estimate is weighted toward the 67 kHz SCA subcarrier.

The proposed remedies are standard. The LP-to-BP transform gives two stagger-tuned biquads. The noise estimate can instead come from the guard bands around the 19 kHz pilot, scaled by the f^2 law of FM discriminator noise, which is correct. The citations are real and relevant: Oppenheim & Schafer for IIR design and frequency transforms, Parks & Burrus "Digital Filter Design" (1987), and ITU-R BS.450 for the pilot-tone stereo system.

Caveats:
- The squelch thresholds were tuned by ear and are marked "Tune this!", so they must be retuned for any new filter.
- Whether SCA or RDS energy actually trips the squelch on real stations depends on those ad-hoc thresholds. That part of (b) is plausible but not proven.
- WBFM is broadcast reception, not core amateur HF/VHF use, which lowers the overall priority. Within the WBFM feature, (a) is a real, user-visible bug, and the "4th-order Butterworth" in (b) is plainly not one.
verdict.corrected_benefit: (a) The de-emphasis on/off and 75/50 us controls currently do nothing until the next sample-rate or buffer-size change. With the fix they take effect immediately, so 50 us regions get about 3.3-3.5 dB more treble at 10-15 kHz, as intended. (b) The squelch noise detector becomes a real 58-75 kHz bandpass, or a guard-band estimator with f^2 scaling. It would no longer peak at 66 kHz (+6 dB, about 7.8 kHz wide, -0.15 dB at the 67 kHz SCA). That makes the squelch less likely to mistake SCA energy for noise and lets it run at lower sample rates. The squelch thresholds must be retuned, and the real-world gain from (b) is plausible but not measured.

kept.title: APF/matched filter: FFTW_PATIENT replanning while holding the DSP lock, and filter swaps that are neither atomic nor crossfaded
kept.file_function: matchedCW.c:SetRXAMatchedFreqs (255-261), CalcMatchedFilter (221-237), calc_size (30-43); firmin.c:setNc_fircore (465-477), plan_fircore (313-318); apfshadow.c:SetRXASPCWSelection (45-90)
kept.current: SetRXAMatchedFreqs enters ch.csDSP and calls CalcMatchedFilter. That calls setNc_fircore whenever calc_size crosses a power of two, which happens on ordinary APF bandwidth moves: 100 Hz gives 579 taps in nc 1024, 50 Hz gives 1158 in 2048, 25 Hz gives 2317 in 4096. setNc_fircore deplans and replans every partition FFT with FFTW_PATIENT; its own comment (line 467) says this 'will probably cause a glitch'. All of that runs while the DSP thread is blocked on csDSP. Separately, SetRXASPCWSelection switches filters through several independently locked calls (old filter run=0, then new filter configured and run=1), so a buffer can go out with no APF at all, at a different gain (matched and gaussian get sqrt(2)*gain). setImpulse_fircore(update=1) also flips mask sets on the next block with no crossfade.
kept.proposed: Build the replacement filter state, including the FFT plan or vDSP setup for that partition size, off the audio thread. Then publish it with one atomic pointer swap at a block boundary. For one block, run old and new filters together and crossfade linearly. Apply a selection change as one swap, not as disable-then-enable. In LyraDSP, create vDSP DFT setups for every power of two from 1024 to 8192 ahead of time so a resize never plans anything on the real-time path.
kept.benefit: Removes audio dropouts, which last as long as FFTW_PATIENT planning takes (often tens to hundreds of ms), and clicks when dragging APF bandwidth or centre, or changing APF type. The DSP itself is unchanged.
kept.risk: Very low. Memory rises briefly while two filter states coexist. The crossfade adds no latency.
kept.evidence: Line-level: csDSP is held across CalcMatchedFilter (matchedCW.c:258-260); plan_fircore uses FFTW_PATIENT (firmin.c:313-318); the setNc_fircore comment at firmin.c:467. FFTW manual on planner cost: PATIENT/EXHAUSTIVE planning can take seconds for large sizes.

verdict.reasoning:
The code paths are cited correctly. SetRXAMatchedFreqs takes csDSP and calls CalcMatchedFilter (matchedCW.c:255-261), and the DSP thread holds the same lock while it processes (main.c:40-58). calc_size crosses powers of two at the bandwidths the proposal gives, because the matched filter runs at dsp_rate (RXA.c:454), so at 48 kHz: 100 Hz gives nc 1024, 50 Hz gives 2048, 25 Hz gives 4096. setNc_fircore deplans and replans with FFTW_PATIENT, and its comment does warn about a glitch. SetRXASPCWSelection really does switch through separately locked calls: it turns the other filters off, then configures the new one, then turns it on. So one block can go out with no APF.

The headline mechanism is wrong, though. In the partitioned overlap-save core (firmin.c:plan_fircore) every FFT has size 2*size, where size is dsp_size, the block size. nc only changes how many partitions there are (nfor = nc/size). It never changes the FFT length. A resize therefore asks FFTW for the same FFT size the filter has used since it was created. That size is already in FFTW's in-process wisdom, and also in the wisdom WDSPwisdom loads or builds at startup for every power of two up to MAX_WISDOM_SIZE = 262144 (wisdom.c, comm.h:134). With wisdom present, FFTW_PATIENT planning is a fast lookup, not a fresh search. The "tens to hundreds of ms" PATIENT dropout does not happen once wisdom is loaded, and the FFTW manual's warning about planning cost applies only without wisdom. The real cost under the lock is 3*nfor+1 plan lookups, plus mallocs and nfor mask FFTs. That is roughly sub-ms to a few ms, and WDSP's I/O ring buffering usually absorbs it. The proposed LyraDSP fix also misreads the design. Creating vDSP DFT setups for 1024 to 8192 ahead of time targets nc, but nc is not the transform size, and the transform size never changes on an APF resize.

Smaller artifacts the proposal does not identify correctly are still real:
(a) setNc_fircore frees the partition history and allocates it again with malloc0. The convolution then restarts from empty, so for about nc/rate seconds (up to around 85 ms at nc 4096, 48 kHz) the narrow-filter output is missing its earlier input. That gives an audible dip or click on the CW tone when a bandwidth drag crosses a power-of-two boundary.
(b) A type change can send one unfiltered block, and gain jumps by sqrt(2) between filter types.
(c) setImpulse_fircore(update=1) swaps mask sets with no crossfade, as filter changes do elsewhere in WDSP.

All three are short transients on user actions that are rare or happen while dragging. They are not dropouts. Building the new filter state off the lock, carrying the history over or crossfading, and doing selection as one locked switch would be modest polish.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This does not remove long dropouts, because there are none to remove: the FFT size is 2*dsp_size, which does not change, and FFTW wisdom already covers it, so replanning is cheap. What it would remove is small transients. One is the dip or click when an APF bandwidth change crosses a power of two in nc, because setNc_fircore restarts the partition history from zero. Others are the brief unfiltered block and gain step when the APF type changes, and the click when masks swap with no crossfade. For LyraDSP the useful lesson is to keep the partition history and swap state atomically. Pre-planning FFTs for 1024 to 8192 is unnecessary, because the transform length does not depend on nc.

kept.title: SAM PLL: arm-filtered, sideband-aware phase detector with carrier-fade flywheel and FFT-aided acquisition
kept.current: The phase detector is det = atan2(corr[1], corr[0]), where corr is the unfiltered counter-rotated input (lines 191-192, 222-223). Everything in the passband, including the sideband that sbmode 1/2 discards, goes through the atan2 nonlinearity before the loop filter. In LSB/USB mode the adjacent-channel interference that made the user pick one sideband still drives the PLL. In a selective-fading carrier null, atan2 stays amplitude-independent, so the loop is steered by sideband noise. Pull-in from a large offset relies on the type-2 loop alone: about T_p = dw^2/(2*zeta*wn^3), which is about 0.3 s at 500 Hz, 2.8 s at 1500 Hz and 5 s at 2000 Hz.
kept.proposed: (1) Add Costas-style arm filters: a 1st- or 2nd-order low-pass at about 150-300 Hz on corr[0] and corr[1] for the PLL path only (audio still uses the unfiltered corr). The phase detector then sees the carrier ±fc, not the full DSB. (2) Add a lock/fade detector: compare |LPF(corr)| with a slow average. When it falls more than about 12-15 dB, hold the omega integrator and drop the g1 term (flywheel on omega) until the carrier returns. (3) For acquisition: when the lock detector reports unlocked, run one short FFT (for example 4096 points at 48 kHz, about 12 Hz bins, with interpolated-peak refinement) over ±fmax, preset omega to the strongest carrier, then let the loop pull in.
kept.benefit: Moderate. Under selective fading, and with a strong adjacent signal on the rejected sideband, SAM has less flutter and fewer phase slips; this is where SAM is most often criticised. Lock is near-instant when the user tunes several hundred Hz off a carrier, instead of seconds. No effect on clean, strong signals.
kept.risk: Each arm-filter pole adds phase lag inside the loop. With the 99 Hz loop pole, a 300 Hz one-pole costs about 18 degrees of the roughly 76 degree margin, so keep the arm corner at least 3x the loop bandwidth or retune omegaN and zeta. The flywheel can hold a wrong frequency if the carrier truly moves during a fade, so cap hold time at about 0.5-1 s. FFT acquisition can lock onto an adjacent carrier, so restrict the search to the passband.
kept.evidence: Costas, 'Synchronous communications', Proc. IRE 1956 (arm filters). Gardner, Phaselock Techniques, 3rd ed. 2005 (pull-in time formula, lock detectors). Rife & Boorstyn, IEEE Trans. IT 1974 (FFT frequency estimation). Pull-in times computed from amd defaults (omegaN 250, zeta 1).

verdict.reasoning:
Code check (amd.c xamd, case 1): corr[0] = ai + bq and corr[1] = -bi + aq are formed from the unfiltered counter-rotated input. det = atan2(corr[1], corr[0]) (lines ~222-223) is fed straight into the type-2 loop (fil_out = g1*det + omega, omega += g2*det, clamped to omega_min/max). The sbmode 1/2 sideband selection only touches the audio path, using the ai_ps/bi_ps/aq_ps/bq_ps all-pass network, never the PLL. RXA.c xrxa runs nbp0 (the user's RX filter) before xamd, so whatever that filter passes reaches the phase detector, including the rejected sideband and any interferer in it. There is no lock detector, fade hold, carrier-amplitude check or acquisition aid in amd.c. fmd.c's PLL also uses bare atan2. WDSP therefore does not already do any of this.

Defaults (RXA.c create_amd): omegaN 250, zeta 1, fmin/fmax ±2000 Hz. Expanding g1 and g2 gives K1 ≈ 2*zeta*wn and K2 ≈ wn^2, a standard 2nd-order loop with wn = 250 rad/s. Gardner's sinusoidal-PD formula then gives 0.32 s at 500 Hz, 2.8 s at 1500 Hz and 5.1 s at 2000 Hz, matching the proposal. Caveat: atan2 is a sawtooth detector, which pulls in somewhat faster than the sinusoidal formula predicts. The numbers are order-of-magnitude right but overstated.

Algorithmic merit: atan2 behaves like a bandpass limiter. When the in-band sidebands, noise or an interferer are comparable to or stronger than the carrier inside the ~5-10 kHz pre-detection bandwidth, the detector suffers limiter suppression and capture. Effective loop gain drops, and at negative pre-detection SNR you get phase wraps and cycle slips. The loop filter cannot undo that, because it sits after the nonlinearity. Narrowing the pre-detection bandwidth to a few hundred Hz improves detector SNR by roughly 10*log10(10k/300) ≈ 15 dB, which is the classical justification for arm or pre-limiter filtering. A flywheel or hold on omega during carrier nulls is a standard and sound enhancement for selective fading. An FFT coarse estimate with interpolated peak, then handoff to the PLL, is standard acquisition practice. None of these add audio latency, because they live only on the PLL path.

The citations are real and relevant: Costas, Proc. IRE Dec 1956; Gardner, Phaselock Techniques 3rd ed., Wiley 2005; Rife & Boorstyn, IEEE Trans. IT 1974.

Weaknesses that reduce, but do not refute, the claim:
(a) A 150-300 Hz arm filter shrinks the effective pull-in range. A carrier 500-2000 Hz off is attenuated and phase-shifted by the arm filter, so without part (3), or bypassing the arm filter while unlocked, pull-in gets worse, not better. The parts are interdependent, and the risk section does not mention this.
(b) The adjacent-interferer benefit applies only when the interferer is comparable to or stronger than the carrier. A weaker interferer at kHz offset is already rejected by the roughly 80 Hz closed-loop bandwidth.
(c) In normal use, broadcast and AM carriers usually sit within a few Hz of the channel, so large-offset acquisition matters mainly while hand-tuning.
(d) The phase-lag estimate is roughly right: 1-pole at 300 Hz against a ~80 Hz crossover costs about 15 degrees. A 2nd-order arm filter would need more care.
Net: the description is accurate and the improvement is genuine for weak, fading and interfered AM/SAM reception. Benefit is moderate and confined to SAM.
verdict.corrected_benefit: For SAM only, with no audio latency added: (1) Arm-filtering the PLL path before the atan2 detector raises detector SNR by roughly 10-15 dB. That cuts cycle slips and flutter at low SNR, during selective-fading carrier dips, and when an interferer in the passband (for example on the rejected sideband) is comparable to or stronger than the carrier. (2) Holding omega while the carrier is in a fade, with a capped hold time, reduces phase wander through nulls. (3) FFT-aided coarse acquisition cuts pull-in from large offsets (about 0.3 s at 500 Hz to a few seconds at 1.5-2 kHz; somewhat less in practice, because atan2 is a sawtooth detector) to near-instant. Part (3), or bypassing the arm filter while unlocked, is required, not optional: the narrow arm filter on its own would shrink the pull-in range. Clean, strong, on-frequency signals see no meaningful change.

kept.title: WBFM: SNR-driven stereo blend with sample-accurate crossfades, and PLL pilot recovery in place of the 8192-tap pilot filter
kept.current: Stereo is a hard switch. mx() picks L=R=LpR or full L±R per buffer, with no crossfade, based only on pilot magnitude hysteresis (0.06 on / 0.03 off, 0.5 s / 1 s frame counts). A weak station with a pilot gets full stereo and its roughly 20 dB worse noise. The squelch gain changes once per buffer (slew = size/(0.05*rate), line 374) and is applied as a constant over the buffer, giving a staircase of about 10% amplitude steps. The 38 kHz reference is the square of a 50 Hz-wide, 8192-tap, AGC-normalised pilot. To align with it, L+R and L-R go through delay lines of agc_delay + 2048 samples (668-673).
kept.proposed: (a) Blend: L = M + g*S, R = M - g*S, where g comes from the pwrNoise that nopwrRun already computes (after the correction in the first proposal). Map it through a soft curve, for example full stereo above one noise level and mono below another 10-15 dB worse, smooth it with tau about 0.1-0.3 s per sample, and optionally add a treble cut at very low SNR. Keep the pilot gate. (b) Ramp sqgain and g linearly per sample between buffer values. (c) Pilot: replace fil19, pAGC_Pilot and the squaring with a narrow 2nd-order PLL at 19 kHz on disc_out (loop bandwidth about 5-10 Hz). Its NCO gives a unit-amplitude coherent sin(2*theta) for 38 kHz, and its in-phase arm gives a lock/pilot-level indicator to replace xindy.
kept.benefit: Weak stations fade smoothly toward mono instead of flipping into hiss, and there are no clicks on the mono/stereo transition or squelch ramps: a clear subjective gain on fringe reception. The pilot PLL removes 2048 + agc_delay samples of latency (about 14.7 ms at 192 kHz, 9.3 ms at 384 kHz) and the largest FIR, 8192 of the 16384 complex taps in the WBFM filter stage. Separation is insensitive to the PLL's phase error (5 degrees still gives about 54 dB). Any noise benefit from the cleaner 38 kHz carrier is marginal.
kept.risk: Blend thresholds are subjective and need listening tests. The PLL needs a reliable lock detector and must acquire within about 100 ms after tuning. Users who want forced stereo need an override.
kept.evidence: Stereo multiplex SNR penalty of about 20-23 dB versus mono: Couch, Digital and Analog Communication Systems, FM stereo section, and standard broadcast references.
