Pilot PLL recovery as in Best, Phase-Locked Loops, 6th ed. 2007, and Gardner 2005. Separation formula (1+cos phi)/(1-cos phi). Latency from calc_wbfm lines 635 and 668-671.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the description of the current code against wbfm.c and it is accurate. mx() (556-570) hard-switches each buffer between L=R=LpR and full L±R. There is no crossfade and no partial separation. The only input to that switch is xindy's pilot magnitude: 0.06 on / 0.03 off, with on_delay of 0.5 s and off_delay of 1.0 s converted to frame counts (lines 72-75). In xwbsquelch, slew = size/(0.05*rate) (line 374). The gain steps once per buffer and mx applies it as a constant across the buffer. At size 1024 and 192 kHz that is about a 0.107 step every 5.3 ms, so the claimed staircase of roughly 10% steps is correct. The 38 kHz reference is the square of the fil19 output: 8192 taps, 18975-19025 Hz, normalised by pAGC_Pilot (dsb_demod). The delay lines are agc_delay + (8192-4096)/2. agc_delay = ceil(rate*4*0.001) is 768 at 192k, giving 2816 samples (14.7 ms); at 384k it gives 3584 samples (9.3 ms). The taps are 4096+8192+4096 = 16384, so the fil19 share is right. The separation figure checks out: (1+cos5°)/(1-cos5°) ≈ 524, about 54 dB. Nothing in WDSP already blends stereo. A grep finds stereo handling only in wbfm.c, and there is no forced-mono or blend setter.

The method is sound and conventional. SNR-driven stereo blend, plus high-cut at low SNR, is standard in commercial FM receivers. The 20+ dB multiplex noise penalty is textbook. Today a weak station with a detectable pilot plays in full stereo until noise crosses the squelch's 0.5 threshold, and xindy's 4 Hz detector keeps detecting the pilot well into the hissy region, so the hiss problem is real. Ramping sqgain per sample is a trivial and correct fix for zipper steps. The hard L-R switch can click when the program has a lot of L-R content, although the hysteresis keeps switching rare.

I have four reservations.
1. The proposed noise metric is flawed for this use. nopwr measures 58-75 kHz on disc_out (calc_bqs 58000-75000). That band overlaps the RDS sidebands (57 ± 2.4 kHz, inside the 4th-order skirt) and the common US 67 kHz SCA subcarrier. Strong stations carrying SCA or RDS would read as noisy and be blended toward mono. A cleaner estimator already exists in the code: the quadrature (imag) output of dsb_demod. The L-R DSB carries no signal in that arm, so it holds only noise within the 23-53 kHz band, which is exactly the noise that stereo adds.
2. Part (c), the PLL, is the weakest piece. The current filter-and-square method cannot false-lock, needs no acquisition logic, and already works. The saving of about 15 ms is irrelevant for broadcast listening. The CPU saving, one FFT-convolved FIR, is modest. Replacing it brings in lock detection, acquisition time and false-lock risk for a 'marginal' noise benefit, which the proposal itself admits.
3. The blend depends on a correction from a separate proposal that I have not verified.
4. WBFM is broadcast reception, not a core amateur mode (speech, CW or digital), which limits the priority. Blend thresholds are subjective and need listening tests.

Citations: Couch's FM stereo noise analysis and Best's Phase-Locked Loops (6th ed. 2007) are real and relevant. 'Gardner 2005' (Phaselock Techniques, 3rd ed.) is real.
verdict.corrected_benefit: An SNR-driven stereo blend, with an optional high-cut, would let weak broadcast FM stations fade smoothly toward mono instead of staying in full stereo with about 20 dB more hiss until squelch. Ramping the squelch gain and blend factor per sample removes the 5 ms, roughly 10% zipper steps. The noise estimate driving the blend should be the quadrature arm of the 38 kHz demodulator, or a band free of RDS and SCA, not the existing 58-75 kHz nopwr band. Replacing the pilot filter with a PLL is optional. It saves about 15 ms and one large FIR, which is of little practical value, and adds lock and acquisition risk. The whole proposal applies only to WBFM broadcast reception, not to amateur modes.

kept.title: NFM: merge the cascaded de-emphasis and audio-bandpass FIRs into one design to halve their latency
kept.file_function: fmd.c:create_fmd (166-179), xfmd (235-238), setSamplerate_fmd/setSize_fmd/SetRXAFMAFFilter; RXA.c:212-215 (nc_de, mp_de, nc_aud, mp_aud defaults)
kept.current: xfmd runs two convolutions in series: pde, the fcimp -6 dB/oct de-emphasis with nc_de = max(2048, size) and mp_de = 0, then paud, the fir_bandpass 0.8*f_low to 1.1*f_high with nc_aud = 2048 and mp_aud = 0. Both default to linear phase, so each adds (N-1)/2 = 1023.5 samples: about 42.6 ms of group delay at 48 kHz, plus two partitioned FFT convolutions. Minimum-phase options already exist for each FIR (mp flags).
kept.proposed: Make one impulse from the product response A(f) = D(f)*B(f) with WDSP's existing frequency-sampling routine (fsamp_exec, which eq_impulse and fcimp already use), and run one 2048-tap fircore. The length is set by the 240 Hz low band edge; the de-emphasis slope is smooth and needs no extra taps. Keep the mp flag so users can still choose minimum phase. Rebuild on SetRXAFMAFFilter, rate changes and size changes, as is done now.
kept.benefit: About 21 ms less NFM audio latency in linear-phase mode, half the FIR compute, and the same magnitude response within design error. Most useful for repeater and duplex work and for keeping audio aligned with the panadapter.
kept.risk: Low. The CTCSS notch, limiter and squelch are unchanged. FMSQ currently gets incidental lookahead because its trigger, fmd->audio, skips about 2048 samples of audio-path delay. Halving that delay to about 1024 samples reduces the lookahead, so check the squelch-tail noise burst.
kept.evidence: Linear-phase FIR group delay (N-1)/2 and frequency-sampling design: Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., ch. 5 and 7. Defaults from RXA.c lines 212-215.

verdict.reasoning:
The proposal mostly describes the code correctly. In fmd.c, xfmd runs xfircore(pde) and then xfircore(paud) in series. pde is built from build_fcimp/exec_fcimp with curve=1 (de-emphasis); its taps go through fsamp_exec with linear-phase sampling, d=(N-1)/2. paud comes from fir_bandpass(nc_aud, 0.8*f_low, 1.1*f_high, ...). The RXA.c defaults at about lines 212-215 set both mp flags to 0. With linear phase, each stage delays the audio by (N-1)/2, about 1023.5 samples, so the cascade adds about 2047 samples, roughly 42.6 ms at 48 kHz. Merging the two is a valid DSP step. In fsamp_exec, A is real and the linear-phase term is applied inside, so a product magnitude D(f)*B(f) can be sampled directly. The cascade's band edges are already limited by paud's 2048 taps, so one 2048-tap design gives essentially the same magnitude and half the group delay. I can't find this done anywhere else in WDSP; emph.c is a separate TX/RX emphasis block.

Inaccuracies and things the proposal leaves out:
(1) nc_aud is max(2048, dsp_size), not a fixed 2048. The same holds for nc_de.
(2) The de-emphasis is not a bare -6 dB/oct curve. exec_fcimp is called with ctfmode=0, which already adds 4th-order (24 dB/oct) skirts below f_low and above f_high. The merge is still easy, because the bandpass already sets the edges.
(3) The two FIRs carry separate scale factors: 1/(2*size) and afgain/(2*size). A combined design must apply one scale of afgain/(2*size), not their product.
(4) The FMSQ risk is understated. FMSQ's trigger is fmd->audio, and FMSQ runs its own linear-phase 2048-tap noise filter (RXA.c, about line 238), which delays detection by about 1024 samples. Today's real lookahead is therefore about 2047 - 1023.5, roughly 1024 samples (about 21 ms), not 2048. After the merge it drops to about 0. The squelch then closes about 1 ms (avtau) plus the 10 ms tdown ramp after the noise reaches the output, which may leave a short click or noise burst at squelch close. That can be fixed by also making the noise filter minimum phase, or by matching delays, but it has to be checked.
(5) Users who need low latency already have a bigger tool: SetRXAFMMPde and SetRXAFMMPaud switch both stages to minimum phase, which removes most of the 42 ms. Linear phase has no audible benefit for NFM speech.

The cited literature is real and relevant: Oppenheim & Schafer cover linear-phase group delay and frequency-sampling design. The improvement is real and costs nothing in magnitude response, but it is incremental, since the minimum-phase options already exist. NFM latency matters only moderately for amateur work.
verdict.corrected_benefit: If the de-emphasis response (with fcimp's ctfmode=0 skirts) and the 0.8*f_low to 1.1*f_high bandpass are combined into one frequency-sampled impulse, one linear-phase fircore of max(2048, dsp_size) taps can replace two. That cuts the default NFM demodulator's added group delay from about 2047 to about 1023.5 samples, about 21 ms less at 48 kHz. It also halves this stage's FIR convolution cost, and the magnitude response stays the same to within window and design error. The scale has to become a single afgain/(2*size). It also removes FMSQ's roughly 21 ms of incidental lookahead, because the squelch's own 2048-tap noise filter already absorbs half of the current delay. Squelch-close behaviour needs testing, or the FMSQ noise filter can be made minimum phase. Setting the existing mp flags (SetRXAFMMPde and SetRXAFMMPaud) already gives larger latency savings, so this mainly improves the linear-phase default.

kept.title: Squelch decisions: make FMSQ deviation-independent, fix SSQL's rate-dependent window, and consider an SPP-based voice squelch
kept.file_function: fmsq.c:xfmsq (150-204) with fmd.c:xfmd (232) and SetRXAFMDeviation (323-331); ssql.c:calc_ssql (139), setSamplerate_ssql (310-315), xftov (70-107), xssql (230-300)
kept.current: FMSQ's trigger is fmd->audio = again*(fil_out - fmdc) with again = rate/(2*pi*deviation) (fmd.c:102, 232). Its 1 ms noise average is compared with absolute thresholds 0.750/0.562 (RXA.c:233-234). Changing deviation from 5 kHz to 2.5 kHz doubles the measured noise at the same RF SNR, moving the squelch opening point by about 6 dB. SSQL counts zero crossings in a ring of rsize = 2400 samples (RXA.c:536). setSamplerate_ssql rebuilds the FTOV with the same rsize, so the window is 50 ms at 48 kHz but 12.5 ms at 192 kHz: the div normalisation follows, but the variance and the time behaviour that WU2O tuned do not. The detector looks for syllabic-rate change in zero-crossing rate (11.3 Hz low-pass, compared with a 0.5 s average) and uses an absolute amplitude gate, eps = 0.01.
kept.proposed: (1) FMSQ: measure noise on fil_out in rad/sample, before again, or divide avnoise by again, so the threshold is in deviation-independent units. (2) SSQL: set rsize = round(0.05*rate) in calc_ssql. (3) Optional SSB voice squelch: decide on a speech-presence probability averaged over the 300-3000 Hz bins and smoothed at syllabic rate (about 4 Hz), with hysteresis. When EMNR is running it already computes the per-bin Gerkmann-Hendriks SPP (nps.PH1y, emnr.c:810), so reuse it. Standalone, use a Sohn/Kim/Sung likelihood-ratio VAD on a 256-point STFT with minimum-statistics noise tracking. A small neural VAD through Core ML is a third option.
kept.benefit: (1) and (2) are deterministic fixes: the same squelch setting behaves the same at any deviation or DSP rate. (3) gives a noise-adaptive, level-independent detector; expect fewer false opens on noise bursts and faster, more consistent opening at low SNR. That size of gain is plausible but unproven against WU2O's tuning, so A/B it on real HF SSB.
kept.risk: (1) changes the meaning of the user's existing FM squelch slider, so rescale it so 5 kHz deviation behaves as before. (3) adds an STFT unless EMNR is on, and may open on music or data signals.
kept.evidence: Line-level for (1) and (2). Gerkmann & Hendriks, IEEE TASLP 2012 (unbiased MMSE noise estimation with SPP). Sohn, Kim & Sung, IEEE SPL 1999 (statistical-model VAD). Martin, IEEE TSAP 2001 (minimum statistics).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked each part against the WDSP 2.11 source.

(1) FMSQ. The description is accurate. fmd.c:102 and SetRXAFMDeviation (fmd.c:328) both set again = rate/(2*pi*deviation). fmd.c:232 writes audio = again*(fil_out - fmdc). RXA.c:224 passes getFMDpAudio() as the FMSQ trigger, so the squelch sees the audio before de-emphasis (pde reads audio and writes to out). In xfmsq, the 5 kHz and up noise filter and the 1 ms average are compared with absolute thresholds. The defaults are 0.750/0.562. SetRXAFMSQThreshold sets tail = thr and unmute = 0.9*thr. Halving the deviation doubles the noise amplitude, which is about 6 dB of CNR above the FM threshold.

Calling this a bug "fixed deterministically" overstates it, for two reasons:
- Measuring noise in units of full-scale deviation means the squelch opens at roughly constant output audio SNR (SINAD). A 2.5 kHz NFM signal really does have about 6 dB worse audio SNR at the same CNR, so the current behaviour is a defensible design choice.
- The user already compensates with the threshold slider.

Making it deviation-independent is a semantic change, not a correction.

(2) SSQL. The description is accurate. RXA.c:536 hard-codes rsize = 2400. setSamplerate_ssql calls calc_ssql, which rebuilds the FTOV with the same ftov_rsize. The ring is therefore 50 ms at 48 kHz and 12.5 ms at 192 kHz. div is renormalised, so the mean output stays the same. The variance does not. A 12.5 ms boxcar has an equivalent noise bandwidth (ENBW) of about 40 Hz against about 10 Hz for 50 ms. After the fixed 11.3 Hz low-pass, the combined ENBW rises from about 7 Hz to about 12 Hz. That is roughly 30% more standard deviation in lpbuff against the fixed wthresh = 0.08, which means more false opens at high DSP rates.

The proposal misses a second rate dependence. The eps = 0.01 gate is applied to the sample-to-sample difference, and near a zero crossing that difference scales as 2*pi*f*A/rate. At 192 kHz it rejects four times more crossings. A complete fix should also scale eps by 48000/rate, or gate on amplitude instead.

The practical impact is limited, because most RX DSP rates in Thetis and Lyra builds are 48 kHz. Still, the fix rsize = round(0.05*rate) is cheap and correct.

(3) SPP/VAD voice squelch. The citations are real and relevant:
- Gerkmann & Hendriks, IEEE TASLP 2012
- Sohn, Kim & Sung, IEEE SPL 1999
- Martin, IEEE TSAP 2001

Reusing the EMNR SPP is feasible: emnr.c:810 computes PH1y per bin, and xssql runs after xemnr in xrxa. The claimed gains on HF SSB are speculative. HF noise (QRN, fading, heterodynes, impulsive noise) is non-stationary, and statistical VADs are known to degrade there. They also open on music, data and carriers. WU2O's syllabic zero-crossing detector was chosen specifically to be level-independent and robust in that environment. This part needs A/B evidence before it carries any weight.

Overall: the current-behaviour claims are correct. Item (2) is a small real fix. Item (1) is a design trade-off described as a bug. Item (3) is unproven.
verdict.corrected_benefit: SSQL: tie the FTOV ring to time with rsize = round(0.05*rate), and scale or replace the sample-difference gate eps (it is also rate-dependent). The syllabic squelch then behaves the same at 48, 96 and 192 kHz DSP rates. It is a small, real consistency fix that only matters when the RX DSP rate is not 48 kHz. FMSQ: normalising noise by again makes the threshold track RF CNR rather than post-detection audio SNR. That is a matter of preference, not a bug fix. The current design arguably holds SINAD constant across deviations, and it changes the meaning of the user's slider. A speech-presence-probability (SPP) squelch built on EMNR's PH1y is feasible because of the processing order, but whether it beats SSQL on real HF SSB is unproven.

kept.title: CW matched filter: match a shaped keying envelope instead of a rectangle
kept.current: The template is a constant-amplitude complex tone (coef = 1.0, line 60) of length ncoef = 1.2067*rate/FWHM, which is matched to a hard-keyed rectangular element. Its |sinc| response has a -13 dB first sidelobe and falls off at only -6 dB/octave. Real transmitters use shaped keying with roughly 4-8 ms raised-cosine edges.
kept.proposed: Use rect(T) convolved with a raised-cosine edge of rise time tau (default about 5 ms, user-adjustable) as the template, and keep T chosen so the -6 dB width still equals FWHM; at tau << T, T barely changes. This is the matched filter for a shaped element. A further step is to link FWHM to the WPM setting (dot = 1.2/WPM s), so 'matched' really matches the operator's dot length.
kept.benefit: Measured with T = 48 ms (FWHM 26 Hz, unchanged) and tau = 5 ms at 48 kHz, as the response envelope relative to peak: 200 Hz -29.5 to -35.4 dB, 300 Hz -33.3 to -47.7 dB, 500 Hz -37.6 to -69.3 dB, 1 kHz -43.7 to -109.5 dB. A hard-keyed signal loses only 0.04 dB of SNR. In practice strong CW signals a few hundred Hz away stop leaking through the sinc skirts, a clear gain for contest and pileup copy.
kept.risk: The impulse grows by tau*rate samples (about 240), adding about 2.5 ms of group delay and occasionally crossing a power-of-two nc. Ringing on very fast hard-keyed CW is essentially unchanged.
kept.evidence: Matched filter theory: North 1943 and Turin, IRE Trans. IT 1960. Window sidelobe and roll-off behaviour: Harris, Proc. IEEE 1978. Response and mismatch-loss figures computed directly from rect and rect-convolved-with-raised-cosine templates at 48 kHz.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is correct. In matchedCW.c, build_matched uses a constant coef = 1.0 (line 60) over ncoef = round(1.2067*rate/fwhm) taps (lines 55-56), and calc_size (30-43) rounds that up to a power of two with a minimum of 1024. 1.2067/T is the half-amplitude (-6 dB) full width of |sinc|, so "FWHM" here really is the -6 dB width. The template is the rect-matched filter, which has a -13 dB first sidelobe and falls off at -6 dB/octave. Nowhere in WDSP is there a shaped-edge matched template. The nearest relative is gaussian.c, a separate CW peaking filter with no sidelobes but more mismatch loss against a keyed element. It is a different trade-off, not the same feature, so the proposal is not already implemented.

Checking the numbers analytically: rect at T = 48 ms gives -29.6 dB at 200 Hz and -37.5 dB at 500 Hz. The 5 ms raised-cosine (Hann) edge multiplies by sinc(f*tau)/(1-(f*tau)^2). That adds 6.0 dB at 200 Hz, about 15 dB at 300 Hz and about 32 dB at 500 Hz, which matches the claimed -35.4, -47.7 and -69.3 dB. The 1 kHz figure of -109.5 dB is overstated: f*tau = 5 lands exactly on a Hann null, and the true envelope there is about -95 dB. The mismatch loss of roughly 0.04 dB and the added group delay of about 2.5 ms (240 taps on a centred, linear-phase filter) are plausible. The citations are real and relevant: North 1943 (RCA report), Turin's IRE Trans. IT 1960 matched-filter tutorial, and Harris, Proc. IEEE 1978.

The practical benefit is overstated, though. In RXA.c the matched filter runs at the very end of the chain: after nbp0 (the main Blackman-Harris-windowed RX bandpass, run before demodulation), after bp1 and after the AGC (xwcpagc). A strong CW signal "a few hundred Hz away" is normally already outside the operator's CW passband (typically 100-500 Hz wide) and has been removed by nbp0 to well beyond 100 dB. The sinc-skirt improvement only counts for interferers inside the main passband. In that range the gain is modest: about 1.4 dB at 100 Hz, about 3.3 dB at 150 Hz and about 6 dB at 200 Hz offset. The large gains at 300 Hz to 1 kHz only apply if someone runs a wide (>=600 Hz) main filter together with a 26 Hz matched filter, which is unusual. An in-passband strong signal has also already captured the AGC upstream, and the matched filter cannot undo that. The WPM-linked FWHM idea is a host/UI matter; WDSP's RX path has no WPM parameter.

Net result: the code claim and the math are sound and the change is cheap and low-risk, but the operational payoff is a few dB of in-passband skirt improvement, not the contest/pileup fix the proposal describes. The low-sidelobe need is already partly covered by the Gaussian filter.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Replacing the rect template with rect convolved with a short raised-cosine edge keeps the matched filter's near-zero mismatch loss (about 0.04 dB against a hard-keyed element) and cuts its sinc sidelobes. In practice that matters only for interferers inside the main nbp0 passband, because the matched filter runs after nbp0 and the AGC. There the improvement is about 1-3 dB at 100-150 Hz offset and about 6 dB at 200 Hz. The 15-60+ dB gains at 300 Hz to 1 kHz are mostly redundant with the main Blackman-Harris RX filter at normal CW widths, and the 1 kHz figure is overstated (about -95 dB, not -109.5). The cost is about 2.5 ms of added delay. It is a modest refinement that sits between the existing rect-matched and Gaussian filters, not a significant pileup or contest improvement.

refuted.title: Float32 hazards in the scalar PLL and leaky-integrator state (SAM, NFM PLL, fade leveler)
refuted.why:
The "current behaviour" in the proposal does not describe WDSP 2.11. Every quantity it names is already double. In amd.c the parameters and state, including phs, omega, fil_out, g1, g2, dc, dc_insert, mtauR and mtauI, are all double, and init_amd uses double exp and cos (lines 77-78). The fmd struct declares phs, omega, fil_out, g1, g2, fmdc, mtau and onem_mtau as double (fmd.c:30-60). xfmd uses double det and corr, and xfmsq uses double noise for avnoise and longnoise. comm.h:141 makes complex a double[2]. So "keep the scalar PLL and leveler state in double" is exactly what WDSP already does. The proposal itself says "In double, every one of these is harmless." The float32 hazards only appear in a hypothetical float32 port. I found none in the Lyra repo: no grep hits for omegaN, fil_out, dc_insert or g2*det.

I recomputed g1 = 0.0103626 and g2 = 2.6986e-5 for omegaN 250, zeta 1 and 48 kHz, and they match. The cancellation is real but costs nothing in double: about 13 significant digits remain.

The zeta > 1 NaN cannot happen. RXA.c:182 and :207 hard-code zeta = 1.0 for both AMD and FMD, no setter for zeta exists anywhere in the source, and sqrt(1 - 1) = 0. The fmd.c:45 comment already documents the limit.

The leaky-integrator bias of about 0.1-0.4% is a float32-only effect. In double, with a 1/(1-a) amplification of about 6.7e4, it is around 1e-11. It is also inaudible either way, because a level offset is not an audible artefact.

Setting FPCR.FZ is unrelated to correctness here. It is about denormal performance, and nothing shows a problem with it.

The cited literature (Higham on expm1 and cancellation, the Arm ARM on FPCR.FZ) is real but irrelevant to WDSP as written. At most this is a porting caution: "don't downcast these scalar recurrences to Float in a Swift port". It is not an improvement to WDSP's algorithms.

summary: Almost every FIR filter in WDSP (bandpass, nbp, eqp, cfir/icfir, doublepole) runs through fircore (firmin.c:290-440). fircore is uniformly partitioned overlap-save: the partition size equals the I/O block, the FFT is 2*size, there is a frequency-domain delay line of past input spectra (fftout ring, idxmask = nfor-1), and two mask sets (fmask[0/1]) are switched by cset under a critical section. Filter design is a windowed sinc. fir_bandpass (fir.c:215-314) uses only a 4-term or 7-term Blackman-Harris window (wintype 2 falls through to the 7-term default) and is cached in a hash-keyed LRU. EQ and CIC compensation use frequency sampling (fsamp_exec, fir.c:653-681, a c2r FFT followed by a BH4/BH7/Kaiser beta=8 window). Minimum phase is cepstral: log|H| on a grid zero-padded by pfactor (16 or 4), then a Hilbert transform via analytic(), with log(1e-300) as the floor (fir.c:385-466, 561-597). Notches in nbp are made by splitting the passband into sub-bands (make_nbp) and summing windowed-sinc bandpasses (fir_mbandpass). The IIR blocks in iir.c are Direct Form I biquads and one-pole filters in double, with RBJ-style designs.

kept.title: SetRXAmpeakNpeaks changes npeaks without reallocating: out-of-bounds read/crash
kept.current: create_mpeak allocates enable/f/bw/gain/pfil with exactly a->npeaks entries (lines 405-413) and calc_mpeak creates npeaks SPEAK objects. SetRXAmpeakNpeaks only does `a->npeaks = npeaks;` under cs_update. xmpeak then loops `for (i = 0; i < a->npeaks; i++) if (a->enable[i]) xspeak(a->pfil[i])`.
kept.proposed: Treat npeaks as a structural change. Take the lock, call decalc_mpeak with the old count, reallocate enable/f/bw/gain/pfil at the new size (copy the old values and default the new ones), then call calc_mpeak. Alternatively, allocate a fixed maximum in create and clamp npeaks to it.
kept.benefit: Prevents a crash or heap corruption. Raising npeaks above the created count (default 2, RXA.c:500-511) dereferences pfil[i] beyond the array. Lowering it and then destroying leaks the SPEAK objects past the new count, because decalc_mpeak only frees i < npeaks.
kept.risk: None functionally. The reallocation must not happen while xmpeak runs, and the existing cs_update lock covers that.
kept.evidence: Line-level: arrays are sized by npeaks at create time (405-413), the setter mutates npeaks without resizing (503), and xmpeak indexes enable[i]/pfil[i] up to the new npeaks (445-449).

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the code is accurate. In iir.c, create_mpeak (395-417) sizes enable, f, bw, gain and pfil to exactly npeaks, and calc_mpeak builds npeaks SPEAK objects. SetRXAmpeakNpeaks (499-505) only sets a->npeaks under cs_update and does not reallocate or rebuild anything. xmpeak, flush_mpeak and decalc_mpeak all loop to the current a->npeaks.

If npeaks is raised above the created count, the code reads past the end of enable[] and pfil[], then calls xspeak on a garbage pointer. That is undefined behaviour and very likely a crash.

If npeaks is lowered, decalc_mpeak (called by destroy, setBuffers, setSize and setSamplerate) frees only the first npeaks filters, so the rest leak. Each later decalc/calc cycle builds only the smaller count, so no further objects leak, but the pfil slots past the new count keep dangling pointers. Raising npeaks again afterwards would then call xspeak on freed memory.

RXA.c (495-511) always creates mpeak with 2 filters, the RTTY mark/space pair at 2125/2295 Hz.

The bug is real but latent. Nothing in WDSP calls SetRXAmpeakNpeaks; it is only exported (wdsp.h:602). The Lyra tree does not call it either: a grep finds only an mpeakRun flag in src/dsp/coach. The fault therefore only happens if a host application calls this exported API with a value other than 2. No realistic receive path in the current integration triggers it.

The proposed fix is sound. The simpler variant (allocate a fixed maximum and clamp npeaks) is lower-risk than reallocating. The sibling setters SetRXAmpeakFilEnable, FilFreq and so on take a filter index with no bounds check, so the same defect class applies to them too.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This hardens an exported API that is currently unused. If a host calls SetRXAmpeakNpeaks with a value above the created count (2), the code reads past the end of enable[] and pfil[] and calls xspeak on an invalid pointer. If a host lowers the count, the extra SPEAK filters leak and later raising it again would use freed memory. No current WDSP or Lyra code path calls this setter, so there is no observed crash today. The fix prevents misuse by future callers. Allocating a fixed maximum and clamping npeaks (including bounds checks on the per-filter setters' fil index) is the simplest safe fix.

kept.title: make_nbp band-deletion loop shifts bands but not the del[] flags, so it deletes the wrong sub-band; also min_notch_width integer-division edge
kept.current: Fully covered sub-bands are flagged in del[i] (line 142). The compaction loop then does `for (i...){ if (del[i]==1){ nnbp--; for (j=i;j<nnbp;j++) bplow[j]=bplow[j+1]...; del[i]=0; } }`. It shifts the band arrays left but leaves del[] in its original indexing, and it advances i past the band that just moved into slot i. del is malloc'd at 1024 ints (line 107), while RXA creates maxpb = 1025 (RXA.c:103), and there is no bound check on bplow[nbp+adds] (147). min_notch_width computes `1600.0 / (a->nc / 256)` with integer nc/256 (lines 88-94).
kept.proposed: Compact with a write index in one pass: w = 0; for i < nbp: if (!del[i]) { bplow[w] = bplow[i]; bphigh[w] = bphigh[i]; w++; } del[i] = 0; nbp = w. Size del from maxpb and check nbp+adds < maxpb before appending. In min_notch_width, use (double)a->nc / 256.0. Better still, derive it from the window's transition width (see the Kaiser proposal).
kept.benefit: Example (offsets removed): passband 0-3000 Hz with notches 900-1100 and 1900-2100 gives bands [0,900], [1100,1900], [2100,3000]. A third, wide notch from -100 to 1950 Hz flags bands 0 and 1. The current loop keeps [1100,1900], which should be notched, and deletes [2100,3000], which is the real passband. It needs overlapping notches that cover two whole sub-bands, so it is rare, but when it happens the audible result is badly wrong. nc < 256 makes min_notch_width divide by zero (inf), so with autoincr every notch removes the whole passband. RXANBPSetNC accepts any nc.
kept.risk: None. Results for the cases that currently work do not change.
kept.evidence: Line-level trace of lines 164-176 with del[0] = del[1] = 1 and nbp = 3 gives the result above. Integer division at 88/91/94, since nc is int.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked nbp.c in WDSP 2.11, lines 82-182. The description of the current code is accurate.

Deletion loop (lines 164-177): when del[i]==1, the loop shifts bplow/bphigh left from slot i, clears del[i] and moves on to i+1. It never shifts del[] and never re-checks slot i. I traced the proposal's case with nbp=3 and del[0]=del[1]=1. At i=0 the arrays become [1100,1900],[2100,3000] and nnbp=2. At i=1, del[1] is still 1, so nnbp drops to 1 with no shift. The result is nbp=1 with only [1100,1900] left. That is the band that should have been removed, and the real passband [2100,3000] is gone, as the proposal says. Two deletions that are not adjacent go wrong too: with nbp=4 and del[0]=del[2]=1, the band in original slot 3 is deleted instead of the one in slot 2. One deletion per notch works correctly, which explains why nobody has noticed. To trigger the bug, one notch has to fully cover two or more sub-bands that earlier notches created. That can happen when a user drags or overlaps notches, or when autoincr widens narrow notches next to existing ones. It is uncommon but realistic, and when it happens the audio output is plainly wrong. make_nbp has no other copy (snb.c only calls the nbp code), and no other mode or option already fixes this.

del sizing: del is malloc0(1024 ints). RXA creates the notch database with at most 1024 notches and maxpb=1025 (RXA.c lines 101 and 122). Each notch can split at most one band, so nbp can reach 1025, and the loop over i<nbp would then read del[1024], one past the end. This only happens with all 1024 notches active, so it is a theoretical off-by-one, not a practical one. The same bound means bplow[nbp+adds] cannot actually exceed maxpb, so the "no bound check" point is only defensive.

min_notch_width: nc is an int, so a->nc/256 is integer division, as claimed. a->rate is a double, so the rate/48000 part is fine. The default nc is max(2048, dsp_size), always at least 2048, and normal sizes are powers of two at or above 256, so truncation does not matter in practice. Only an nc below 256, set through RXANBPSetNC (which does no validation), would divide by zero and give an infinite minimum width, so that autoincr notches wipe out the passband. That is a real but marginal edge case.

The proposed one-pass compaction with a write index is correct, simple, and gives the same results for every case that works today.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The fix corrects a real bug in make_nbp. When a single notch fully covers two or more existing sub-bands, the compaction loop deletes the wrong sub-band, leaving a band that should be notched and removing the real passband. Rewriting the loop as a one-pass compaction with a write index fixes this, and results for the single-deletion cases that work today stay the same. The other changes are minor hardening. Sizing del from maxpb fixes an off-by-one read that only happens with all 1024 notches active. Using floating-point nc/256 in min_notch_width only matters if a caller sets nc below 256, which the default (2048 or more) never does.

kept.title: Impulse/min-phase cache LRU list is mutated without a lock
kept.file_function: fir.c:fir_bandpass (239-241, 311) and fir.c:mp_imp (401-411, 465) -> impulse_cache.c:get_impulse_cache_entry (128-162), add_impulse_to_cache (164-185), remove_impulse_cache_tail (93-111)
kept.current: get_impulse_cache_entry takes _cs_use_cache only to read the _use_cache flag (lines 133-135). It then walks the list and moves the hit to the head (prev->next = e->next; _cache_heads[bucket] = e) with no lock, and memcpy's e->impulse. add_impulse_to_cache can evict and free the tail (remove_impulse_cache_tail frees (*pp)->impulse), also with no lock. fir_bandpass is called from many PORT setters that do not hold csDSP while designing (for example SetRXABandpassFreqs, bandpass.c:399, and RXANBPSetFreqs, nbp.c:539), for both RX and TX channels.
kept.proposed: Hold one mutex across the entire get (walk, move to head, copy) and the entire add (evict, insert). os_unfair_lock is fine on Apple platforms because design runs off the audio thread. For LyraDSP, consider dropping the cache for fir_bandpass entirely: a 2048-tap windowed sinc is a few thousand sin/cos calls, tens of microseconds. Keep it only for the costly 16x-padded min-phase FFTs.
kept.benefit: Removes a real data race. Two threads redesigning filters at once (two receivers, RX and TX, or a GUI thread and a tuning thread) can corrupt the bucket list or memcpy from a freed entry. That is a rare crash or a garbage impulse that is very hard to reproduce.
kept.risk: Negligible. Lock hold time is a memcpy of at most nc complex values.
kept.evidence: Line-level: the only lock in impulse_cache.c guards the _use_cache flag (89, 133-135, 169-171). The list pointers _cache_heads/_cache_counts (87-88) are read and written outside any lock.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code in /Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source/impulse_cache.c and it matches the proposal.

- **The lock only guards the flag.** `_cs_use_cache` is taken only to read or write `_use_cache` (lines 133-135, 169-171, 193-195, 267-269, 278-280).
- **The cache list is changed with no lock.** `get_impulse_cache_entry` (128-162) walks `_cache_heads[bucket]` and moves a hit to the head without a lock: `prev->next = e->next; e->next = head; head = e`. It then copies `e->impulse`.
- **Eviction frees memory with no lock.** `add_impulse_to_cache` (164-185) can call `remove_impulse_cache_tail`, which runs `_aligned_free` on both the entry and its impulse, then edits the head and count, all unlocked.
- **The cache is one global object.** It is shared by every channel: FIR_CACHE and MP_CACHE are fixed bucket indices.

The callers do not serialise design work either.

- `SetRXABandpassFreqs` (bandpass.c:394-410) calls `fir_bandpass` before it takes csDSP.
- `RXANBPSetFreqs` (nbp.c:537-549) calls `calc_nbp_impulse` with no lock at all.
- Even callers that do hold csDSP hold a per-channel lock (`ch[channel].csDSP`). Two channels (RX1, RX2, TX) are not excluded from each other.
- `fir_bandpass` is also called from resample.c, varsamp.c, delay.c, fmd.c, fmmod.c, wbfm.c, dexp.c and nnrbypass.c. So the shared list is touched from many paths.

**What can go wrong.** Two threads designing at once can corrupt a bucket list. One thread's eviction can also free an entry while another thread is copying from it, which reads freed memory. Possible results are a crash, a lost or looping list, or a garbage impulse.

**The cache is on in Lyra.** src/wdsp_native.cpp:1195 calls `init_impulse_cache(1)`, so `_run` is 1 and the unlocked path runs.

**What I could not confirm.** I did not find out whether Lyra calls all WDSP setters from a single thread. src/wire/wdspcalls.cpp has no thread or mutex usage, which hints that they may be serialised. If they are, the race is latent in Lyra today, though still real in the library. That is why this is not high priority.

**Notes on the fix.**
- One mutex held across the whole get (walk, move to head, copy) and the whole add (evict, insert) is correct and cheap.
- `save_impulse_cache` and `read_impulse_cache` also walk and rebuild the lists without a lock. They should take the same mutex. Lyra calls save during unload, so this matters less there.
- The CRITICAL_SECTION shim already in WDSP's Linux/macOS port can be reused instead of `os_unfair_lock`.
- Dropping the cache for `fir_bandpass` is a fair optional simplification: a windowed-sinc design is cheap. It is a separate change, not needed to fix the race.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This fixes a real data race in WDSP's global impulse cache. The cache's linked lists are updated, and entries evicted and freed, with no lock. Only the `_use_cache` flag is protected. Filter-design calls on different channels, and setters such as `SetRXABandpassFreqs` and `RXANBPSetFreqs` that design before taking csDSP or without it, can therefore corrupt a cache bucket or copy from freed memory. The result would be a rare crash or a corrupted filter impulse that is very hard to reproduce. Lyra turns the cache on (`init_impulse_cache(1)`), so the unlocked code runs there. How likely the race is in Lyra depends on whether its WDSP setters really run on more than one thread, which I did not confirm. The fix is one mutex held across the whole get and the whole add, and the same mutex should also cover `save_impulse_cache` and `read_impulse_cache`. Lock hold time is small, and filter design does not run on the audio thread.

kept.title: Click-free filter exchange in fircore: crossfade old and new mask outputs for one block
kept.current: A new impulse is transformed into the inactive mask set, and then cset is flipped (line 343 or 490). The next xfircore applies the new masks to the whole frequency-domain delay line immediately, so the output switches instantly from old filter * x to new filter * x. That is a step discontinuity whenever the response changes a lot: dragging passband edges, nbp lightweight recalculation on every tune step with notches (nbp.c:184-215), EQ edits, or CW bandwidth changes.
kept.proposed: Keep the previous cset for one block after a flip. In that block, run the spectral MAC twice (old and new masks over the same FDL), do two IFFTs, and crossfade the two outputs over the block with a raised-cosine or equal-gain ramp. The FDL holds input spectra, so both outputs are exact and no state is lost. Cost is one extra MAC pass and one IFFT, only on blocks where the filter changes. For very small blocks, crossfade over 2-4 blocks. This is the time-domain filter-exchange method used in partitioned-convolution engines.
kept.benefit: Removes the audible ticks and zipper noise when filters are dragged or retuned with notches active. This is the most audible improvement in this area for an interactive UI. Steady-state quality is unchanged.
kept.risk: For one block the output is a blend of the two filters, so a notch reaches full depth one block later (about 1.3 ms at 48 kHz with size 64). Needs an atomic generation counter instead of the bare masks_ready int.
kept.evidence: Mueller-Tomfelde, 'Time-varying filter in non-uniform block convolution', DAFx 2001. Wefers, 'Partitioned convolution algorithms for real-time auralization', PhD thesis, RWTH Aachen 2015 (ch. on filter exchange / crossfading). Code: the single cset is read at line 423 and swapped at 343/490, with no crossfade path.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description matches it. calc_fircore (firmin.c 323-347) FFTs the new impulse into fmask[1-cset] and, when flip is set, toggles cset under the critical section. setUpdate_fircore (485-494) does the same toggle when masks_ready is set. xfircore (412-440) reads one cset and runs the spectral MAC over all nfor partitions of the frequency-domain delay line (FDL) with that mask set only. No crossfade, ramp or dual-output path exists in fircore or in its callers. SetRXABandpassFreqs and SetRXABandpassWindow (bandpass.c ~396-425) compute the impulse, then call setUpdate_fircore. calc_nbp_lightweight (nbp.c 184-215) calls setImpulse_fircore(...,1) on every tune or shift change while a notch is or was in the passband. RXAbp1Set and RXAbpsnbaSet only flip cset. The only slewing in WDSP is the channel on/off ramp, which does not cover filter changes.

The physics is right. The FDL holds the spectra of the full input history, so right after the flip the output equals the steady-state output of the new filter. The output therefore jumps by (h_new - h_old)*x at a block boundary. That is the same as switching on a band-limited difference signal with a rectangular gate, which spreads energy across the band as a click. The jump is large when a strong carrier or CW signal crosses a dragged edge, when a notch is inserted on a strong carrier, or when CW bandwidth is narrowed next to a strong signal. It is small when an edge moves through noise only. Crossfading the outputs of the old and new mask sets over the same FDL is the standard filter-exchange method for uniformly partitioned convolution. Both outputs are exact, so no state is lost. Both citations are real and relevant: Müller-Tomfelde, DAFx-01, and Wefers' 2015 RWTH thesis, which covers filter exchanges by time-domain crossfading.

The claim has four weaknesses.
1. The claimed benefit is overstated. With small edge steps in noise the click is small. The worst case in practice is a strong signal crossing an edge or a notch, which is real but occasional. I could not verify that this is "the most audible improvement in this area".
2. The cost is understated. During the exchange block the second MAC runs over all nfor = nc/size partitions, which with nc=4096 and size=64 means 64 partitions. That doubles the dominant cost on that block. During a continuous drag or a VFO spin with notches active, updates can arrive about every block, so the extra cost can be sustained rather than occasional.
3. Concurrency needs more than an atomic counter. calc_fircore writes into fmask[1-cset] with no lock. Once the old set must stay readable for the crossfade, a quick second update would overwrite it mid-read. That needs a third mask set (3x mask memory) or a rule that holds back the next flip until the fade has finished.
4. A one-block fade at size 64 lasts only about 1.3 ms, so it reduces splatter but does not remove it. Fading over several blocks makes the buffering harder.

For nbp tuning there is a separate problem the crossfade does not fix: the tune or shift change and the mask flip are not applied on the same sample. That misalignment can let a notched carrier leak through briefly whether or not a crossfade is used.

Net: the description is accurate, no equivalent exists, the method is sound and backed by real literature, and it would help amateur-radio use (speech, CW, digital modes) at no latency cost in steady state. It is a modest but real quality gain with moderate implementation complexity.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Removes the step discontinuity, (h_new - h_old)*x switched on at a block boundary, that every fircore filter exchange produces today: bandpass edge drags, window changes, nbp notch recalculation on tune steps, EQ and CW bandwidth changes. Clicks become clearly less audible when a strong carrier or CW signal crosses a moving edge or a notch is inserted; with noise only, the change is barely noticeable. Steady-state output and latency do not change. Costs: one extra full MAC pass (all nc/size partitions) and one extra IFFT on each exchange block, which can be every block during a continuous drag or VFO spin with notches active. Safe overlap with the next update needs a third mask set or a hold-off on the next flip. A one-block fade at size 64 (about 1.3 ms) only partly suppresses splatter, and a longer fade adds buffering complexity. It does not fix the leak caused by applying the nbp tune shift and the mask flip at different samples.

kept.title: Kaiser window sized to a target attenuation in fir_bandpass/nbp, for sharper skirts or fewer taps (lower linear-phase delay)
kept.current: fir_bandpass supports only BH 4-term (case 0) and BH 7-term (case 1/default). wintype 2 silently becomes BH7 because `case 1: default:` shares the code at 282-283, even though get_fsamp_window implements Kaiser for the EQ/CFIR path, with beta fixed at 8.0 (line 93). RXA bp1 and the TX bandpasses use wintype 1 (BH7, RXA.c:404-416, TXA.c:241-253). nbp's minimum notch width is a hard-coded table, 1600 or 2200 Hz per 256 taps at 48 kHz.
kept.proposed: Add a Kaiser window whose beta comes from a requested stopband attenuation A: beta = 0.1102(A - 8.7) for A > 50. The transition width is then about (A - 8)/14.36 bins of fs/N. Default A to about 120-130 dB for the float32 port; a lower-level window cannot be realized anyway once coefficients and FFT products are float32 (floor roughly -130 to -140 dB). Derive min_notch_width from the same formula instead of the table. Optionally offer constrained least-squares or Parks-McClellan equiripple design for the static TX filters, where design time is unimportant.
kept.benefit: Classic windows have transition widths of roughly 0.9 times their main-lobe width. BH4 (main lobe about 8 bins, about -92 dB) gives about 7 bins; Kaiser at 92 dB gives about 5.9 bins (about 20% narrower). BH7 (main lobe about 14 bins, sidelobes far below what float32 can realize) gives about 13 bins; Kaiser at 130 dB gives about 8.5 bins (about 35% narrower). At nc = 2048 and 48 kHz that is roughly 300 Hz down to 200 Hz transition and correspondingly narrower minimum notches. Alternatively, keep the current skirts with about 25-35% fewer taps, which cuts the linear-phase group delay nc/2 (21 ms at 2048 taps and 48 kHz) by the same fraction. A moderate, real improvement.
kept.risk: Users who have tuned against BH7's extreme stopband will see a higher (but still sub-noise-floor) stopband. Keep BH4/BH7 as options. Equiripple design of 2048+ tap filters with Remez can fail to converge, so use least squares or Kaiser for real-time redesign.
kept.evidence: Kaiser, 'Nonrecursive digital filter design using the I0-sinh window function', Proc. IEEE ISCAS 1974. Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., section 7.5 (Kaiser formulas, window transition widths). Harris, 'On the use of windows for harmonic analysis with the DFT', Proc. IEEE 1978. Parks and McClellan, IEEE Trans. Circuit Theory 1972.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is accurate. In fir.c:fir_bandpass the window switch has only `case 0` (BH 4-term) and `case 1: default:` (BH 7-term), so wintype 2 silently gives BH7. get_fsamp_window (fir.c:59-109) has a Kaiser case 2 with `const double beta = 8.0`, but only the frequency-sampling path (EQP and CFIR) uses it. The EQP blocks pass wintype 2 (RXA.c:277, TXA.c:126). RXA bp1 (RXA.c:415) and TXA bp0/1/2 (TXA.c:252/273/295) pass wintype 1, so they get BH7. nbp.c:min_notch_width is a fixed table: 1600 Hz (wintype 0) or 2200 Hz (others) per 256 taps at 48 kHz. That works out to about 8.5 and 11.7 bins, which matches the full windowed-sinc transition widths. No path in WDSP builds a fir_bandpass impulse with an attenuation-sized Kaiser, so the feature does not already exist.

I checked the benefit numerically with a pure-Python evaluation of the windowed-sinc response (N=513, transition measured in bins of fs/N from the -0.001 dB passband edge to where the response stays below the target level):
- BH4 reaches -92 dB in 7.1 bins. Kaiser with A=92 does it in 5.9 bins, about 17% narrower.
- BH7 reaches -130 dB in 11.15 bins. Kaiser with A=130 does it in 7.95 bins, about 29% narrower.
- Kaiser with A=120 reaches -120 dB in 7.55 bins, against 10.95 for BH7.
- The existing fixed beta=8 Kaiser reaches only about -80 to -90 dB, which is why it is no substitute.

So the direction and rough size of the claim hold, but the BH7 figure is overstated. The real transition is about 11 bins, not 13, so the gain is about 29%, not 35%. At nc=2048 and 48 kHz (23.4 Hz per bin) that is about 260 Hz down to about 190 Hz to reach -130 dB, not 300 down to 200. The formulas beta = 0.1102(A - 8.7) and transition width (A - 8)/14.36 bins are the standard Kaiser design equations.

The citations are real and relevant:
- Kaiser, ISCAS 1974, the I0-sinh window paper.
- Oppenheim and Schafer, 3rd ed., chapter 7: windowing in 7.5, Kaiser design examples in 7.6.
- Harris, Proc. IEEE 1978.
- Parks and McClellan, IEEE Trans. Circuit Theory 1972.

Why the practical value is modest:
1. Users can already set the tap count (SetRXABandpassNC, RXANBPSetNC, SetTXABandpassNC). The change is equivalent to about 1.2 to 1.4 times more taps for free, which saves compute and linear-phase delay but brings no new capability.
2. A minimum-phase option exists (SetRXABandpassMP, RXANBPSetMP). Users sensitive to latency can use it, which weakens the delay argument.
3. The main RX filter nbp0 uses BH4 (wintype 0). There the gain at matched about 92 dB is only about 17%, and about 92 dB is marginal against very strong adjacent signals. Raising A costs back much of the width advantage: K100 gives about 6.4 bins and K120 about 7.5 bins, against 7.2 bins for BH4 at -100 dB.
4. Stock WDSP builds the coefficients in double precision. The float32-floor argument applies only to a float32 port, but -130 dB is beyond the ADC and signal-chain dynamic range in either case, so BH7's deeper far stopband buys little.

The risk is low: compute I0 once per redesign, keep BH4 and BH7 as options, and derive min_notch_width from the same formula. The caution against real-time Remez is sound. Overall this is a real, low-risk, textbook improvement in tap efficiency for the same skirts, but the benefit for HF/VHF speech, CW and digital modes is incremental, not a capability change.
verdict.corrected_benefit: A Kaiser window with beta = 0.1102(A - 8.7), sized to the stopband attenuation actually needed, gives a transition about 17% narrower than BH4 at the same -92 dB level, and about 29% narrower than BH7 at the -120 to -130 dB levels that matter in practice. At nc=2048 and 48 kHz that is roughly 260 Hz down to 190 Hz to reach -130 dB. Equivalently, the same skirts need about 20-30% fewer taps, with proportionally lower compute and linear-phase delay. It also gives fir_bandpass a real wintype 2 (today it silently falls back to BH7) and a min_notch_width derived from a formula instead of a table. The gain is modest because users can already raise nc or turn on minimum phase, so it improves efficiency, not capability.

kept.title: Run the doublepole CW filter as an exact recursive complex one-pole instead of an nc-tap FIR (up to 16384 taps)
kept.current: The impulse actually used is h[i] = scale*alpha*exp(-alpha*i) * e^{-j*omega*i} with alpha = pi*(bw/1.7)/rate (lines 150-160). That is exactly the impulse response of one complex pole, truncated at nc. It is executed through fircore with nc from calc_dpole_nc: 2048 at 100 Hz bandwidth, up to 256*4*16 = 16384 at bandwidths under about 17 Hz at 48 kHz. When the bandwidth crosses a threshold, setNc_fircore runs inside csDSP (SetRXADoublepoleFreqs, 295-301). That re-plans every FFTW_PATIENT plan, and fircore's own comment says this 'will probably cause a glitch in audio' (firmin.c:467).
kept.proposed: Implement y[n] = g*alpha*x[n] + p*y[n-1] with p = exp(-alpha) * e^{-j*omega} (sign matched to the impulse convention above) and g = gain, dropping the 1/(2*size) FFT normalization. This is one complex multiply-add per sample, with no truncation, no nc selection and no re-planning. Keep the state in double, which costs nothing for a scalar recursion on Apple Silicon. If a true 2-pole response is wanted (the unused H() / build_doublepole_1sided/2sided path), cascade two such poles or use a complex biquad.
kept.benefit: Identical response (more exact, since there is no truncation tail error, about -90 dB at the nc limits) at about 1/100 to 1/1000 of the cost. It also removes the audio dropout from FFTW re-planning under the DSP lock when the operator changes CW bandwidth. Latency is unchanged (both are causal with no added delay).
kept.risk: With a complex one-pole the pole radius gets very close to 1 at narrow bandwidths (1 - 3.9e-4 at 10 Hz/48 kHz). It is stable and fine in double; in float32 the bandwidth error is tiny but the state should still be double. The mode 1/2 input manipulation (lines 203-212) must be preserved.
kept.evidence: Line-level: build_doublepole_1eff is a sampled exp(-alpha*n)*e^{j*theta*n}, the impulse response of 1/(1 - p z^-1). Standard one-pole resonator theory: Smith, 'Introduction to Digital Filters', 2007, ch. on one-pole/complex resonators.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description holds. build_doublepole_1eff (doublepole.c:142-162) fills h[i] = scale*alpha*exp(-alpha*i) * e^{-j*omega*i}, with alpha = pi*(bw/1.7)/rate and omega = -2*pi*fc/rate. That is exactly the impulse response of one complex pole, p = e^{-alpha} e^{+j2*pi*fc/rate}, cut off at nc. It runs through create_fircore(size, in, out, nc, mp=0, 4, impulse), a partitioned overlap-save convolver. With mp=0 the impulse is used unchanged and nothing else shapes it.

The nc figures are right. At 48 kHz, calc_dpole_nc gives 2048 taps at the default 100 Hz and 16384 taps for any bandwidth under 17 Hz. It scales with sample rate, so 192 kHz reaches 65536 taps.

Per block, fircore does a forward FFT, then nfor = nc/size complex multiply-accumulates (MACs) over 2*size bins, then an inverse FFT. With a 64-sample buffer that is about 64 complex MACs per sample at nc=2048 and about 512 at nc=16384, plus the FFTs. The recursion costs one complex MAC per sample. So the claimed 100x to 1000x saving is about right.

The re-planning claim is also correct. When a bandwidth change moves nc across a threshold (136, 68, 34 or 17 Hz), CalcDoublepoleFilter calls setNc_fircore under csDSP. That frees and re-allocates every partition buffer and re-plans about 3*nfor+1 FFTW_PATIENT plans plus a minphase plan of size nc*4. It also starts the filter from zeros, so the output jumps. The author's own comment (firmin.c:467) warns of a likely audio glitch. One caveat: WDSP's wisdom file makes PATIENT planning fast, so the dropout is shorter than the claim implies. The state reset still happens.

The truncation figure in the proposal is wrong, and it understates the gain. The tail at the cut is exp(-alpha*nc). For bandwidths just above each threshold (bw/1.7 just above 10, 20 or 40 Hz) alpha*nc is only about 5.36, so the tail is about -46 dB, not -90 dB. Above the top threshold it reaches about -46 dB again at about 68 Hz (bw/1.7 = 40). The worst-case truncation leakage is therefore about -46 dB. The recursion has no truncation error at all.

The response match is exact. Using p^n with g = gain*alpha reproduces the impulse after removing the 1/(2*size) normalization that fircore needs. The difference at the passband centre is only the tail factor (1 - e^{-alpha*nc}). Latency is the same, because both process the same block with no extra lookahead.

The CWU sign flip and the mode 2 Q=I copy (lines 203-212) happen on the input before filtering, so they carry over unchanged. A pole radius of 1-6.5e-4 is no problem in double. The recursive form also keeps its state when coefficients change, which is better than setNc's reset.

Nothing elsewhere in WDSP already does this. iir.c has real biquad peak filters, not a complex one-pole version of this filter. The citation (Smith, Introduction to Digital Filters, one-pole and complex resonator sections) is real and relevant.

Two things limit the priority. The FIR is not a big CPU load on modern hardware. The glitch only happens when the bandwidth crosses a threshold. So this is a solid, low-risk improvement but not urgent.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The doublepole CW filter is exactly a truncated complex one-pole. Running it as y[n] = gain*alpha*x[n] + p*y[n-1], with p = e^{-alpha} e^{+j2*pi*fc/rate}, gives the same response with no truncation error. The current FIR's truncation error is as high as about -46 dB just above each nc threshold, not the -90 dB the proposal says. The recursion costs about 1/60 to 1/500 of the current CPU work, more at high sample rates where nc reaches 65536 taps. It removes the nc selection, the setNc_fircore re-allocation, the FFTW re-planning under csDSP and the zeroed state when the bandwidth crosses 136, 68, 34 or 17 Hz. Wisdom makes the re-planning fairly quick, but the state reset still causes a discontinuity. Latency is unchanged. The CWU sign flip and the mode 2 Q=I copy run before the filter and stay as they are. Keep the recursion state in double.

kept.title: Non-uniform partitioned convolution for the long (16384-tap) EQ and other long kernels, so small blocks are affordable
kept.file_function: firmin.c:plan_fircore/xfircore (290-321, 412-440); eq.c:create_eqp (255-284) with nc = max(16384, dsp_size) (RXA.c:269, TXA.c:118)
kept.current: fircore is uniformly partitioned (UPOLS): nfor = nc/size partitions, each costing one 2*size complex MAC pass per block (lines 427-435). The RX and TX EQ use 16384 taps, so at size 64 that is 256 partitions, about 512 complex MACs per output sample for the EQ alone, plus 32 partitions each for nbp, bp1 and cfir. nfor must be a power of two (idxmask = nfor - 1, lines 297/434), so nc and size must both be powers of two (comment at eq.c:258).
kept.proposed: Use a non-uniform partition scheme: small partitions (size B) at the head, then partitions growing 2x or by an optimised sequence, each scheduled at its own block rate (Gardner; Garcia's optimal partitioning; Wefers' 'NUPOLS'). Input-output latency stays at B while cost becomes close to logarithmic in the filter length. Alternatively, because the EQ is minimum phase (mp = 1), split its impulse into a short head through UPOLS and a long tail through one large-FFT partition. When porting, also lift the power-of-two nfor constraint with a modulo index.
kept.benefit: Typically 3-10x less spectral-MAC work for 16k-tap kernels at B = 64. Honest magnitude: on Apple Silicon the current UPOLS cost (a few hundred MFLOP/s per channel) is affordable at B = 64. The gain matters when you shrink the block to 16-32 for lower latency (UPOLS cost grows as nc/B per sample) or run several receivers or a TX/RX pair at once.
kept.risk: Higher complexity, plus scheduling of the long-partition FFTs across blocks to avoid CPU spikes (the long partitions must be computed ahead in a background or interleaved fashion). Not worth it if block size stays at 64+ and only one receiver runs.
kept.evidence: Gardner, 'Efficient convolution without input-output delay', J. AES 43(3), 1995. Garcia, 'Optimal filter partition for efficient convolution with short input/output delay', AES 113th Conv., 2002. Wefers, PhD thesis RWTH Aachen, 2015.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the code is accurate. plan_fircore (firmin.c:290-321) sets nfor = nc/size and idxmask = nfor-1, so nfor has to be a power of two. xfircore (412-440) runs one forward FFT of size 2*size, then nfor passes of 2*size complex MACs, then one inverse FFT. That is uniformly partitioned overlap-save with a frequency-domain delay line. create_eqp gets nc = max(16384, dsp_size) on both RX (RXA.c:269) and TX (TXA.c:118), with mp = 1. SetRXAEQNC and SetTXAEQNC are marked 'DEPRECATED' and do nothing, so the host cannot shorten the EQ. At size 64 that gives 256 partitions, or 512 complex MACs per sample. nbp0, bp1 and cfir use max(2048, size) taps, which is 32 partitions at size 64. WDSP has no non-uniform or multi-rate partitioned convolution anywhere; grep finds only UPOLS 'Partitioned Overlap-Save' kernels. So nothing in WDSP already does this.

The literature is real and on topic. Gardner, JAES 43(3), 1995, introduced zero-delay and non-uniform block convolution. Garcia, AES 113th Convention, 2002, covers optimal non-uniform partitioning. Wefers' 2015 RWTH Aachen thesis is the standard reference for NUPOLS. A rough cost check for N = 16384 and B = 64 bears out the speed-up: UPOLS costs about 4k flops per sample, mostly the 256x128 spectral MACs. A NUPOLS with about 12-16 partitions across 4-5 FFT sizes costs about 0.8-1.2k flops per sample. So 3-5x less work is realistic; 10x is the optimistic end.

Why it is still not worth much in practice:
1. The EQ is off by default (xeqp just memcpy's when run = 0), so the saving only applies when someone turns the EQ on.
2. At B = 64 the cost is about 200 MFLOP/s per EQ at 48 kHz, or about 400 at a 96 kHz TX rate. Apple Silicon handles that easily, and larger DSP buffers cost proportionally less.
3. The stated reason, smaller blocks for lower latency, is weak in WDSP. The main RX filter nbp0 is linear phase (mp = 0) with 2048 taps, which is about 21 ms of group delay at 48 kHz. The TX bp0/bp1/bp2 and cfir are also linear phase with 2048 taps. Each of those adds far more delay than the block does. Going from B = 64 to B = 16 saves about 1 ms against more than 20 ms of filter delay. The minimum-phase 16k EQ also has a lot of low-frequency group delay of its own.
4. For the 2048-tap kernels (32 partitions) the gain is small, maybe 1.5-2x.
5. Implementation risk is real. fircore uses double-buffered masks (cset, fmask[2]) for glitch-free coefficient changes. A non-uniform scheme has to switch every partition rate on the same sample. Its large FFTs have to be spread across blocks or run on another thread, which WDSP's single-thread-per-channel model doesn't support today. flush and setSize would also need rework.

The proposal states its own magnitude honestly and is technically correct, so I don't refute it. It is a niche optimisation with low priority. Lifting the power-of-two constraint on nfor is trivial and has nothing to do with the main idea.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Non-uniform partitioned convolution, or the simpler minimum-phase head/tail split, would cut the spectral work of the fixed 16384-tap RX/TX EQ by about 3-5x at B = 64 with no added latency. It would give little for the 2048-tap bandpass, nbp and cfir kernels (about 1.5-2x). It helps only when the EQ is turned on, and the current cost (about 200-400 MFLOP/s per EQ) is already affordable on Apple Silicon. Its only real use is cutting CPU when many receivers run EQ at once, or making very small blocks affordable. Small blocks would not noticeably cut end-to-end latency, because the default linear-phase 2048-tap bandpasses add about 21 ms of group delay each.

refuted.title: Numerical hazards for the float32 port: cepstral min-phase floor, Direct Form I IIR at low frequency, half-bin frequency-sampling grid
refuted.why:
I read the cited code. Most of the line references are correct, but the proposal's main premise does not apply to how WDSP is actually used.

(a) and (b) only matter for a float32 port, and none exists. WDSP 2.11 does all filter design and all IIR state in double: fir.c mp_imp/mp_imp_exec, fsamp_exec, eq_impulse and the snotch/speak biquads in iir.c. Lyra links WDSP/FFTW unchanged. Its specs say audio leaves WDSP as "interleaved stereo double" and that WDSP/FFTW are "unchanged". So the proposed fix, "do design in double, keep IIR state in double", is what WDSP already does. The proposal itself says that in double the CTCSS-notch round-off is inaudible and the min-phase change is "marginal". The NaN from log(1e-300f) only happens if someone writes a naive float port. It is not a WDSP defect.

The detail in (a) is also partly wrong. The 1e-100 floor in eq_impulse applies to the target magnitude A[k]. A[k] then goes through fsamp_exec: c2r, then a Blackman-Harris window. firmin.c's mp_imp_exec takes the log of the FFT of that windowed, zero-padded impulse, not of A[k]. The stopband magnitudes the log sees are therefore set by window leakage, not by the 1e-100 floor, so the floor does not produce "-2000 dB spikes" in the cepstrum. Exact zero bins (the log(1e-300) branch) are practically never hit for a windowed double FIR. Clamping at about -150 dB relative is a reasonable textbook refinement, but nothing shows an audible effect for amateur-radio speech, CW or digital modes.

(c) is the one accurate observation. fsamp_exec, like the original fir_fsamp even-N branch, places A[k] on integer bins k*fs/N (phase -2*pi*((N-1)/2)*k/N). But eq_impulse's even-N branch samples the curve at (i+0.5)/mid, and cfir_impulse/icfir_impulse use offset = 0.5 for even N. The designed curve is therefore shifted down by fs/(2N): about 1.5 Hz for the 16384-tap EQ (RXA.c/TXA.c use max(16384, dsp_size)) and about 12 Hz for a 2048-tap CFIR. The EQ curve is a smooth user curve and the CFIR is a smooth CIC-droop compensator, so this changes the response by hundredths of a dB or less. It is a cosmetic consistency fix that would also break bit-exactness with the reference, not a meaningful improvement.

The cited literature is real and generally relevant: Damera-Venkata et al. 2000, Oppenheim & Schafer on cepstral aliasing, Jackson on DF-I round-off, and Simper's SVF note. However, it supports concerns about a float port that the project does not have.

Net: no actionable benefit for the existing double-precision WDSP in Lyra. The only real finding, the half-bin grid offset in (c), is negligible.

summary: resample.c is a classic rational L/M polyphase FIR (calc_resample L35-78): GCD-reduced L/M, a Blackman-Harris-7 windowed sinc from fir_bandpass (wintype 1) with ncoef = 140*full_rate/min_rate (L64) and a -6 dB cutoff at 0.45*min_rate (L57), giving about 0.1*min_rate of transition band centred on fc. reshb.c (new in 2.11) is a cascade of decimate-by-2 half-band FIRs with Dolph-Chebyshev windows (140 dB design, L345-382) and folded symmetric taps (xhbres L134-164). The stage lengths come from a hard-coded table of rate pairs (L179-344), and they agree closely with Kaiser's length estimate for protecting a 0-24 kHz final passband. Those stages are well designed and float32-safe. varsamp.c is an arbitrary-ratio resampler. It linearly interpolates coefficients from a table oversampled by R=1024 (hshift L114-124, about -120 dB coefficient error), and it tracks output timing with two double accumulators (isamps, h_offset) that stay exactly consistent only because inv_cvar is truncated to 36 mantissa bits by type-punning (L151-153). rmatch.c wraps varsamp in a ring buffer: var = feed_forward(count ratio, 262144-call window, EMA 0.01) - pr_gain * boxcar_mean(fill deviation, 16384 calls), clamped to +/-4% (control L256-273), with raised-cosine fades on under- and overflow. shift.c is a recursive complex-rotation NCO reseeded from a double phase every buffer. delay.c is a fixed polyphase windowed-sinc fractional delay (20 ns step) plus up to 1024 whole samples.

kept.title: rmatch control loop: averaging windows are counted in callbacks, not seconds, so loop stability depends on buffer size
kept.file_function: rmatch.c:control (L256-273), xmav (L56-69), calc_rmatch pr_gain (L147), create_rmatchV defaults (L519-524), xrmatchIN/xrmatchOUT control calls (L359, L464)
kept.current: control() runs once per xrmatchIN and once per xrmatchOUT. The proportional term is pr_gain * av_deviation, where av_deviation is a boxcar mean over the last prop_ringmax=16384 calls (xmav). pr_gain = 4e-6*48000/nom_outrate is normalised for sample rate but not for block size. Plant: d(n_ring)/dt ~= nom_outrate*(var - var_true), so the P loop has k = 4e-6*48000 ~= 0.19 s^-1 (time constant about 5.2 s) at any rate. The boxcar adds a delay of half its window, which is 16384/(2*call_rate) seconds.
kept.proposed: Make the loop time-based and design it explicitly as a 2nd-order (type-II) loop: a DLL/PI controller on the fill-level error, updated at a fixed time cadence or with per-call time weighting (dt = blocksize/rate). Set an explicit bandwidth (for example 0.02-0.05 Hz) and damping of about 0.707, following Adriaensen's DLL and adaptive-resampling designs (zita-ajbridge / alsa_in). The integral term removes the need for the 262144-call count-ratio feed-forward window. Keep the count ratio only as a one-shot initial estimate at lock. If a smoothing filter is kept in the loop, use a 1-pole whose time constant is much shorter than the loop time constant, not a long boxcar.
kept.benefit: Linear analysis (needs confirming in simulation) for 48 kHz in and out. With 64-sample blocks (about 1500 calls/s) the boxcar is about 10.9 s and the phase margin is about 38 deg: underdamped, slow fill-level hunting. With 256-sample blocks (about 375 calls/s) the boxcar is about 44 s; at the about 0.09 rad/s gain crossover the phase is about -203 deg, so the linear loop is unstable and only ring over/underflows or the +/-4% clamp bound it. The deprecated legacy constructor already notes this: L734 cuts gain to 1e-6 'to help Primary buffers > 512'. A time-based PI loop behaves the same at every buffer size, locks in seconds rather than after the 3 s startup plus a 4096-call ringmin, and holds the fill tightly enough to shrink the ring. That directly lowers VAC/rmatch latency, since latency is about rsize/2.
kept.risk: Changes the documented tuning parameters (ffmav_*, prop_*), so expose new bandwidth/damping parameters and map the old API onto them. A loop bandwidth that is too wide modulates pitch, so keep it well under 0.1 Hz. Test against real devices with bursty USB/network delivery.
kept.evidence: Loop algebra from L262 and L269 plus the boxcar transfer function sinc(wT/2)e^{-jwT/2}. Corroborated by the W4WMT comment at rmatch.c L734. F. Adriaensen, 'Using a DLL to filter time', LAC 2005. F. Adriaensen, 'Controlling adaptive resampling', LAC 2012. F. M. Gardner, Phaselock Techniques (type-II loop design).

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the code is accurate. control() (rmatch.c L256-273) runs on every xrmatchIN call (L359) and every xrmatchOUT call (L464). It pushes the instantaneous fill deviation into a boxcar xmav (L56-69) with prop_ringmax=16384 calls (create_rmatchV L519-524), and sets var = feed_forward - pr_gain*av_deviation, clamped to +/-4%. pr_gain = prop_gain*48000/nom_outrate (L147) cancels the dependence on sample rate, so the plant gain is k = nom_outrate*pr_gain ~= 0.192 s^-1 at any rate. Nothing scales the window by block size. The feed-forward term is an open-loop count ratio (in vs. out sample counts), not part of the fill loop, so the loop is effectively the integrator k/s in series with a boxcar of length 16384/call_rate seconds.

I redid the linear analysis. At 64/64 blocks and 48k (1500 calls/s, T ~= 10.9 s), crossover is ~0.166 rad/s with ~38 deg phase margin. At 256/256 (375 calls/s, T ~= 44 s), crossover is ~0.09 rad/s with phase ~ -202 deg, so the loop is linearly unstable. Gain at the -180 deg point is ~1.7.

I also ran a time-domain simulation of the exact update law: alternating in/out calls, a perfect feed-forward, a 500-sample initial offset, and the clamp. Peak |deviation| over the last 100 s of a 600 s run:
- 64-sample blocks: 32 (decays)
- 128-sample blocks: 95
- 256-sample blocks: ~36,000
- 512-sample blocks: ~73,000
- 1024-sample blocks: ~19,000 (clamp-bounded limit cycle)

In real code the growth is bounded instead by the over/underflow handlers (L318-336 force n_ring to rsize; dslew resets it near outsize). The result is periodic glitches plus up to +/-4% pitch swings, which is exactly what the proposal says.

The W4WMT comment at L734 (gain cut to 1e-6 'to help Primary buffers > 512') corroborates it. Hosts can work around it via setRMatchPropRingMax and setRMatchFeedbackGain, but WDSP does not normalise these itself, so the defaults are block-size dependent. That is not 'already done'.

The literature is real and relevant: Adriaensen's LAC 2005 DLL paper and LAC 2012 adaptive-resampling paper (zita-ajbridge), alsa_in's PI controller, and Gardner's type-II loop design. This matters for amateur radio because VAC/rmatch carries audio to and from digital-mode software (FT8 and others) and voice. Ring glitches and drift in the resampling ratio hurt decoding, and a tighter fill lock lets the ring and its latency shrink.

Caveats: the latency benefit is plausible but not demonstrated. A full PI/DLL redesign is more than the fix needs. Making prop_ringmax and ff_ringmax time-based (scaled by the actual call rate), or swapping the boxcar for a short 1-pole, already removes the block-size dependence with a far smaller API change.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
The rmatch fill-level loop has a fixed loop gain (~0.19 s^-1) but a smoothing delay that depends on block size. With the default parameters it is underdamped at 64-sample blocks and linearly unstable at about 256 samples per call or more. There it falls into a clamp- and over/underflow-bounded limit cycle: periodic ring glitches and up to +/-4% resampling-ratio (pitch) swings. My simulation confirms this.

Two fixes would make loop behaviour independent of buffer size. The minimal one is to express the averaging windows in seconds and scale them by the call rate, or to replace the boxcar with a short 1-pole. The fuller one is the proposed time-based type-II (PI/DLL) loop with explicit bandwidth well under 0.1 Hz. Either should remove periodic VAC under/overflows for larger buffers. Tighter fill control may also allow a smaller ring and lower latency, but that is unverified.

kept.title: xaamav divides by zero after an input stall and latches feed_forward at +inf
kept.file_function: rmatch.c:xaamav (L101-126, division at L117), control (L260-262, L269-271)
kept.current: *output = (double)a->neg / (double)a->pos with no guard. If the input side stalls (radio disconnected) while the audio output keeps calling xrmatchOUT, every positive entry eventually leaves the 262144-entry window (about 350 s with 64-sample output blocks at 48 kHz). Then pos == 0 and the ratio is +inf. feed_forward = 0.01*inf + 0.99*ff = inf, and once ff is inf it stays inf on every later update. var = inf - pr_gain*dev, which is clamped to 1.04 on every call.
kept.proposed: When pos == 0 (or neg == 0), hold the previous output instead of dividing. Reject non-finite values before the EMA (isfinite). Better still, freeze the feed-forward and P/I state while either side has not been called for more than N ms, and re-acquire when both resume. The new loop in the previous proposal should have the same freeze-on-stall rule.
kept.benefit: Without the fix, after a long input dropout the resampler stays 4% fast until something calls reset_rmatch or setRMatch*. The result is continuous overflows, crossfade glitches and a pitch shift. The fix costs nothing.
kept.risk: None meaningful. Holding the last ratio is the natural behaviour.
kept.evidence: Line-level: L117 has an unguarded division. L262 is an EMA that cannot recover from inf because 0.99*inf = inf. The L270 clamp hides the problem instead of fixing it.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code in rmatch.c and the description is accurate.

1. control() runs from both sides: xrmatchIN calls control(a, insize) and xrmatchOUT calls control(a, -outsize). If the input stalls, the output side keeps pushing negative entries into ffmav.
2. xaamav removes the oldest entry once load >= ringmax. Within 262144 consecutive output-only calls (create_rmatchV sets ffmav_max = 262144), every positive entry leaves the window, so pos becomes 0. Time to reach that is 262144 * outsize / 48000: about 350 s with 64-sample blocks, about 23 min with 256-sample blocks.
3. On that path (load >= ringmin) there is no guard. *output = neg/pos = +inf under IEEE arithmetic (no trap). The startup branch does guard neg>0 && pos>0, so the author handled the zero case there and not in steady state.
4. In control(), current_ratio stays inf after multiplying by inv_nom_ratio. feed_forward = 0.01*inf + 0.99*ff = inf, and stays inf on every later update. No NaN appears, since nothing computes inf - inf or 0*inf.
5. var = inf - pr_gain*av_deviation = inf, which the existing clamp pins to 1.04. Nothing in WDSP calls isfinite or resets ff. Only reset_rmatch, setRMatch* or recreating the object recovers it.
6. In varsamp.c, cvar = var * nom_ratio, so var = 1.04 produces about 4% more output samples. With the feedback path overwhelmed, that means repeated overflows and blend crossfades in xrmatchIN, plus the resampled pitch error. The claimed symptoms follow.

Realism: this needs the input side (radio → DSP → xrmatchIN) to stall while the audio-device callback keeps calling xrmatchOUT, for several to tens of minutes. A network drop or the radio going away while the sound card stream stays open is plausible. If the host app tears down and recreates rmatch on power-cycle, the user never sees it, which limits how often it happens.

Caveats:
- The neg==0 guard is not needed for the latch. An output stall gives ratio 0, which is finite and recovers.
- The freeze-on-stall and re-acquire idea is a reasonable refinement, not a required fix. Its reference to a "new loop" from another proposal is outside this check.
- The minimal fix (hold the last output when pos==0, plus isfinite before the EMA) is cheap and has negligible risk.
verdict.corrected_benefit: If the input side stalls for 262144 consecutive output calls (about 6 min at 64-sample blocks, about 23 min at 256), xaamav returns +inf. feed_forward latches at inf and var stays clamped at 1.04 until the rmatch is reset or recreated, which causes continuous overflows, crossfade glitches and about 4% resampling error after input resumes. Adding a pos==0 hold in xaamav and an isfinite check before the EMA in control() prevents the latch at almost no cost. Freezing the loop during a stall is an optional improvement. How often this happens depends on whether the host keeps the output stream running and does not recreate rmatch after a long input dropout.

kept.title: varsamp timing accumulators: replace the bit-truncation trick with one 64-bit fixed-point phase (needed for the float32 port; removes undefined behaviour)
kept.current: Output timing is tracked twice. isamps accumulates inv_cvar (L172) and h_offset accumulates delta = 1 - inv_cvar, wrapped to [0,1) (L160-162). The two stay exactly consistent (h_offset = frac(-isamps)) only because L151-153 cast &a->inv_cvar to uint64_t*, mask off the low 16 mantissa bits, and cast back. That makes every addend a multiple of about 2^-36, so the double sums are exact. The pointer cast is a strict-aliasing violation, which is undefined behaviour; clang's TBAA at -O2 may reorder the double store at L150 against the uint64 load at L152.
kept.proposed: Use a single unsigned 64-bit fixed-point time accumulator (Q32.32, or a Q0.64 fraction plus an integer carry). The step is round(inv_cvar * 2^32); varmode adds a fixed-point per-sample increment. The polyphase table index (top log2(R) bits of the fraction) and the linear-interpolation weight (the next bits, converted to float) are both read from the same word, so the two can never disagree and no bit-punning is needed. If type-punning is still wanted anywhere, use memcpy.
