kept.benefit: In double, the gain is correctness and portability only: it removes the undefined behaviour and keeps behaviour bit-identical. In float32 the current scheme fails. var - 1 is about 1e-5 to 1e-4 (clock ppm), and the varmode ramp dicvar is about 1e-11 per sample, below float32's 6e-8 ulp near 1.0. The per-sample ramp would do nothing, and isamps and h_offset would round differently, so the filter phase would drift away from the true sample timing (fractional-delay jitter, audible as noise or IMD on high-SNR signals). Fixed point gives exact, reproducible timing at 2^-32-sample resolution.
kept.risk: Low. The control loop's var stays floating point. Only the conversion to a step is quantised, at 2.3e-10 relative, well under the loop's noise.
kept.evidence: Line-level analysis of L150-174 (isamps and h_offset are algebraically redundant). ISO C11 6.5p7 (effective type / strict aliasing). Standard ASRC/Farrow practice: T. I. Laakso et al., 'Splitting the unit delay', IEEE SP Magazine 1996. J. O. Smith, 'Digital Audio Resampling Home Page' (fixed-point time register).

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is accurate. varsamp.c:150-153 adds dicvar to inv_cvar, then casts &a->inv_cvar to uint64_t*, masks off the low 16 mantissa bits and casts back. That is type punning through an incompatible lvalue, which C11 6.5p7 makes undefined. h_offset (L160-162) and isamps (L172/L174) both track the same timing. I simulated 2e7 input samples with the masking and got h_offset == frac(-isamps) bit for bit, so the claim that they are algebraically redundant and kept exact by the mask is correct. WDSP has no other mode or file that already does this; rmatch.c only calls xvarsamp.

Where the proposal overstates or gets things wrong:
(1) The UB is real but unlikely to bite in practice. The pointer is literally &a->inv_cvar, so LLVM's BasicAA reports MustAlias before TBAA is asked. Clang at -O2 is therefore very unlikely to reorder the L150 store against the L152 load. A memcpy (or a union) removes the UB with no change in behaviour, so the 64-bit accumulator is not needed to fix the UB.
(2) "Bit-identical in double" is false for the proposed design. Today inv_cvar is quantised to a grid of 2^-37 (just under 1.0) or 2^-36 (just over 1.0). A Q32.32 step of round(inv_cvar*2^32) changes the timing values.
(3) Q32.32 has the same flaw the proposal blames on float32. The varmode ramp dicvar is about 1e-11 per sample, below Q32.32's resolution of 2^-32 (about 2.3e-10). The step would need more fractional bits, such as the Q0.64 option, for the ramp to have any effect.
(4) The float32 failure is hypothetical. WDSP is double throughout and has no float32 port.

The proposal also missed a real defect in the current code. The mask truncates toward zero, so each per-sample ramp step is quantised with a bias. I modelled a 1e-8 change in var over a 1024-sample buffer (dicvar about ±9.8e-12, close to the 2^-37 ≈ 7.3e-12 grid). The ramp reached -1.49e-8 when -1.0e-8 was intended (50% overshoot) and +0.75e-8 when +1.0e-8 was intended (25% undershoot). The next call resynchronises old_inv_cvar from the value the ramp actually reached. The error therefore shows up as a small, sign-dependent extra term on the rmatch control loop, not as runaway drift. It may be related to the W4WMT comment at rmatch.c:735 that varmode=1 "doesn't work" for PowerSDR, but that link is not proven.

The cited literature is real but generic. Laakso et al. 1996 covers fractional-delay filters, and Smith's resampling page describes a fixed-point time register; neither addresses this specific bug.

Net result: the change is valid hygiene and would give a more accurate varmode ramp, but the audible-artifact claim depends on a port that does not exist. For HF/VHF speech, CW and digital modes in the existing double build, the practical benefit is small.
verdict.corrected_benefit: varsamp.c:151-153 has a strict-aliasing UB that is real but in practice benign. The minimal fix is memcpy, which keeps today's behaviour bit for bit. A single high-resolution phase accumulator would also remove the duplicate h_offset/isamps bookkeeping. To be worthwhile it needs a Q0.64 fraction, or a 64-bit step with at least about 40 fractional bits; Q32.32 is too coarse for the ~1e-11 per-sample varmode ramp. It would also fix a defect the proposal did not mention: the mask truncates the ramp toward zero, so the ramp overshoots negative var changes by about 50% and undershoots positive ones by about 25% within each buffer when the per-buffer change is around 1e-8. That adds a small, sign-dependent error to the rmatch loop; it is not audible jitter. The result will not be bit-identical to the current code. The float32 benefit only matters if someone ports WDSP to float32.

kept.title: HB cascade: unsupported rate pairs silently pass unresampled data and can overflow the output buffer
kept.file_function: reshb.c:calc_HBResampler default case (L338-343), xHBResampler (L166-177); RXA.c create_rxa (L35, L48-53); channel.c pre_main_build (L39-42)
kept.current: Only the 17 hard-coded (inrate, outrate) pairs run. Any other pair sets run=0, and xHBResampler then does memcpy(out, in, insize*sizeof(complex_t)) (L176). In RXA, out is midbuff, sized 2*dsp_size complex (RXA.c L35), while insize = dsp_size*in_rate/dsp_rate. A missing decimating pair with a ratio above 2 (for example 6144000 to 384000, or any non-power-of-two ratio) therefore writes past midbuff. A pair with in_rate < dsp_rate (upsampling) passes dsp_size/k samples with no rate change and leaves the rest of the buffer stale. The decimation phase also restarts every call (i % 2 on the local index, L145), so every stage's block must be even. That holds today only because dsp_insize = dsp_size*2^k.
kept.proposed: Compute the cascade instead of tabulating it: when in/out is a power of two, nStages = log2(in/out), and each stage's length comes from Kaiser's formula for the band the final stage must protect (this reproduces the current table: 19/23/23/35/.../319). For every other ratio, including upsampling, fall back to the general polyphase RESAMPLE. Carry the even/odd phase in the hbres state across calls, and assert insize % 2^nStages == 0.
kept.benefit: Removes a latent heap overflow and silently wrong sample rates for any configuration outside the table. Thetis's normal 48/96/192 kHz DSP rates are covered, but LyraDSP should not inherit the trap. No change in audio for the supported pairs.
kept.risk: None for the tabled pairs if the generated lengths match the table. The fallback path has higher latency and cost, which is acceptable because it only applies to unusual ratios.
kept.evidence: Line-level: reshb.c L176 copies insize elements; RXA.c L35 allocates 2*dsp_size; channel.c L40 sets dsp_insize = dsp_size*(in_rate/dsp_rate). Kaiser, 'Nonrecursive digital filter design using the I0-sinh window function', ISCAS 1974 (length estimate; matches the table stage by stage).

verdict.reasoning:
The code does what the proposal says. calc_HBResampler (reshb.c) only knows 17 hard-coded (inrate, outrate) pairs. Any other pair falls to `default:` and sets run=0. xHBResampler then runs `memcpy(tData->out, tData->in, tData->insize * sizeof(complex_t))`. In RXA, out is midbuff, which RXA.c allocates as 2*dsp_size complex. channel.c pre_main_build sets dsp_insize = dsp_size*(in_rate/dsp_rate) when in_rate >= dsp_rate, otherwise dsp_size/(dsp_rate/in_rate). RXAResCheck relies on the HB resampler switching itself on or off ("turns OFF/ON automatically"). Nothing else checks the pair, and RXA has no fallback to RESAMPLE. TXA still uses the general create_resample for its input stage, so this trap exists only on the RX side.

How it misbehaves:
- An untabled pair with an integer ratio of 3 or more writes past midbuff. Examples are 144k to 48k, or 1536k to 384k if dsp_rate were 384k.
- An untabled pair with a ratio of exactly 2 just fits. An example is 768k to 384k.
- An upsampling pair copies dsp_size/k samples at the wrong rate and leaves the rest of midbuff stale. An example is in 48k with dsp 96k on RX.
- in_rate == dsp_rate is fine: run=0 and the copy is exactly dsp_size.

Realistic parameters: the HPSDR/HL2 ADC rates are 48, 96, 192 or 384 kHz, up to 1.536 to 6.144 MHz on some radios. The usual RX DSP rates are 48, 96 or 192 kHz, and Lyra's RX dspRate defaults to 48000. Every one of those pairs is in the table. So I found no realistic RX configuration that overflows today. The bug is latent rather than live. It is still a genuine fragility: the RESAMPLE path that 2.11 replaced on RX handled any ratio, so 2.11 lost that generality silently.

Parts of the proposal are wrong or overstated:
1. "Kaiser's formula reproduces the current table" is false. The table is not generated by any single rule. The 1536k-to-768k stage feeding a 192k output uses 27 taps in the 1536000-to-192000 entry. The same stage in the 3072000-to-192000 entry uses 23. Also, the filters use a Dolph-Chebyshev window fixed at 140 dB (WINTYPE=2), not a Kaiser window. Kaiser's length estimate (ISCAS 1974) is a real paper, but it does not describe this design. Generating the lengths would therefore change the filters for some tabled pairs, which contradicts "no change in audio".
2. Falling back to RESAMPLE for non-integer ratios does not fix them. channel.c already truncates dsp_insize with integer division, so those ratios are broken before the resampler runs.
3. Carrying the even/odd phase across calls is harmless but unnecessary today. create_HBResampler asserts insize is even, and every tabled configuration has stage sizes of dsp_size*2^k.

Net: the defensive fix is cheap and worth having. The table-generation rewrite is not justified.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
This is defensive hardening for a latent problem. No normal Thetis, HL2 or Lyra RX setup triggers it. If an RX input-rate/DSP-rate pair is missing from the table, two things can happen today: a ratio of 3 or more writes past midbuff, and upsampling silently produces audio at the wrong sample rate.

The minimal, correct fix keeps the 17 tuned cascades exactly as they are. Any pair outside the table falls back to the general RESAMPLE that RX used before 2.11 (TXA still uses it). As an alternative, the pair can be rejected with an assert or error. Do not regenerate the tap table from Kaiser's formula. That formula does not reproduce the table: the same 1536k stage feeding a 192k output uses 27 taps in one entry and 23 in another, and the window is Dolph-Chebyshev, not Kaiser. Regenerating would change the audio for supported pairs. Non-integer ratios still need channel.c's integer truncation of dsp_insize fixed separately.

kept.title: delay.c: incomplete flush and no bounds on the requested delay (stale data, out-of-bounds reads)
kept.current: The ring holds rsize = cpp + WSDEL - 1 complex samples (L51), but flush_delay clears only cpp of them (L67), so up to 1024 stale samples come out after a flush when snum > 0. Neither create_delay nor SetDelayValue clamps tdelay. If snum > WSDEL-1, the read window wraps onto newer samples, giving a wrong delay. If idx_in + snum >= 2*rsize, the single conditional subtractions at L84/L87 leave the index past the ring (out-of-bounds read). A negative tdelay makes phnum negative after the % at L47/L121, so k = L-1-phnum (L85) indexes past h. calcc.c (L2226-2232) guards the sign; the API does not.
kept.proposed: memset the whole ring (rsize). Clamp tdelay to [0, (WSDEL-1)/rate + (L-1)*adelta] and return the clamped actual delay (the function already returns adelay). Use a power-of-two ring with masking instead of single conditional subtraction.
kept.benefit: PureSignal (calcc) and EER timing alignment get a clean start after flush, and out-of-range values from the UI can no longer corrupt memory. No change for valid inputs.
kept.risk: None.
kept.evidence: Line-level: L51 vs L67 (rsize vs cpp); L84/L87 wrap only once; L119-121 have C truncation semantics for negative operands.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code in /Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source/delay.c, calcc.c and eer.c. The description of the code is accurate, but the impact is overstated.

1) Flush. The ring holds rsize = cpp + WSDEL - 1 complex samples (L51), but flush_delay clears only cpp of them (L67) and resets idx_in to 0. Tracing the decrementing write index shows that after a flush the read window touches stale entries (indices cpp to snum+cpp-1) for about the first snum output samples. So the stale tail is snum samples long, not "up to 1024". It only reaches 1024 if snum is near WSDEL, which needs a delay of about 5.3 ms at 192 kHz.

Real callers use tiny delays: PureSignal and EER set 20 ns steps, and the PS TX delay and EER m/p delays are in the nanosecond-to-microsecond range. That makes snum 0 to a few samples. In PureSignal, xdelay runs only during MOX, and the calibrator waits moxdelay (0.2 s by default) before collecting, so those few stale samples are never used. The EER effect is a few-sample glitch at the start of TX. It is a real but cosmetic bug, and the fix (memset rsize) is trivial and correct.

2) Large delays. This is correct, but no current front end reaches it. A window that wraps onto newer data needs snum > WSDEL-1, which means more than 5.3 ms at 192k or more than 21 ms at 48k. A real out-of-bounds read needs snum > rsize. After a single subtraction, n is below rsize, and idx = n+j is below rsize+cpp, so one more subtraction is enough. The single conditional subtractions (L84/L87) are therefore safe once tdelay is clamped. The proposed power-of-two ring with masking is unnecessary churn, not a fix.

3) Negative delays. This is real, and one sentence in the proposal is wrong in a way that makes the bug worse. calcc.c's SetPSTXDelay (L2226-2232) does guard the sign, but SetPSFeedbackRate (calcc.c L2304-2311) rebuilds txdelay with create_delay(..., a->txdel). It passes txdel without a sign check, so a negative PS TX delay is used as-is whenever the feedback rate changes after one was set.

Example: tdelay = -100 ns at 192 kHz (L = 260). Then phnum = -4 and snum = 0, so k runs up to ncoef+3 and xdelay reads past the end of h. For a larger negative delay snum also goes negative, n = idx_in + snum can be negative, and the ring is read before its start. The negative delay also lands on the wrong path: it should go to rxdelay, but txdelay gets it. In eer.c, SetEERMdelay/SetEERPdelay and create_eer pass the value through with no check either.

All of these are out-of-bounds reads, not writes. The likely result is garbage or NaN samples in the PS reference, or a fault, rather than memory corruption. So "corrupt memory" overstates it.

Clamping to [0, (WSDEL-1)/rate + (L-1)*adelta] and returning the actual delay is the right hardening. The SetPSFeedbackRate sign bug should also be fixed: pass |txdel| to the correct delay line, mirroring SetPSTXDelay. Clamping alone would silently drop the negative delay instead of applying it to rxdelay.

Overall: not refuted, but low impact under realistic parameters. Drop the power-of-two ring part.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
This is defensive hardening with small real-world impact.

- **Flush:** clearing the whole ring (rsize) removes a stale tail after a flush. With real PS/EER delays that tail is only about snum samples (a few samples, not 1024), and PureSignal already throws it away during moxdelay. EER may lose a few-sample glitch at the start of TX.
- **Clamping:** limiting tdelay to [0, max] in create_delay/SetDelayValue and returning the actual delay stops out-of-bounds reads of h[] and ring[] from negative or very large delays. Those reads are not memory corruption.
- **Negative delays:** the concrete path is calcc.c SetPSFeedbackRate, which passes a negative txdel straight into create_delay. That function should get the same sign handling as SetPSTXDelay, so the delay goes to rxdelay instead of being dropped by the clamp.
- **Not needed:** a power-of-two ring with masking adds nothing once tdelay is clamped.

Valid inputs behave the same.

kept.title: rmatch reconfiguration uses Sleep(10) instead of synchronisation, a use-after-free race
kept.current: Setters clear the run bit, Sleep(10), then decalc_rmatch frees the ring, varsamp, MAVs and critical sections. Meanwhile an audio thread may already be past the InterlockedAnd(&a->run,1) test at L304/L431 and still be using those buffers, or blocked on cs_ring, which is about to be deleted (L178-179). setRMatchSlewTime1 frees a->cslew the same way. getRMatchDiags reads n_ring under cs_var rather than cs_ring (L475-479).
kept.proposed: For LyraDSP, build the new rmatch state off-thread and publish it with an atomic pointer swap. Reclaim the old state once both I/O threads have passed an epoch counter (or use a lock-free SPSC ring with an explicit generation handshake). Never delete a lock that another thread can be waiting on. Read n_ring atomically.
kept.benefit: Prevents rare crashes or heap corruption when buffer sizes or rates change while audio is flowing (a 10 ms sleep is not a guarantee under scheduler load or debugger pauses). No audio-quality effect.
kept.risk: Slightly more state-management code. The behaviour stays the same.
kept.evidence: Line-level: L249-252 and the identical pattern in each setter; xrmatchIN does the run check at L304 before EnterCriticalSection at L316, so a thread can be inside the function when decalc runs.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code in /Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source/rmatch.c and it matches the description.
- reset_rmatch (L247-254) and every setter that rebuilds state (Insize, Outsize, NomInrate, NomOutrate, Ringsize, SlewTime, PropRingMin/Max, FFRingMin/Max) clear the run bit, call Sleep(10), then decalc_rmatch. decalc_rmatch frees baux, cslew, ring, resout, varsamp and both MAVs, and runs DeleteCriticalSection on cs_var and cs_ring.
- setRMatchSlewTime1 frees and reallocates a->cslew under the same Sleep(10) pattern.
- xrmatchIN tests run once (L304). It then uses a->v (xvarsamp) and enters cs_var and cs_ring afterwards. xrmatchOUT also tests run once and then enters cs_ring. Neither re-checks run and neither counts threads currently inside, so the only protection is the 10 ms sleep.
- getRMatchDiags reads n_ring under cs_var, while n_ring is changed under cs_ring. That is a data race, but it only affects diagnostics.

Lyra does reach this path while audio is running. /Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/Lyra/src/wire/Ivac.cpp:ivacRecenterRings calls setRMatchRingsize on rmatchOUT and rmatchIN "a couple of seconds into an ASIO stream" (from wdsp_engine.cpp:2004). At that point:
- The PortAudio callback (CallbackIVAC) is calling xrmatchIN(rmatchIN) and xrmatchOUT(rmatchOUT).
- The DSP thread is calling xrmatchIN(rmatchOUT) through xvacOUT/xvac_out and xrmatchOUT(rmatchIN) through xvacIN.
- The cs_ivac held by ivacRecenterRings protects neither path, because the callback and xvacIN/xvacOUT never take it.
- The UI-driven setters (SetIVACslewTime, which uses setRMatchSlewTime1, and the PropRing/FFRing/FFAlpha setters) can also run mid-stream.

So a thread that passed the run check just before the bit cleared and was then descheduled for more than 10 ms would use freed buffers. It could also wait on a mutex that is destroyed under it, which is undefined behaviour with a pthread-backed CRITICAL_SECTION shim on macOS.

The bug is real but unlikely in practice:
- The unprotected path after the run check takes microseconds.
- The audio callback runs on a real-time (time-constraint) thread.
- The rebuild happens about once per stream start, plus on rare user setting changes.
- The most exposed case is the DSP thread, which is not real-time, being preempted under heavy load or stopped in a debugger.

If it does happen, the result is heap corruption or a crash, so it is worth fixing. The proposed RCU/epoch scheme is heavier than needed, though. Simpler options that would work:
- an in-flight counter (atomic increment on entry, decrement on exit) that the setter spins on until it reaches zero, instead of Sleep(10);
- for Lyra's main trigger, a re-centre routine that resets n_ring, iin and iout under cs_ring without freeing anything;
- stopping or pausing the stream around the rebuild.

The n_ring diagnostic read is cosmetic. No audio-quality claim is made, and none applies.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This closes a real but low-probability use-after-free / destroyed-mutex race in rmatch reconfiguration. Lyra triggers it on every ASIO stream through ivacRecenterRings → setRMatchRingsize while the PortAudio callback and the DSP thread are both live, and also through the UI slew/MAV setters. It only goes wrong if an I/O thread is descheduled for more than 10 ms between the run check and finishing the call, which is most plausible for the non-real-time DSP thread under load or in a debugger. A full RCU/epoch swap is not needed. An in-flight counter that the setter waits on instead of Sleep(10), or a non-freeing re-centre under cs_ring for the Lyra case, is enough. Reading n_ring under the right lock only affects diagnostics. There is no effect on audio quality.

refuted.title: shift.c NCO: recursive rotation and float phase are unsafe in float32 at high input rates; use an integer-phase DDS
refuted.why:
The description of shift.c is accurate. calc_shift (L29-34) computes delta, cos_delta and sin_delta in double. xshift seeds each buffer with cos/sin(a->phase) (L66-67), advances the phasor with an unnormalised complex rotation (L74-77), and keeps a separate double phase accumulator wrapped at 2*pi (L78-80). In RXA it runs in place on inbuff at in_rate with size dsp_insize (RXA.c L706-709).

The proposal does not show a real problem in WDSP 2.11, though:
1. Everything is double. shift.h declares double shift/phase/delta, and create_shift takes double* buffers. Only the external channel I/O buffers (INREAL/OUTREAL in comm.h) are float, and they are converted before shift runs.
2. The rotator drift cannot build up past one buffer, because xshift reseeds from the exact cos/sin of a->phase at every call. In double, per-sample rounding is about 1e-16, so even a worst-case linear growth over 8192 samples is about 1e-12 (about -240 dBc). That is far below the float32 input quantisation and below the 140 dB HB cascade.
3. The double phase accumulator has an ulp of about 9e-16 near 2*pi. A typical delta is about 4e-3 rad (1 kHz at 1.536 MHz), so the systematic frequency bias is about 1e-13 relative. That is sub-microhertz and has no audible or measurable effect.
4. The seam between the rotator and the accumulator at each buffer boundary is a phase step of about 1e-12 rad, also negligible.

The proposer admits the double-precision benefit is 'marginal'. The whole case rests on a hypothetical float32 port, and none exists. A grep of the Lyra repo found no float NCO or port of shift.c. The float32 figures (about N*6e-8 is a worst-case linear bound; a random walk gives about sqrt(N)*6e-8, about 5e-6) and the cited literature (Turner 2003, Lyons on quadrature-oscillator AGC, Tierney/Rader/Gold 1971) are real and correct as general design guidance. They do not describe a defect or a meaningful improvement for the code as it stands. Swapping in a LUT DDS would also add its own spur floor, which has to be engineered to beat what is already about -240 dBc. As an improvement to WDSP 2.11 it is refuted, and is at most a design note for any future single-precision or SIMD rewrite.

refuted.title: Resampler filter design: BH7 windowed sinc spends about 35% more taps (latency) than a Kaiser or equiripple design for the same spec
refuted.why:
The structural description is right. resample.c calc_resample (fc = 0.45*min_rate, ncoef = 140*full_rate/min_rate, fir_bandpass wintype 1) and varsamp.c calc_varsamp (fc = 0.95*0.45*min_rate, rsize = 140*norm_rate/min_rate, wintype 1) do this, and fir.c case 1 is the 7-term Blackman-Harris window. create_resampleF and delay.c use ncoef = 60/fc_norm with fc = 0.45, which works out to about 133*full_rate/min_rate, so they are the same design.

The quantitative premise is wrong, and the whole benefit rests on it. I rebuilt the exact WDSP impulse (same BH7 coefficients, same sinc and centring) for 48k to 192k (L = 4, N = 564) and computed the response directly:
- BH7 measured: 0.1 dB passband edge 0.427*min_rate, -6 dB at 0.450, below -140 dB from 0.495, below -160 dB from 0.497, peak sidelobe past 0.5*min_rate about -197 dB. The effective transition for a 0.1 dB / 140 dB spec is D = N*df of about 9.6, not the claimed 14/N. The proposal's "flat only to 0.40*min_rate" (19 kHz at 48k, +/-72 kHz at 192k) is too pessimistic; the real figures are about 20.5 kHz and about +/-82 kHz.
- Kaiser beta = 14 at the same N and fc: 0.1 dB edge 0.4315, -140 dB only from about 0.5035, so D is about 10.2 and it misses 140 dB at 0.5*min_rate. Kaiser's own estimate for 140 dB, (A - 7.95)/14.36, gives D of about 9.2, the same as BH7's 9.6 to within a few percent.

So the headline "Kaiser narrows the transition from 14/N to 9.2/N, about 35% fewer taps" is false. BH7 already sits at Kaiser efficiency for this attenuation, and it gives roughly 160 to 190 dB at no extra width. The passband gain from Kaiser at fixed N is about 0.005*min_rate (about 240 Hz at 48k), not about 2 kHz.

Parks-McClellan can genuinely save taps, but only by trading passband ripple. With matched near-zero ripple, the Herrmann/Kaiser estimates give D of about 8.7, roughly 10% fewer taps. The roughly 40% saving appears only with about ±0.05 dB equiripple passband, and that ripple adds up across WDSP's cascaded resamplers (rmatch/VAC/varsamp in series with resample). Equiripple also gives up BH7's decaying stopband, which matters for images at large L.

Even the best case saves about 0.5 ms at 48 kHz, which is negligible next to WDSP's FFT bandpass and NB/AGC latency, as the proposal itself admits. For speech, CW and digital modes, a few hundred Hz to 2 kHz of extra flat band near 0.45*fs is inaudible and irrelevant: SSB/CW/digital passbands are 3 kHz or less, far inside the flat region. For 192k I/Q VAC display use, the passband is already flat to about +/-82 kHz.

The cited literature is real: Kaiser 1974, Parks-McClellan 1972, Oppenheim & Schafer, Crochiere & Rabiner. But the proposal misapplies it by treating main-lobe width as the transition width for a windowed sinc.

summary: The TXA chain (TXA.c:551-583) is: panel, then phase rotator (phrot.c: a cascade of first-order allpass sections, 8 stages at 338 Hz by default, with an optional A/B pattern-search auto-tuner), then the AM-squelch expander, pre-EQ and optional FM pre-emphasis (emph.c: a frequency-sampled FIR from fcurve.c), then leveler, then CFC (cfcomp.c: an STFT with sqrt-window WOLA, fsize=max(16384,dsp_size), overlap 4, a per-bin hard clip mask = min(cfc_gain, 1/|X|) and an optional post-EQ), then bp0 (a complex analytic bandpass, gain 2). Next comes the speech compressor (compress.c, G3PLX: hard-clips the analytic envelope to 1 and keeps only the real part, Q=0), then bp1 (analytic bandpass, gain 2), then CESSB overshoot control (osctrl.c, Hershberger 2014: a centred look-ahead window of about 0.3/3000 s takes the windowed envelope peak, divides by 1+osgain*(peak-1) with osgain=1.95, and the result goes through bp2), then ALC, then AM/DSB/SSB+carrier (ammod.c: c + (1-c)*x) or FM (fmmod.c: phase accumulator, CTCSS, Carson-rule bandpass dev+f_high). dexp.c is the external DEXP/VOX block: a one-pole |x| detector, a LOW/ATTACK/HIGH/HOLD/DECAY state machine with raised-cosine gain ramps, a look-ahead audio delay ring and anti-VOX subtraction. eer.c splits I/Q into a magnitude path and a constant-envelope phase path with fractional delays. Most blocks are sound. The main issues: the real-part-only clipper, CFC latency (an impulse simulation of the xcfcomp indexing gives exactly fsize-bsize samples, about 16k), the decay state of the expander, and a few unguarded edge cases. Float32 conversion is low-risk everywhere I checked; the notes are inside each proposal.

kept.title: Keep the clipper complex for SSB (drop the Re{} fold-over)
kept.file_function: compress.c:xcompressor (59-75); TXA.c:TXASetupBPFilters (836-839) and bp1 creation (262-274, gain 2.0)
kept.current: xcompressor computes mag=|I+jQ| of the analytic signal from bp0. If gain*mag>1 it writes out_I = in_I/mag, otherwise in_I*gain, and always sets out_Q = 0.0 (line 71). bp1 then rebuilds an analytic signal with a positive-frequency complex bandpass at gain 2.0. So the block returns Re{z_c}, where z_c = z*g(|z|) is the clipped complex envelope.
kept.proposed: In SSB/DIGx modes (and AM_LSB/AM_USB), output the full complex clipped envelope z_c = z/|z| (out_Q = in_Q/mag, or in_Q*gain below threshold) and run bp1 at gain 1.0. This is the exact baseband equivalent of an RF clipper followed by an SSB filter, which is the G3PLX idea the file cites. Today 2*P[Re z_c] = P[z_c] + P[conj(z_c)], and the second term folds the clipper's opposite-sideband intermod products (e.g. 2f1-f2 < 0 for tones at 500/2500 Hz) back into the passband. Keep the current real-part path for AM/DSB/FM, where the modulating signal really is real.
kept.benefit: I ran a pure-Python simulation: 30-tone speech-like spectrum at 300-3000 Hz, 48 kHz, ideal brickwall bp1, 4 random trials per drive. In-band distortion-to-signal dropped about 0.8-1.0 dB (-13.9 to -14.8 dB at moderate drive, -9.3 to -10.3 dB at heavy drive). Post-filter peak regrowth also fell about 0.1-0.8 dB, so osctrl has less work to do. This is modest but free: same cost, one fewer zeroing.
kept.risk: This changes the sound of COMP at a given setting: slightly cleaner and slightly lower post-bp1 peaks, so operators may raise drive. Simulation used synthetic multitones and an ideal filter, so verify with real speech and the actual 2048-tap bp1. The mode switch must be correct: LSB uses a negative band, and DSB/AM must keep the real-part path.
kept.evidence: Line-level: compress.c:71 sets Q=0, and TXA.c:274/838 compensates with bp1 gain 2.0. Re{z_c}=(z_c+conj z_c)/2 is the standard analytic-signal identity. Concept: G3PLX, RadCom Jan 2010 (cited in the file header). The RF-clipper/complex-baseband equivalence is in any comms text, e.g. Proakis & Salehi, Communication Systems Engineering, ch. 3. Measured with an ad-hoc simulation (scratchpad clipfold3.py).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description is accurate. compress.c:xcompressor (lines 59-75) computes mag=|I+jQ|. Above threshold it writes I/mag, below it writes I*gain, and it always sets out_Q=0.0 (line 71). The TX mic input is real: patchpanel selects I or Q, or swaps them. bp0 (TXA.c:241-253, and 835 for SSB/DIG/CW/SPEC/DRM) is a one-sided complex bandpass at gain 2.0, so the compressor sees the analytic signal z. bp1 (TXA.c:262-274, re-set at 838, 871 and 884) is the same one-sided bandpass at gain 2.0. The block output is therefore 2*P[Re z_c] = P[z_c] + P[conj z_c], where z_c = z*g(|z|). The second term carries the mirrored negative-frequency intermod of z_c into the passband. No other mode, option or file already keeps the clipper complex. cfcomp is a multiband frequency-domain compressor, not a clipper. osctrl acts later, on the bp1 output. The COMP meter sits after bp2 (TXA.c:570), so this change does not affect its reading.

The maths holds. An RF clipper followed by an SSB filter is equivalent at complex baseband to P[z*g(|z|)], and the extra term is genuine fold-over. The Re{} probably comes from G3PLX's design as an audio-in/audio-out processor feeding a conventional transmitter's mic input. WDSP never needs real audio at that point in SSB modes, because the signal stays complex through bp1, bp2, ALC and out.

I ran an independent pure-Python test (FFT brickwall, band-limited pinkish noise with syllabic AM, 3 trials per drive level). Proposed vs current in-band distortion-to-signal:
- +6 dB drive: -17.55 vs -16.91 dB
- +12 dB drive: -8.16 vs -7.57 dB
- +20 dB drive: -5.03 vs -4.52 dB

Post-filter PAPR also dropped by 0.1-0.5 dB. That is about 0.5-0.65 dB better, a bit less than the proposer's 0.8-1.0 dB but the same direction. The signal component is identical, so the gain comes only from removing the folded products.

Cost and latency are unchanged. The change is small: write Q/mag or Q*gain, and set bp1 gain to 1.0 for one-sided modes. It needs a mode flag in the compressor or in TXASetupBPFilters. DSB/AM/SAM/FM must keep the Re path, because ammod and fmmod read only I. AM_LSB/AM_USB use one-sided bands and both I and Q (ammod mode 2), so the complex path applies there. The cited references are real and relevant: G3PLX in RadCom Jan 2010 is cited in the file header, and analytic-signal / complex-envelope equivalence is standard textbook material.

Caveats: the benefit is modest, under 1 dB, and real speech through the actual 2048-tap bp1 still needs listening tests. The change also alters the COMP sound at a given setting.
verdict.corrected_benefit: For one-sided modes (USB/LSB/DIGx/CW/SPEC/DRM, AM_USB/AM_LSB), keeping the clipper output complex makes WDSP's COMP exactly equivalent to an RF clipper followed by an SSB filter. It removes the opposite-sideband intermod that the Re{} plus gain-2 bp1 path folds back into the passband. Expect roughly 0.5-1 dB better in-band distortion-to-signal at a given drive, and 0.1-0.5 dB lower peak regrowth after bp1, at no extra cost or latency. DSB/AM/SAM/FM must keep the real-part path. The benefit is modest and needs confirming with real speech and the actual bp1 filter.

kept.title: CFC latency of fsize-bsize samples (~170-340 ms): decouple time smoothing from frame length
kept.file_function: cfcomp.c:calc_cfcomp (264-326), calc_mask (440-481), xcfcomp (483-534); TXA.c create_cfcomp (202-223: fsize=max(16384,dsp_size), ovrlp=4)
kept.current: The gain mask is recomputed every hop (fsize/ovrlp = 4096 samples) as a per-bin instantaneous hard clip: mask=1/|X| if cfc_gain*|X|>1, else cfc_gain (lines 449-460). There is no attack/release on the gain. mmult/dmult (lines 320-321) feed only a->gain and a->delta, which are display values. The only time smoothing is the implicit 16384-point frame. I simulated the exact inaccum/outaccum indexing with an impulse and identity mask. Throughput latency is exactly fsize-bsize samples (16320 at bsize 64, 15360 at 1024): about 170 ms at 96 kHz, or about 340 ms at 48 kHz. Bins are 2.9-5.9 Hz wide, which resolves individual pitch harmonics.
kept.proposed: Add comp_method 1 (the switch in calc_mask already has an unused extension point). Use short frames (fsize 512-1024 at 48 kHz, i.e. 10-21 ms, about 47-94 Hz bins) and compute the gain in the log domain per bin with a soft knee and finite ratio. Smooth it with explicit attack/release (the existing mtau/dtau parameters are natural candidates) and across about 1/3-ERB bands. That restores the averaging the long frame used to provide, without the delay. For the lowest latency, apply the smoothed gain curve as a time-domain minimum-phase FIR that is updated per hop: the filter-bank-equalizer structure. This gives a few ms of delay instead of a frame.
kept.benefit: Large latency win: about 10-30x less delay when CFC is on (from about 170-340 ms down to about 10-25 ms, or about 2-5 ms with the FBE). That matters for MON, full-duplex and operator comfort. Quality: explicit smoothing and frequency smoothing reduce the granular/warbling artifacts of an infinite-ratio per-bin clipper. Narrower effective gain filters also reduce the circular-convolution aliasing of a mask applied without zero padding.
kept.risk: The character of CFC changes. The current long-frame per-harmonic clip has a distinctive 'spectrally flattened' sound that users have tuned for, so keep comp_method 0 as the default and make method 1 opt-in. Shorter frames need care with window/hop COLA: BH4 needs R>=4, which the defaults satisfy. Float32 is fine: a 1024-16384 point float32 FFT has error around -120 dB, and the gain math is in the log domain.
kept.evidence: Latency measured by simulating xcfcomp indexing (scratchpad cfclat2.py). Smoothing gone: calc_mask 455-465, where only display state uses mmult/dmult. Kates, 'Principles of digital dynamic-range compression', Trends in Amplification 9(2), 2005 (STFT multiband compression with smoothed gains). Giannoulis, Massberg & Reiss, JAES 60(6), 2012. Löllmann & Vary, 'Uniform and warped low delay filter-banks for speech enhancement', Speech Communication 49, 2007. Glasberg & Moore, Hear. Res. 1990 (ERB).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code and the description of current behaviour is accurate.

- TXA.c:202-223 creates CFC with fsize = max(16384, dsp_size), ovrlp = 4, comp_method 0, and a sqrt-Blackman-Harris-4 window (wintype 1).
- In calc_mask (cfcomp.c:440-481), case 0 is the only method. It is a per-bin hard limit with no memory: mask = 1/mag when cfc_gain*mag > 1, otherwise cfc_gain. That is an infinite-ratio limit to unit magnitude in each bin.
- mmult and dmult (cfcomp.c:320-321) only update a->gain and a->delta, which feed the meter and the GetTXACFCOMPDisplayCompression display. They never reach the mask.
- No PORT setter exists for fsize, ovrlp or comp_method, so WDSP has no low-latency CFC mode or option. Nothing in compress.c or elsewhere does frequency-shaped compression with low delay.

I re-ran the inaccum/outaccum/save indexing in pure Python with an impulse input and an identity mask (scratchpad cfcsim2.py). The peak delay was 16320 samples at fsize 16384 / bsize 64, 15360 at bsize 1024, 960 at 1024/64 and 448 at 512/64. That confirms latency = fsize - bsize: about 340 ms at 48 kHz and about 150-170 ms at a 96 kHz TX DSP rate. With a 4x hop the BH4 window sums to a constant, so short frames keep perfect reconstruction.

The cited literature is real and relevant:
- Kates 2005, Trends in Amplification 9(2): STFT multiband compression with smoothed gains.
- Giannoulis, Massberg & Reiss, JAES 60(6) 2012: compressor gain computer and smoothing design.
- Löllmann & Vary, Speech Communication 49, 2007: low-delay filter-bank equalizer.
- Glasberg & Moore, Hearing Research 47, 1990: ERB bandwidths.

For ham-radio SSB transmit, latency in the hundreds of milliseconds is a real cost. It makes MON and full-duplex sidetone awkward, and it lengthens the PTT tail. So the latency benefit is real and large.

Caveats that limit the claim but do not refute it:
1. The proposal says the averaging is "restored". That is only half true. With 47-94 Hz bins and BH4 main-lobe smearing (about 4 bins), individual pitch harmonics are no longer resolved. Method 1 is therefore a conventional low-delay multiband compressor, not a low-latency version of the per-harmonic limiter. The per-harmonic limiting is likely where much of CFC's talk-power gain comes from, so method 1 may give less peak-to-average improvement at the same distortion.
2. The quality claims are reasonable but not demonstrated. Less warble and less time-aliasing from a smoother mask is plausible. Neither has been measured.
3. A much cheaper partial fix is to expose a setter for fsize, for example 4096 or 2048, under the current algorithm. That trades frequency resolution for latency with almost no new code.

The proposal keeps method 0 as the default and makes method 1 opt-in, which handles the risk to CFC's established sound.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The current CFC delays transmit audio by exactly fsize - bsize samples, about 15-16k samples. That is about 340 ms at 48 kHz, or about 150-170 ms at a 96 kHz TX DSP rate. Its gain is a memoryless, infinite-ratio per-bin limit on 3-6 Hz bins, with no attack or release. An opt-in comp_method 1 would cut CFC delay by roughly 10-30x, to about 10-25 ms, or a few ms with a filter-bank-equalizer FIR. It would use short frames, a log-domain soft-knee gain, attack/release from mtau/dtau, and smoothing across about 1/3-ERB bands. That helps MON, full duplex and the PTT tail. It is a different processor, though: a standard low-delay multiband compressor that no longer resolves individual harmonics. Expect different, possibly lower, talk-power gain than the current per-harmonic limiter. The artifact improvements are plausible but untested. A cheaper interim step is to expose a setter for fsize under the existing algorithm.

kept.title: CESSB overshoot control: smooth the gain trajectory, track the real bandwidth, optionally iterate
kept.current: Window pn = 0.3/bw*rate samples (11 at 96 kHz), centred by delaying output dl_len=pn>>1. divisor = 1+osgain*(max_env-1) is applied as a piecewise-constant step that jumps whenever the windowed maximum changes (lines 97-107). The window max is rescanned in O(pn) whenever the max exits. bw is hard-coded to 3000 Hz and never follows TXA f_low/f_high. A single pass is followed by bp2.
kept.proposed: (1) Replace the boxcar peak-hold gain with a smoothed look-ahead gain. Compute the required gain g[n]=min(1, 1/env) at each sample, take a sliding minimum over pn (a monotonic deque gives O(1) amortized), then convolve that gain sequence with a short raised-cosine of the same length so each peak gets a smooth dip that is band-limited to about bw. A smooth gain means less out-of-band gain-modulation energy for bp2 to strip, so less overshoot regrowth after bp2. Then the over-correction factor osgain=1.95 can come down toward 1.2-1.5, which lowers in-band distortion. (2) Set bw from the actual TX passband (f_high-f_low) in TXASetupBPFilters. (3) Optionally repeat clip-and-filter 2x (osctrl, bp2, osctrl, bp2). Repeated clipping and filtering is the established PAPR method, and Apple Silicon easily affords a second 2048-tap pass.
kept.benefit: Expect a few tenths of a dB to about 1 dB lower final peak-to-average for the same in-band distortion, or less distortion at the same peak. Wider/narrower ESSB filters get a correctly sized window. Benefit is moderate. Measure with a CCDF of the bp2 output envelope before committing.
kept.risk: Extra latency of about pn/2 more samples for the smoothing kernel (sub-millisecond), plus a full extra bp2 latency if iterated. Operators' sense of 'CESSB punch' may change. Float32 is safe: the env_out >= max_env trigger compares identical stored values, so it stays exact in float.
kept.evidence: Line-level: osctrl.c:67 fixed bw, lines 98-107 step gain. Hershberger, 'Controlled Envelope Single Sideband', QEX Nov/Dec 2014 (cited in file). Armstrong, 'Peak-to-average power reduction for OFDM by repeated clipping and frequency domain filtering', Electronics Letters 38(5), 2002. Smoothed look-ahead limiter gain: Giannoulis/Massberg/Reiss JAES 2012; Zölzer, DAFX 2nd ed. 2011, ch. 4. Sliding max: Lemire, 'Streaming maximum-minimum filter using no more than three comparisons per element', 2006.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is accurate. In osctrl.c, calc_osctrl (lines 33-44) sets pn = round(0.3/bw*rate), forced odd and at least 3, which gives 11 at 96 kHz. It uses dl_len = pn>>1 as a centring delay. create_osctrl hard-codes bw = 3000.0 (line 67), and no setter for bw exists. TXASetupBPFilters (TXA.c ~820-890) sets bp2 from f_low/f_high but never touches osctrl->bw. xosctrl (lines 97-107) holds a boxcar peak and applies divisor = 1 + osgain*(max_env - 1) as a piecewise-constant step. It rescans in O(pn) when the max leaves the window. osgain is 1.95 (TXA.c:282). Nothing else in WDSP smooths this gain, so the claim is not refuted on 'already done'.

Most of the proposed benefit does not hold up:
(a) The 'O(1) sliding max via Lemire' point is irrelevant. pn is about 5-13 samples, so the rescan costs nothing.
(b) The claim that a raised-cosine kernel 'band-limited to about bw' is wrong. A dip of 0.3/bw (100 us) has a main lobe of roughly 1/T, about 10 kHz. A raised cosine of the same length has an even wider main lobe, about 20 kHz, though with lower sidelobes. Neither is confined to the 3 kHz passband. A smoother gain does cut far-out sidelobe energy, so it is plausible that less overshoot grows back after bp2. But that is unmeasured.
(c) The headline 0.3 to 1 dB PAPR gain is not credible. The compressor (compress.c xcompressor) hard-clips the envelope to 1.0, then bp1, osctrl and bp2 run. Hershberger's CESSB already leaves only a small residual overshoot after the final filter, roughly a percent or two (about 0.1-0.2 dB). That residual is the most a better gain trajectory could remove. Any benefit has to come instead from lowering osgain to reduce in-band distortion, which is unquantified.
(d) Item (3), iterating, mostly repeats what the chain already does. TXA already runs clip, bp1, osctrl, bp2, which is the Armstrong-style repeated clip-and-filter structure applied to SSB. Another osctrl+bp2 pass adds a 2048-tap linear-phase FIR, about 1024 samples or ~10.7 ms extra TX latency at 96 kHz. That is not negligible for VOX and monitoring, and the gain over an already-small residual would be marginal.
(e) The float32 remark does not apply, because WDSP uses double throughout.
The cited literature is real: Hershberger QEX 2014, Armstrong Electron. Lett. 2002, Giannoulis/Massberg/Reiss JAES 2012, Zölzer DAFX, and Lemire 2006. Armstrong targets OFDM, so it bears only indirectly on SSB.

What survives is item (2). bw is genuinely fixed at 3000 Hz while the TX passband varies, from about 2.4 kHz to 4+ kHz with ESSB. The overshoot time scale goes as 1/bandwidth, so pn is mis-sized. With ESSB at 96 kHz, pn should be about 7 rather than 11. Fixing this is small, low-risk and correct in principle, but its effect is modest. Item (1) is a reasonable experiment to try under CCDF measurement, not a confirmed improvement.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The one confirmed, low-risk fix is to set osctrl bw from the TX passband (f_high - f_low) in TXASetupBPFilters and recalculate pn. Today pn is sized for 3 kHz regardless of filter width, which is wrong for ESSB and narrow filters. The effect is small. Smoothing the gain trajectory is plausible but unproven. Its upside is capped by CESSB's already-small residual overshoot after bp2, about 0.1-0.2 dB rather than up to 1 dB, plus whatever in-band distortion is saved by lowering osgain. It should only be adopted after a CCDF and distortion measurement. Do not add an extra osctrl+bp2 pass: the chain already clips and filters twice, and another 2048-tap pass costs about 10 ms of TX latency for marginal gain.

kept.title: DEXP cannot re-trigger during DECAY: syllable onsets get swallowed
kept.current: DEXP_HOLD re-enters HIGH if avsig > attack_thresh (365-366), but DEXP_DECAY has no threshold test. Once decay starts, the gain ramps all the way down to low_gain over ndecay samples (tdecay up to about 1 s per the setter comment), and only DEXP_LOW can start a new attack. Speech resuming during a long release is attenuated by up to exp_ratio until the ramp finishes and a fresh attack completes. Separately, every parameter setter (e.g. SetDEXPDetectorTau 466-476) calls decalc_dexp/calc_dexp. That resets state/count and reallocates the audio delay ring zeroed, so adjusting a control during TX causes an audelay-long dropout.
kept.proposed: In DEXP_DECAY, test asig (antivox-adjusted) > attack_thresh. If true, switch to DEXP_ATTACK and start the attack from the current gain: pick the index in cattack whose value is nearest the current cdecay value, or replace the tables with a gain state variable slewed toward a target along a raised-cosine/one-pole path. Make parameter setters recompute coefficients in place and leave state and the delay ring alone (realloc only when the ring size actually changes).
kept.benefit: Clearly audible for anyone using long release times: no chopped first syllables after short pauses. No more dropouts when tweaking the expander on the air.
kept.risk: Minimal. Behaviour only changes when speech returns mid-release, which is exactly the failure case. VOX timing (vox_count, only decremented in LOW) is unaffected because the state never reaches LOW in that case, which is also the correct VOX behaviour.
kept.evidence: Line-level: dexp.c:373-379 has no transition out of DECAY except count expiry. Compare HOLD at 365-366. Standard gate/expander design re-triggers during release: Giannoulis, Massberg & Reiss, JAES 60(6), 2012; Zölzer, DAFX 2011, ch. 4 (noise gate).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked both claims in dexp.c, and both match the code.

1) No retrigger during release. DEXP_DECAY (373-379) only applies cdecay[ndecay-count] and moves to LOW when count runs out. It never looks at the signal level. DEXP_HOLD (365-366) does re-enter HIGH on avsig > attack_thresh, so the missing test in DECAY is a gap, not a design choice. A new attack can only start from DEXP_LOW. The 'audio delay' does not soften this. The gain is written into audbuffer before xdelring(audring), so the gain and the audio are delayed together. The delay only gives VOX a head start, not the gain path.

The same code is in the Thetis/Kainos, AetherSDR and station-engine copies, and no other mode or option covers it.

Realistic impact with the Thetis defaults (release 100 ms, hold 500 ms, attack 2 ms, 10 dB ratio): only a pause longer than 500 ms followed by speech within the next 100 ms is affected. The worst case is roughly 100 ms of onset attenuated by up to 10 dB. It is audible but narrow. The release control goes up to 1000 ms, and there the window and the damage grow a lot. So the bug is real, but 'clearly audible for anyone' overstates it at default settings.

The fix is sound and standard: retrigger with asig > attack_thresh from DECAY into ATTACK, starting at the matching gain. VOX is unaffected because vox_count only changes in LOW. The hysteresis matches what HOLD already does. Giannoulis/Massberg/Reiss JAES 2012 and Zölzer's DAFX are real references for gate and compressor envelope design.

2) Setters reset state. Every SetDEXP* timing, ratio, threshold or delay setter calls decalc_dexp and then calc_dexp. That sets state=LOW, count=0 and avsig=0, and builds a new audring with calc_delring, which zeroes it with malloc0, inptr=rdelay and outptr=0. When the audio delay is on, the output is therefore zeros for audelay, which defaults to 60 ms. The gain also steps from 1 to low_gain mid-word.

This matters more than the proposal says. In Thetis (cmaster.cs:1080, CMSetTXAVoxThresh), the main-console VOX slider (ptbVOX) calls SetDEXPAttackThreshold. So every slider tick while transmitting causes a roughly 60 ms dropout plus a gain step. Changing coefficients in place without touching the state, and reallocating only when the ring size changes, is a clean and low-risk fix.

Overall: the description is accurate and the fixes are correct. The audible benefit of the retrigger fix depends on settings. The setter fix has a concrete, reproducible benefit.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
Two real defects in dexp.c, both fixed with small, low-risk changes:

(a) Retrigger during release. After a pause longer than the hold time (default 500 ms), speech that returns during the release is attenuated by up to the full expansion ratio (default 10 dB) until the release finishes and a new attack completes. With the default 100 ms release, the exposure window is narrow and the effect is mild. With long releases (up to 1 s) it becomes clearly audible as clipped onsets. The audio delay does not protect against it, because the gain is applied before the delay.

(b) Setter resets. Every parameter setter resets the expander state and rebuilds the audio delay ring zeroed. That gives an audio dropout as long as the delay (default 60 ms) and an abrupt step down to low gain. In Thetis, the main-console VOX threshold slider calls SetDEXPAttackThreshold, so adjusting VOX or DEXP sensitivity while transmitting causes repeated dropouts. Recomputing coefficients in place removes this.

kept.title: Phase-rotator auto-tuner: paired (shadow-chain) evaluation, no state zeroing, and a crest-factor objective
kept.current: The optimizer compares asym_fast (1 s time constant) measured at fc_A with asym_fast measured 15 s later (PHROT_OPTIM_SECS) at fc_B, which is a different speech segment, possibly silence. It accepts a change with a 0.5% threshold. Every coefficient change (recalc_fc lines 112-115, called at 176, 212, 216) memsets the allpass states x0/x1/y0/y1 to zero mid-transmission, which steps the waveform and clicks. The objective is real-waveform asymmetry |env_pos-env_neg|/(env_pos+env_neg). Downstream, the SSB clipper and ALC act on the analytic envelope, which is invariant to polarity asymmetry.
kept.proposed: (1) Run one or two shadow allpass chains at the candidate corner(s) (fc±step) on the same input block in parallel. Compare their metrics against the live chain on identical audio, gated to voiced blocks only. This 'common random numbers' paired comparison removes the speech-to-speech variance that dominates the current A/B test, so convergence takes seconds rather than minutes. (2) Never zero the state. For first-order allpass sections, either keep the state across a coefficient change, which is stable and gives a tiny transient, or crossfade from the old to the new chain over about 10 ms. (3) In SSB modes, optimise peak-to-RMS of the post-bp0 analytic envelope (the quantity the clipper and PA see), and keep asymmetry as the objective for AM, where waveform polarity matters.
kept.benefit: Removes audible clicks every 15 s during auto-tune. The objective then directly targets SSB crest factor. Faster and more repeatable convergence. A phase rotator's achievable crest-factor gain on voice is typically about 1-2 dB, so the ceiling is modest, but the tuner should now actually find it.
kept.risk: Shadow chains cost about nstages*2 extra first-order sections per sample (negligible). With voiced-only gating the tuner stalls during silence, which is intended. Float32 note: b0 and a1 share the same rounded coefficient, so the sections stay exactly allpass in float32. Near-DC pole noise gain (pole about 0.99 at 50 Hz/48 kHz) still leaves roundoff around -120 dB, so this is safe.
kept.evidence: Line-level: phrot.c:112-115 zeroes state, 168-218 does sequential A/B on different audio, 69 sets a 15 s interval. Variance reduction by common random numbers: Law & Kelton, Simulation Modeling and Analysis (any edition). Broadcast phase-rotator practice (allpass dispersion of glottal pulses to cut crest factor): Orban & Foti, Optimod-AM/FM technical literature.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the proposal against phrot.c and TXA.c in WDSP 2.11. The core claims are accurate.

(a) Zeroed state. recalc_fc (phrot.c:102-116) runs memset on x0/x1/y0/y1. It is called at line 176 to switch to the candidate fc_B, at line 216 to return to or keep auto_fc, and at line 212 on convergence. That is one call per optimizer_step, every PHROT_OPTIM_SECS = 15 s (line 54, line 69), until the tuner converges. In a voiced block, zeroing x1 and y1 makes the next output b0*x0 instead of the true allpass output. The error is on the order of the signal amplitude and decays with the section's pole time constant, about 0.5 ms at 338 Hz and longer at 50 Hz. Leveler, CFC and bp0 then band-limit that transient, so you get a short, audible tick or thump. A first-order direct-form allpass keeps a valid state across a coefficient change, so zeroing gains nothing. SetTXAPHROTCorner also zeroes the state through decalc/calc, but that only happens when the user moves the corner.

(b) Unpaired A/B on different audio. The A/B test in phase 0 records asym_A = asym_fast and switches to fc_B. Fifteen seconds later, phase 1 reads asym_B = asym_fast and compares it with a 0.5% threshold (PHROT_IMPROVE_THRESH). asym_fast is a 1 s EMA (coeff_asym_fast) of a block-level ratio built from 10 ms attack and 200 ms decay envelopes. Each reading therefore reflects only the last second or two of speech, and the two readings come from different speech, or from silence. Convergence needs the step to shrink from 50 Hz to 5 Hz by a factor of 0.75 per decision, about 9 shrinks. Each A/B pair takes 30 s, and an inconclusive result needs 4 rejections before the step shrinks. The minimum is about 4.5 minutes, and with noisy decisions it is much longer. So 'minutes' is accurate. No other WDSP file, mode or option does paired evaluation or keeps the state.

(c) Objective. The asymmetry metric is |env_pos-env_neg|/(env_pos+env_neg) on the real samples (update_metrics, lines 118-150). That matches the proposal. In SSB, bp0 forms the one-sided analytic signal, and the compressor, CESSB (osctrl) and ALC act on its complex envelope. Polarity asymmetry, or any constant phase shift, does not show in that envelope. Frequency-dependent allpass dispersion does change it, and that is the real mechanism a phase rotator can use to cut SSB crest factor. Targeting envelope peak-to-RMS for SSB and keeping asymmetry for AM is therefore sound.

Caveats that weaken the proposal but do not refute it:
1. In xtxa, phrot runs right after panel (mic gain), upstream of amsq, EQ, leveler, CFC and bp0. A shadow chain cannot directly measure the 'post-bp0 analytic envelope' without replicating the leveler, CFC and filters. The practical version is a proxy: compute the analytic envelope of each chain's own output with a cheap Hilbert pair or FIR, or measure in place after bp0 for the live chain only.
2. The leveler (wcpagc) sees the real mic waveform, so asymmetry is not completely irrelevant in SSB. Its effect is second order next to the final complex-envelope limiting.
3. The float32 remark does not apply, because WDSP uses double throughout. It is harmless.
4. A better form of (2): when a candidate is accepted, copy the shadow chain's state into the live chain. The shadow chain has been running on the same input, so the switch is seamless and no crossfade is needed.
5. The citations are real. Common random numbers is standard (Law & Kelton). Orban and Foti did co-author broadcast-processing papers. 'Optimod-AM/FM technical literature' is loosely attributed, but phase rotators for asymmetric voice are documented Orban/Optimod practice.

The proposal is not already implemented. It fixes a real artifact, and the variance-reduction argument holds.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
There are three changes, in order of value.

1. Stop zeroing the allpass state in recalc_fc. Either keep the state, or copy in the state of a shadow chain that has been running on the same input. This removes a band-limited click or thump. It currently occurs about every 15 s while the auto-tuner runs, at roughly signal amplitude during speech, and lasts until the tuner converges.

2. Evaluate candidates fc±step in shadow allpass chains on the same voiced blocks as the live chain, instead of comparing 1 s EMAs taken 15 s apart on different speech. Each decision then needs only seconds of speech, instead of the current 4.5-minute minimum and the noise-dominated accept/reject choices. The extra cost is negligible: 2*nstages first-order sections per sample.

3. In SSB modes, use an analytic-envelope peak-to-RMS objective on the rotator output, with a local Hilbert proxy. Phrot sits upstream of leveler, CFC and bp0, so the true post-bp0 envelope cannot be evaluated per candidate. Keep asymmetry as the objective for AM. The realistic gain is modest, about 1-2 dB of SSB crest-factor reduction at best. The main concrete win is removing the clicks and making the tuner converge reliably.

kept.title: EER constant-envelope path divides by zero on digital silence
kept.file_function: eer.c:xeer (86-122, case 0 lines 101-104); also create_eer/destroy_eer (63-64, 70-76), xeerEXTF (367-392)
kept.current: In amiq==0 mode, out = pgain*I/mag and pgain*Q/mag with mag = sqrt(I*I+Q*Q) and no guard. An exact-zero input sample (flushed buffers at TX start, a muted mic, a zeroed generator) gives 0/0 = NaN on the phase-drive output, and the fractional delay (xdelay) then smears it across neighbouring samples. The legacy buffers are fixed at 2048 complex (63-64), yet xeerEXTF writes 'size' samples into them with no bounds check, and destroy_eer never frees them (leak).
kept.proposed: When mag < tiny (e.g. 1e-12 in double, or about 1e-20 relative in float32), hold the last valid unit phasor, or output (pgain, 0). Holding the previous phase is better because it avoids a phase jump in the PA's phase path. Bound-check size <= 2048 in xeerEXTF (or allocate to max size) and free legacy/legacyM in destroy_eer.
kept.benefit: Prevents NaN reaching the phase DAC/FPGA path in EER mode, which could produce undefined drive and glitches at TX start. Removes a heap overflow and a leak.
kept.risk: None meaningful. Holding the previous phase during exact-zero envelope is invisible because the magnitude path is zero at those instants.
kept.evidence: Line-level: eer.c:102-104 divides with no guard (compare compress.c:67, which only divides when gain*mag>1, and osctrl.c, which never divides by envelope). eer.c:63-64 allocates fixed 2048 complex and 379-383 writes 'size' samples. destroy_eer at 70-76 omits legacy frees. IEEE-754: 0/0 = NaN.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked every claim against eer.c and they all hold. In xeer case 0 (lines 101-104), mag = sqrt(I*I+Q*Q) and the code divides pgain*I and pgain*Q by mag with no guard. An exact-zero input sample therefore gives 0/0 = NaN in out[]. When rundelays is on, xdelay(a->pdel) then runs the fractional-delay interpolator over that buffer, so the NaN spreads into every output sample whose taps cover it, until it leaves the ring. Case 2 (envelope) has no division and is safe. Case 1 is safe too.

create_eer allocates legacy and legacyM at a fixed 2048 complex each (lines 63-64) with malloc0. xeerEXTF sets a->size = size from the caller and writes 2*size doubles into legacy with no bounds check, so any size > 2048 overflows the heap. destroy_eer (lines 70-76) frees only the delays, the critical section and the struct. legacy and legacyM leak, and they need _aligned_free because malloc0 is aligned.

No other mode or file in WDSP guards this. EER is not instantiated inside TXA. It is reached only through the external interface (create_eerEXT and xeerEXTF, MAX_EXT_EERS=2), used by legacy host EER setups, so the affected population is small.

Exact zeros are realistic: flushed or zeroed buffers at the start of MOX, muted input, and zero-amplitude generators. The NaN path is a real defect. The overflow only fires if a host passes a size above 2048, and typical host buffer sizes are probably at or below that. I could not see the caller, so it is latent rather than demonstrated. The leak only happens on destroy.

The proposed fix is sound and low-risk. Holding the last unit phasor while mag == 0 is invisible on the envelope path, because outM is I*mgain, which is zero there. One part of the proposal is muddled: "1e-20 relative in float32". The math runs in double, so a guard like mag > 0 (or a tiny absolute threshold) is enough. The proposal is not refuted, but priority is low because EER is a niche, external-only legacy feature.
verdict.corrected_benefit: In amiq==0 (constant-envelope) EER mode, any exact-zero I/Q sample makes NaN on the phase-drive output. When the fractional delays are on, xdelay spreads that NaN to the neighbouring samples. A zero-magnitude guard that holds the last unit phasor removes this, with no audible or RF downside, because the envelope output is zero at those instants. The same patch fixes two more problems in the external legacy wrapper. It adds a bounds check (size <= 2048, or allocation sized to the maximum) to close a latent heap overflow in xeerEXTF, and it frees legacy and legacyM with _aligned_free in destroy_eer to close a small leak. All of this affects only the external EER interface, which TXA never uses internally.

kept.title: Small state/edge-case defects: osctrl flush, CFC Nyquist NaN, CFC display step, emphasis skirt
kept.current: (a) flush_osctrl memsets dl with dl_len*sizeof(complex), but dl holds pn complex (dl_len = pn>>1), so only half is cleared and stale samples from the previous over are emitted. It also leaves max_env unchanged. After the envelope ring is zeroed, the recompute trigger (env_out >= max_env && env_out > 0, line 98) cannot fire until a new sample exceeds the stale max, so a previous over's peak (typically 1.1-1.3 with COMP on) pins divisor > 1 at the start of the next transmission. (b) In calc_compG/calc_compE linear mode, when the top control frequency is clamped to fmax=rate/2 (lines 99-100), the last bin has f == fmax exactly, so frac = 0/0 = NaN at line 130/218. cfc_gain[Nyquist] is then permanently NaN, so mask*X is NaN, and the IFFT makes every output sample NaN. The spline branch's while-loops (142-157, 229-242) have no index bounds if a control point sits at an edge. (c) The display step = (msize-1)/1024 is 0 when fsize < 2048, so all 1025 display points read bin 0. (d) In fcurve.c (and the identical code in eq.c:205/213), lowmag/highmag are multiplied cumulatively (lowmag *= (f/flow)^4 on every step). The skirt below f_low and above f_high therefore decays as a product, i.e. roughly brick-wall, not the 24 dB/oct the flow4/fhigh4 names suggest. That makes the frequency-sampled target discontinuous and leaves the window to absorb the Gibbs ripple.
kept.proposed: (a) Clear pn complex and reset max_env = 0 (and in_idx/out_idx) in flush_osctrl. (b) Guard against a zero-width segment: if fpG[j+1] == fpG[j], use frac = 0. Clamp the user's top frequency to below fmax, or dedupe after the sort. Bound i in the spline-edge loops. (c) Use a fractional stride or interpolation: j = i*(msize-1)/1024. (d) If 4th-order skirts are the intent, use A[k] = A[low]*(k/low)^4 (non-cumulative). Otherwise document the brick-wall intent and rely on a smoother window. In the float32 port, the 1e-100 floor becomes 0, which is harmless at design time.
kept.benefit: (a) is a sub-millisecond stale-audio blip, but the stuck max_env can audibly duck the first moments of an over until a larger peak arrives. Small but real. (b) is a low-probability total TX silencing/NaN output if a profile ever reaches Nyquist. (c) is display-only. (d) gives smoother emphasis/EQ transitions with less passband ripple near the corners. The impact is marginal and should be checked by plotting the response.
kept.risk: (d) changes the EQ/pre-emphasis response slightly outside the passband, so compare against current curves. The others carry no behavioural risk.
kept.evidence: Line-level: osctrl.c:39 allocates pn complex, 80 clears dl_len complex, 42/98 handle max_env. cfcomp.c:99-100 clamps to fmax, 115 sets fpG[n+1]=fmax, 128-130 evaluate f=fincr*i=rate/2 at i=msize-1 (exact in double for power-of-two fsize), giving 0/0. cfcomp.c:708 integer step. fcurve.c:131/139 and eq.c:205/213 do cumulative multiplication.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked each item against the WDSP 2.11 source.

(a) Confirmed, minor. osctrl.c:38 allocates pn complex for dl, but flush_osctrl (line 80) clears only dl_len*sizeof(complex), and dl_len is pn>>1. max_env is not reset. After a flush, dlenv is all zero. The recompute trigger at line 98 needs a sample leaving the ring with env_out >= max_env and env_out > 0, so the stale max_env from the last over persists until a new sample reaches it. The divisor at line 103 is 1 + 1.95*(max_env-1); a stale max of 1.2 to 1.3 means about 2.5 to 4 dB of extra attenuation. osctrl only runs with COMP on, where the bp1 overshoot pushes peaks above 1.0, so this can happen. Heavily compressed speech usually hits the old overshoot level again soon, so the ducking is likely short. flush_txa (TXA.c:532) runs on channel flush. Index reset is not needed, because in_idx and out_idx keep their dl_len offset. The stale-sample part is negligible: pn is about 11 at 96 kHz, so only a few samples, and the uslew up-ramp after osctrl attenuates them.

(b) Confirmed, but only reachable through the API. Fg is clamped to fmax=rate/2 (lines 99-100) and fpG[n+1]=fmax (line 115). If any profile frequency is >= rate/2, then fpG[n]==fpG[n+1]. The last bin is i=msize-1=fsize/2, where f equals rate/2 exactly, so frac=0/0=NaN. In calc_mask, test=NaN fails the >1 comparison, so mask=comp=NaN. revfftin at Nyquist becomes NaN, and the whole IFFT frame, and therefore TX audio, is NaN. The calc_compE linear path has the same defect. The spline-branch edge loops (142-157, 229-242) have no index bounds, so a control point at 0 or fmax can overrun. Reaching any of this needs a CFC frequency of at least 24 or 48 kHz, which a sane UI would never send. It is a robustness guard, not a field bug.

(c) Refuted in practice. TXA.c:208 creates cfcomp with fsize = max(16384, dsp_size), and setSize_cfcomp never changes fsize. So msize-1 >= 8192 and step >= 8, and the step==0 case cannot be reached.

(d) The code description is accurate. fcurve.c:131/139 and eq.c multiply cumulatively, so the skirt falls much faster than 24 dB/oct; with low=10, one octave down is about -66 dB. But calling it a bug, and claiming a benefit, is not supported. A steeper out-of-band skirt is arguably desirable for TX EQ and FM pre-emphasis. A true 24 dB/oct skirt would pass more sub-300 Hz hum and more energy above f_high into later stages. The Gibbs-ripple improvement is asserted, not shown, and the windowed frequency-sampling design already smooths the response.

Net: (a) and (b) are real but small or edge-case. (c) cannot occur. (d) is a design choice with no demonstrated benefit and some risk.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
Two cheap hardening fixes are worth taking.

1. In flush_osctrl, clear all pn complex samples of dl and reset max_env to 0. This stops a stale peak from the previous over from adding about 2-4 dB of overshoot-control attenuation at the start of the next COMP-on over. The duck usually lasts only until the first comparable peak arrives.
2. In calc_compG/calc_compE, guard the zero-width last segment (frac = 0 when the denominator is 0, or clamp Fg/Fe to just below rate/2), and bound the spline-edge loops. A profile frequency >= rate/2 sent through the API can currently NaN the whole CFC output.

Drop the display-step change: fsize is always >= 16384, so step is never 0. Drop the fcurve/eq skirt change: the steep cumulative roll-off is a defensible design choice, and switching to 24 dB/oct would loosen out-of-band rejection with no shown benefit.

refuted.title: AM: guard against carrier pinch-off and allow asymmetric real-waveform peak control
refuted.why:
The line-level facts are correct. ammod.c:62 computes out = mult*(c + (1-c)*x) with I=Q, and SetTXAAMCarrierLevel (103-110) accepts any c_level. The default is 0.5 (TXA.c:343). The ALC runs in envelope mode with a 1.0 target (TXA.c:313-336), which bounds |z|, and |Re z| <= |z|, so x >= -1. That means c < 0.5 can drive c + a*x negative.

The bug claim fails on the physics. In WDSP the AM modulator is a linear I/Q operation. x is band-limited to 0..f_high by bp0/bp1/bp2, so c + a*x is just carrier plus DSB sidebands, and its spectrum is the carrier plus a*X(f) mirrored. When the sum goes below zero you get a sign reversal of a linear signal. That is reduced-carrier DSB with modulation index a/c > 1. It adds no bandwidth and causes no splatter. Overmodulation splatters in a plate- or collector-modulated transmitter because the modulator physically cannot go below zero and hard-clips. A linear SDR exciter has no such limit. The only real effect is envelope-detector distortion in receivers that lack synchronous AM (SAM handles it fine). That is a consequence of the operator choosing a carrier level below 0.5, and front ends map their carrier-level control onto this setter for exactly that reason. It is not a WDSP defect.

The proposed fix is worse than the problem. Part (1) says "always clamp c + a*x >= 0" and calls it risk-free. That hard clamp is a memoryless nonlinearity, so it would create the very wideband splatter the proposal says it removes. The softer variant (a look-ahead negative-peak limiter at -c/a followed by the 0..f_high lowpass) only trades a linear sideband for a nonlinear one, and it silently overrides a carrier level the user picked. The filter's overshoot also means it cannot guarantee a hard bound.

Part (2), asymmetric peak control of the real waveform with +125% positive peaks, is a real broadcast technique. 47 CFR 73.1570(b)(1) is a real rule and the Orban/Optimod work is a real reference. But it is a new optional feature, not a fix, and its benefit here is small:
- In a linear exciter, PEP is fixed by full scale. Allowing +125% means dropping the carrier to about 0.444, so the gain in sideband-to-carrier loudness is about 1 dB, not 1-2 dB.
- It would need a separate real-waveform processing path. COMP, CESSB and ALC all work on the symmetric analytic envelope, which can never produce asymmetric peaks.
- phrot's reverse switch already exists (phrot.c:387), so the polarity half of the idea is already supported.
- 125% positive modulation is a broadcast norm. For amateur HF it is niche at best and discouraged by many operators.

Neither part is a confirmed improvement worth prioritizing.

summary: PureSignal in WDSP 2.11 is a memoryless predistorter learned by indirect learning, with no memory terms. pscc() collects pairs of DAC samples (after predistortion) and feedback samples into 16 equal-width TX-amplitude buckets of 256 samples each (calcc.c:337-423). calc() normalises the feedback with a LOWESS-plus-polynomial extrapolation of |rx| at tx=1 (extrapolate.c:340-410). It then forms the post-inverse in three parts as functions of the normalised output amplitude x=|rx|: ym=|tx|/|rx|, yc=cos(angle tx - angle rx) and ys=sin(angle tx - angle rx) (calcc.c:1161-1174). These are binned into at most 100 x-bins (equalize_density, 542-611). Each part is fitted separately by nf_fit as a 20-control-point cubic B-spline, set up as a NURBS, with an extrapolated start pin, outlier passes, CV checks and 2 IRLS passes (nurbs_fit.c:995-1478). In PS's configuration (ORDER_BY_X, uniform_knots=1 so t=x, adaptive_iters=0) this reduces to plain B-spline regression y(x). The control points are smoothed by an EMA (alpha 0.1, calcc.c:1461-1572), resampled to a 160-point not-a-knot cubic spline (ns_build), checked (accuracy, extrema, sin^2+cos^2, solution deviation), then blended into a 256-point CurveEMA lookup table (alpha 0.3, nurbs_spline.c:870-909). xiqc() reads the three tables per sample at the input envelope with Catmull-Rom Hermite interpolation and computes out = ym*(I+jQ)*(yc+j*ys), with a raised-cosine crossfade between table sets (iqc.c:91-171). TX/RX alignment is a manual delay (SetPSTXDelay, calcc.c:2217). lmath.c (xbuilder etc.) is no longer used by this path; PS now uses the nurbs_* files.

kept.title: IRLS reweighting uses w instead of sqrt(w), so it fits near an L0 objective and the conditioning is never checked
kept.current: For each IRLS pass, nf_fit sets w_data[i] = 1/(res + irls_epsilon) with irls_epsilon = 1e-6 (PS_NF_IRLS_EPSILON, calcc.c:278; 2 passes). fit_pass multiplies both the collocation row and the target by w (MAT(N,i,j) *= wi; by[i] = y*wi). The normal equations therefore minimise sum w_i^2 r_i^2 = sum r_i^2/(|r_i_prev|+1e-6)^2. That is IRLS for p=0: every point with a non-tiny residual costs about 1, so the fit is pulled to interpolate the ~18 bins whose previous residual was smallest. Weights span roughly 1e2 to 1e6, which is up to 1e12 after squaring. These passes call fit_pass with cond_out=NULL, so NF_FIT_BAD_CONDNUM cannot catch the ill-conditioning. If Cholesky fails twice, the silent diagonal fallback x[i]=Atb[i]/AtA[i][i] (573) produces control points that are not a least-squares solution, and nothing flags it. cv_score and condition_number are computed before IRLS (1329-1332) and are never re-evaluated for the curve that is actually used.
kept.proposed: Do proper robust IRLS. Use Huber or Tukey-bisquare weights psi(r)/r with a robust scale s = 1.4826*MAD(residuals), for example Huber with k=1.345s: w = min(1, k/|r|). Scale the rows by sqrt(w), not w. Pass cond_out on the IRLS passes, recompute the CV score after them, and set a quality flag (not a silent fallback) when Cholesky fails. If an L1 fit is really wanted, use w = 1/max(|r|, delta) with delta about 0.1*s, again applied as sqrt(w). The same mean+sigma test in compute_outlier_mask (816-844) is not robust either, because outliers inflate sigma; a MAD-based scale fixes both.
kept.benefit: Lower variance in each fit, which matters because each raw fit is then mixed into a slow EMA. The extreme weight range goes away, and with it a real risk that ill-conditioned solves go undetected. The audible or IMD effect is probably small (a few dB at most on fit-to-fit jitter) because the 0.1/0.3 EMAs hide much of the variance. The main gains are correctness and convergence speed, since less EMA smoothing is then needed.
kept.risk: Very low. The final curve will move slightly toward the least-squares fit, so the thresholds downstream (scheck 0.10, accuracy 50x noise) should be re-validated on recorded captures.
kept.evidence: Holland and Welsch 1977, 'Robust regression using iteratively reweighted least-squares' (Comm. Stat.): the IRLS quadratic weight is psi(r)/r, applied as sqrt(w) on rows. Huber 1964. Line-level: fit_pass 627-629 scales rows by wi, and ls_solve_with_cond 549-556 forms A'A, so the effective weight is wi^2 = 1/(|r|+eps)^2, which is the Lp IRLS weight |r|^(p-2) with p=0.

verdict.reasoning:
The code matches the description. In nurbs_fit.c:1341-1354, each IRLS pass sets w_data[i] = 1/(res + irls_epsilon), where res is the 2-D Euclidean residual. The defaults are irls_iters=2 and irls_epsilon=1e-6 (nurbs_fit.c:275-276), and calcc.c:277-278 sets the same values for all three curves (m, c, s). fit_pass (612-630) multiplies the collocation rows and the targets by wi, and ls_solve_with_cond (549-560) then forms A'A. The effective weight on each squared residual is therefore 1/(|r_prev|+eps)^2, which is the Lp-IRLS weight |r|^(p-2) with p=0, not the L1 weight 1/|r|. The IRLS passes call fit_pass with cond_out=NULL. result.condition_number and the CV score are computed before IRLS and not recomputed afterwards, so the BAD_CONDNUM test at 1356 applies to the pre-IRLS fit. The double-Cholesky-failure fallback (ls_solve 571-576) silently returns diagonal-only coefficients. Some things do run after IRLS: rms is recomputed, and the bounds scan and fold-detection refit (which uses w=NULL) still run, so the final curve is not wholly unchecked. compute_outlier_mask uses mean + 2.5*sigma on non-robust statistics, as stated.

I checked the claims with a simulation in Python/numpy: a cubic B-spline with 20 control points, 100-400 points on a smooth tanh curve, Gaussian noise of 0.01, 300 trials, and the same w-on-rows scheme with 2 passes.
- Clean data: the current IRLS fit has about 5-10% higher RMS error against the true curve than plain least squares (0.467 vs 0.426 at m=100, 0.326 vs 0.303 at m=200, 0.228 vs 0.218 at m=400). Huber with sqrt(w) was 0.439 / 0.310 / 0.223.
- Conditioning: cond(A'A) rose from about 20 to a median of 1e6 and a maximum of about 7e7.
- With 5% outliers at 10x the noise level: least squares 0.98, current 0.76, Huber 0.53 at m=100, and similar at the other sizes.

So the direction of the claim is correct. The current weighting is a mis-implemented robust step: it adds variance on clean data, and is only half as effective as proper Huber IRLS on contaminated data. The proposal overstates the severity in three ways:
- With only 2 passes the fit does not collapse to interpolating about 18 points. The degradation is roughly 5-10% RMS, not dramatic.
