- Conditioning reaches about 1e6-4e8, not 1e12. That is well within what Cholesky in double precision handles, so the silent fallback should be rare in practice.
- The 2.5-sigma outlier mask runs before IRLS and removes the worst outliers, which reduces the robustness gain from Huber.

The remedy cited is real and standard (Holland & Welsch 1977 IRLS; Huber 1964; MAD scale). It costs essentially nothing in latency, because this is the slow PureSignal calibration fit and not the audio path. Even so, the benefit at the predistortion output is likely small once the 0.10/0.30 control-point EMAs are applied. The parts that matter most are correctness and diagnostics: weight by sqrt(w), recompute the condition number and CV score after IRLS, and flag a Cholesky failure. A large measurable IMD improvement is not established. Downstream thresholds would need re-validation on real captures.
verdict.corrected_benefit: nf_fit's IRLS weights rows by w = 1/(|r|+1e-6) instead of sqrt(w), so it effectively minimises sum (r/r_prev)^2 (p=0) rather than L1 or Huber. Switching to Huber weights (MAD scale, k=1.345s) applied as sqrt(w) has two effects in simulation: on clean data the per-fit RMS error falls by about 3-6% (back close to plain least squares), and on data with 5% outliers it falls by about 30-50% compared with the current scheme. cond(A'A) drops from about 1e6-1e8 back to about 1e1-1e2. Since cond_out=NULL is passed during IRLS, the condition number and CV score now describe the pre-IRLS fit; they should be recomputed after IRLS, and a Cholesky failure should set a quality flag. At the PureSignal output the effect is probably small because of the 2.5-sigma pre-masking and the 0.10/0.30 control-point EMAs. This is mainly a correctness and diagnostics fix with a modest gain in fit variance, and it needs validation on recorded captures.

kept.title: Rejected fits still update the control-point and pin EMA state; the table clip only applies on the first cycle
kept.file_function: calcc.c:calc (pin commit 1452-1459, ctrl EMA 1461-1572, later rejections 1575-1661); nurbs_spline.c:curve_ema_update (901-905)
kept.current: The pin EMAs (m/c/s_y_pin_ema) are committed at 1452-1459. The control-point EMAs are blended (alpha=0.10) and written back into the nurb at 1484-1496. Both happen before ns_build (1575), ns_accuracy_check (1582), count_extrema (1596), sin_cos_identity_check (1650) and scheck (1657). Any of those can 'goto cleanup' and mark the iteration failed (scOK=0), but the rejected fit has already gone into m/c/s_ctrl_ema_x/y and the pin EMAs. It then makes up 10% of every later fit and decays over about 10 iterations. Separately, m_ctrl_n is recorded (1479) but never compared with nc. The fold refit path can shrink n_ctrl by 2 (nurbs_fit.c:1444-1446, 1474), which would mix control points from different knot vectors. In curve_ema_update, the y_clip_lo/hi limits are applied only when count==0 (901-902); later blended tables are never clipped.
kept.proposed: Do the EMA in a scratch copy. Build and validate the candidate (ns_build, accuracy, extrema, identity, scheck) from scratch EMA values. Copy scratch into the persistent ctrl and pin EMA state only when every check passes, just before curve_ema_update. Reset the control-point EMA (or refuse the blend) when nc != m_ctrl_n or the knots differ. Apply y_clip on every update. A cleaner alternative: since t=x and the knots are uniform and fixed, keep exponentially-forgotten normal-equation statistics (A'WA, A'Wy) per curve and solve once per iteration. That is recursive least squares with forgetting factor lambda. It weights each iteration by how much data it actually contributed and replaces the stacked ctrl EMA (0.1) and curve EMA (0.3).
kept.benefit: One bad capture (a PA fault, an ALC transient or a mis-scaled feedback cycle) can no longer degrade the correction for the next ~10 cycles after being rejected. The RLS form also shortens tracking time. The two stacked EMAs currently give a time constant of about 13 calibration cycles for thermal or band drift, while cold start already takes the first fit directly. The effect is moderate and shows mostly in robustness under bad feedback, not in steady-state IMD.
kept.risk: Low. Re-tune alpha or lambda after the change so steady-state jitter does not increase.
kept.evidence: Line-level ordering in calc(): the EMA writes at 1486-1496, 1524-1534 and 1561-1571 come before the rejecting gotos at 1588-1600, 1650-1661. RLS with exponential forgetting: Haykin, 'Adaptive Filter Theory', ch. 10.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked each claim against the code in "/Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source".

1. Ordering in calcc.c:calc. The pin EMAs (m/c/s_y_pin_ema and the valid flags) are committed at 1452-1459, right after the three nf_fit calls pass their NULL and NF_FIT_BAD checks. The control-point EMAs are blended with alpha=0.10 and written back into the nurbs at 1461-1572. After that, ns_build or NULL (1575), ns_accuracy_check at more than 50x the noise estimate (1582-1592), count_extrema > 2 (1596-1601), sin_cos_identity_check (1650) and scheck (1656) can each `goto cleanup`. The cleanup block (1725) only frees the nurbs and splines and sets scOK=0. Nothing rolls back the ctrl EMA or the pin EMA. The only resets are at init (918-941) and on restart/reset (1909-1914). The cold-start paths leave partial state too: if the magnitude cold start succeeds and the cos cold-start gate (1508) then rejects, m_ctrl_ema_valid is already 1 and holds a fit that was never validated. The description is accurate.

2. n_ctrl mismatch. m_ctrl_n is set to the configured n_ctrl at 1280 (and again at 1479 on cold start) and is never compared with nc. In nurbs_fit.c, the final fold-refit loop drops n_refit by 2 when fold_relative > 0.05 and cond > 200 (1444-1446). It rebuilds the knots with make_knots_uniform(n_refit) and sets c->n_ctrl = n_ctrl_final (1474-1475). PS_NF_FOLD_DETECT=1 and PS_NF_UNIFORM_KNOTS=1, so this path is live. The EMA loop then blends the first 18 coefficients of a 20-point B-spline basis with coefficients from an 18-point basis on different knots. When the next cycle returns to 20, entries 18 and 19 are stale. This is a real, though probably rare, correctness bug.

3. Clipping. In curve_ema_update (nurbs_spline.c 901-905), the y_clip_lo/hi limits are applied only when count==0. Later updates blend the unclipped new_y in, so a spline that overshoots can push the table past the clip range. This is real but minor, because the extrema and scheck gates usually catch such curves first.

4. Impact. The checks run on the already-blended curve. A rejected cycle therefore leaves its raw fit at 10% weight in the ctrl EMA, decaying by 0.9 per cycle. The applied table (calavg) is only updated on success, with alpha 0.3. So the bad capture reaches the correction at roughly 0.1 x 0.3 = 3% on the next good cycle and fades over about 10 cycles. The pin EMA contamination behaves the same way. This is real but modest, which matches the proposal's own "moderate, robustness only" framing. The "about 13 cycles" time constant is roughly right: cascading a 0.1 EMA and a 0.3 EMA gives a mean delay of about 9 + 2.3 ≈ 11 cycles.

5. RLS alternative. With uniform_knots, t is x clamped to [0,1] and the knots are uniform and fixed for a given n_ctrl, so the premise holds. Haykin's Adaptive Filter Theory does cover exponentially weighted RLS, so the reference is real. But the fitter also does IRLS, outlier and local-outlier masking, CV holdout, pinned start and end points, flat or horizontal end constraints, fold truncation, and a 2-D (wx, wy) fit. Accumulating A'WA directly does not reproduce that robust pipeline without real redesign, and its benefit is speculative. The bug fix (scratch EMA committed only on success, reset on an nc or knot mismatch, clip on every update) is the solid part.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
This fixes three confirmed state-integrity bugs in the PureSignal calc() loop.

1. Iterations that are later rejected (accuracy, extrema, sin/cos identity, scheck, or a later curve's cold-start gate) still commit to the pin EMA and the control-point EMA. Each one stays in the state at 10% weight, decaying over about 10 cycles. It reaches the applied correction table at about 3% on the next accepted cycle.
2. A fold refit that shrinks n_ctrl from 20 to 18 gets blended coefficient by coefficient with an EMA built on a different knot basis.
3. curve_ema_update applies y_clip only on the first cycle.

Staging the EMA in a scratch copy, committing it only after every check passes, resetting it when nc or the knots differ, and clipping on every update removes these at low risk. The gain is robustness after bad feedback cycles and occasional fold-refit cycles. Steady-state IMD should not change. The RLS replacement is a speculative redesign that conflicts with the robust IRLS, outlier and pinned fitting pipeline, so it should not be part of this change.

kept.title: Cold-start sanity check reads a NULL spline and never fires
kept.current: On the first valid fit, calc() rejects the fit if ns_eval_near_clamped(a->m_spline, 0.04, ...) > 1.8 (and |cos| or |sin| > 1.1). At that point a->m_spline, c_spline and s_spline are always NULL. After a successful calc they are handed to iqc and nulled (1838-1840). After a failed calc they are freed and nulled (1734-1736). LRESET frees them too (1897-1899). The new splines are only built later, at 1575/1605/1628. ns_eval_near_clamped returns 0.0 for NULL (nurbs_spline.c:653), so 0.0 > 1.8 and |0.0| > 1.1 are never true. The guard is dead code and an unchecked first fit seeds the control-point EMA.
kept.proposed: Evaluate the candidate NURBS itself: nf_eval at t=0.04 (t=x under uniform_knots), or move the check after ns_build and evaluate the new spline. Better still, check the pinned start value and the left 10% of the curve against the physical bounds already used elsewhere (mag in [0.1, 2.0], cos/sin within ±1.05).
kept.benefit: Restores a guard the author intended against a wild first fit, which otherwise sets the EMA baseline and can take ~10 cycles to wash out. The benefit is small but this is a real correctness gap.
kept.risk: None beyond occasionally rejecting a first fit that the current code would accept.
kept.evidence: Data flow: a->m_spline is NULL at 1467 on every path, per lines 1734-1736, 1838-1840 and 1897-1899. The NULL return is at nurbs_spline.c:653.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the data flow and it holds. calc() is called from one place only, case 3 at calcc.c:1823. If scOK is set, the splines go to SetTXAiqcStart or SetTXAiqcSwap and are set to NULL without condition (1838-1840). If scOK is clear, cleanup frees them and sets them to NULL (1732-1736). LRESET frees them when no calc is running (1897-1899), and it is also where the ctrl_ema_valid flags go back to 0 (1909-1911). Destroy frees them too (1104). So when calc() reaches the cold-start branch at 1464/1502/1540, a->m_spline, c_spline and s_spline are always NULL. The new splines are only built afterwards, at 1575, 1605 and 1628. ns_eval_near_clamped returns 0.0 for a NULL spline (nurbs_spline.c:653), so `0.0 > 1.8` and `fabs(0.0) > 1.1` can never be true, and binfo bit 0b00100000 can never be set. The guard is dead code.

Some later checks soften the impact. For cos and sin, sin_cos_identity_check covers x in 0.05-0.95. For mag, count_extrema applies. ns_extend_left limits the left extension to [0.1, 2.0] for mag and ±1.1 for cos/sin, and the CurveEMA is bounded. So a wildly wrong first fit is usually caught before it reaches iqc.

There is a second problem that makes the proposal more relevant. m/c/s_ctrl_ema_valid is set to 1 before ns_build, the extrema check, the identity check and scheck run. A first fit that those later checks reject has therefore still seeded the control-point EMA. Its control points then carry 0.9^n weight in later fits, so with alpha=0.10 it takes roughly 10-20 calcs to wash out. The order also allows partial seeding: if mag seeds and the cos guard (once it works) rejects, mag's EMA is already seeded.

Two corrections to the proposal. First, "t=x under uniform_knots" is not guaranteed: the default in nurbs_fit.c:267 is 0, and calcc sets it from PS_NF_UNIFORM_KNOTS. The safest form of the fix is to move the check after ns_build. On a cold start the EMA'd control points equal the candidate's, so the new spline is exactly the candidate. Second, any failure later in that same cold-start calc must clear ctrl_ema_valid (or set it only once the calc succeeds); otherwise the fix still leaves a rejected fit as the EMA seed.

The bug is real, but the practical benefit is small because later checks and the bounds partly cover it.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The cold-start check is dead code because the splines it reads are always NULL. The fix: on a cold start, run the check on the new spline after ns_build, comparing it against the physical bounds (mag in [0.1, 2.0], cos/sin within ±1.1). Also set ctrl_ema_valid only after the whole calc succeeds, or clear it on any failure in that calc. Today any first fit seeds the control-point EMA, including one that later checks reject. The identity check, the extrema check and the bounded extension already catch most bad first fits before they reach iqc. What the fix mainly stops is a bad seed slowing convergence for about 10-20 calcs after a reset.

kept.title: Apply phase correction as a unit phasor: fit unwrapped phase (or renormalise cos/sin) and use one complex table
kept.file_function: calcc.c:calc (separate c/s fits 1297-1450, sin_cos_identity_check 803-822), nurbs_spline.c:curve_ema_update, iqc.c:xiqc 103-107
kept.current: cos and sin of the AM/PM correction are fitted, EMA-smoothed and tabulated independently, each with its own pins, outlier masks and IRLS. xiqc applies ym*(yc + j*ys) without normalising, so any |yc+j*ys| != 1 becomes AM/AM error. The identity check allows |s^2+c^2-1| up to 0.05 (SC_IDENTITY_TOL), which is about ±2.5% (±0.2 dB) amplitude error depending on amplitude. That check runs on the new spline only, not on the blended CurveEMA table that is actually applied. A linear EMA of cos/sin also shortens the phasor whenever the phase moves between cycles: averaging unit vectors Delta apart gives magnitude about cos(Delta/2). The constant loop phase offset is also left in, so one of cos/sin sits near ±1, where it carries little information.
kept.proposed: Minimum, at zero runtime cost: after curve_ema_update, renormalise the stored c/s tables to unit magnitude, building a complex table G[k] = ym[k]*(c[k]+j*s[k])/|c[k]+j*s[k]|, and have xiqc do one complex Hermite lookup and one complex multiply instead of three lookups. Better: remove a reference rotation (the circular mean of tx*conj(rx) over the top buckets), compute phi(x) = atan2 on the binned circular means, and fit and EMA the unwrapped phi(x) as a single scalar curve. Then |correction| = ym exactly and the sin^2+cos^2 check becomes unnecessary.
kept.benefit: Removes an amplitude-dependent gain error of up to about 0.2 dB that the current checks tolerate, most often after phase drift (thermal, band or antenna change) when the EMA averages differing phasors. Halves the fitting work (two curves instead of three) and reduces per-sample cost. The IMD gain is small, probably 1-3 dB at the -50 dBc level where PS operates, but it costs nothing.
kept.risk: Phase unwrapping needs care at very low x, where the feedback phase is noisy. Keep the existing low-x pin and extrapolation logic on phi. Correction files would need a format version bump or must keep cos/sin.
kept.evidence: iqc.c:106-107: |PRE| = ym*|yc+j*ys|*|in|. calcc.c:304 sets SC_IDENTITY_TOL to 0.05. For the chord-averaging shrinkage of unit phasors see Fisher, 'Statistical Analysis of Circular Data' (1993). Polar AM/AM plus AM/PM table forms: Cavers 1990, IEEE Trans. Veh. Technol. 39(4), 'Amplifier linearization using a digital predistorter with fast adaptation and low memory requirements'.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code, and the description of current behaviour is accurate.

**What the code does now**
- calcc.c:1170-1173 builds yc and ys for each sample as the unit-normalised Re and Im of tx*conj(rx).
- Cos and sin then get completely separate NURBS fits (calcc.c:1297-1450). Each fit has its own extrapolated pin and pin EMA, its own outlier, CV and IRLS settings, and its own clamp to ±1.05.
- calcc.c:1663-1667 runs curve_ema_update separately on m, c and s, with a linear EMA at alpha=0.30 (nurbs_spline.c:904).
- sin_cos_identity_check (calcc.c:803-822) tests only the new a->c_spline and a->s_spline, not the blended c_calavg/s_calavg tables that are actually applied. Its tolerance is SC_IDENTITY_TOL 0.05 (calcc.c:304). A 0.05 error means |phasor| up to sqrt(1.05), about +0.21 dB, so that figure is right.
- iqc.c:103-107 does three separate table lookups and applies ym*(yc+j*ys) with no normalisation, so any |yc+j*ys| != 1 really does become AM/AM error.
- Nothing in calcc.c, iqc.c or nurbs_spline.c renormalises the phasor. The only atan2 is in the display path (calcc.c:1706, 1712). WDSP does not already do this.

**Where the benefit is overstated**
1. **0.2 dB is the limit, not the typical error.** It is the rejection threshold. Each per-sample phasor is exactly unit length, so a good separate fit should leave only a small identity error. The worst case is unlikely in normal operation.
2. **Phase drift shortens the phasor only a little.**
   - Slow drift: if the phase moves by delta per cycle, the EMA settles at a magnitude of about 1 - (1-alpha)*delta^2/(2*alpha^2). At alpha=0.3 and 2°/cycle that is about 0.995, roughly 0.04 dB.
   - A sudden step: the shortening is real but temporary. A 30° step gives |0.3e^{j30°}+0.7| ≈ 0.971 (-0.25 dB), and it recovers within a few cycles.
3. **A uniform phase shift only changes overall gain.** If the phase shifts by the same amount at all amplitudes (cable or antenna change, or the constant loop offset), the phasor shrinks by the same factor everywhere. That is a flat gain change and produces no IMD. Only shrinkage that varies with amplitude matters, and that comes from AM/PM shape drift between cycles (small per cycle) or from the next point.
4. **Phase noise at low drive is the stronger case, and the proposal underplays it.** Averaging noisy unit phasors gives a magnitude of about exp(-sigma^2/2). That biases the low-amplitude correction short. Low amplitudes contribute little to IMD, though.
5. **"Halves the fitting work" is wrong.** Going from three curves to two saves a third, not half.
6. **"1-3 dB IMD gain" is unquantified speculation.**

**The "better" variant (fitting unwrapped phase) carries real risk.** Phase unwrapping at low amplitude, where the feedback is noisy, plus reworking the pins and extrapolation for a new quantity, is a substantial change for a gain nobody has demonstrated.

**The minimal variant is sound and nearly free.** Renormalise the blended c/s tables after the EMA (or build one complex table G = ym*u/|u|). This is a circular-mean EMA, which is the standard fix. It costs nothing at run time, slightly reduces per-sample lookups, and needs no change to the correction-file format if c/s stay stored. It removes a real error that the identity check does not monitor.

**The citations are real and relevant.** Cavers 1990, IEEE Trans. Veh. Technol. 39(4), covers amplitude-indexed complex-gain predistortion lookup tables. Fisher 1993, *Statistical Analysis of Circular Data* (Cambridge), is the standard source for mean resultant length shrinking.

**Verdict:** The description is accurate and the minimal fix is technically correct, but the practical benefit is small. Low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: After the CurveEMA update, renormalise the blended cos/sin tables to unit magnitude, or build one complex table G = ym*u/|u|, and have xiqc use it. This removes a real AM/AM error in the correction table that is not monitored, because the identity check only looks at the new spline. The error comes mainly from phase-noise bias at low drive and from temporary EMA averaging after sudden phase steps. In steady state it is typically well under 0.05 dB, and a phase shift that is the same at every amplitude only changes overall gain, not IMD. 0.2 dB is the rejection limit, not a typical value. The change costs essentially nothing and saves a little per-sample work. Expect at most a marginal IMD improvement, not a confirmed 1-3 dB. The full unwrapped-phase refit is not justified by the evidence.

kept.title: Automatic sub-sample TX/RX time alignment each calibration cycle
kept.file_function: calcc.c:pscc lines 1882-1888 (manual delay), SetPSTXDelay 2217-2236; new alignment step before putSample
kept.current: Alignment between the DAC samples and the feedback samples is a fixed user-set delay (txdel), applied through the WDSP delay line in 20 ns steps (create_delay at 1056-1071). Nothing estimates or tracks the actual loop delay. Any residual misalignment tau makes the measured phase error proportional to the envelope slope, which shows up as amplitude-dependent scatter (a hysteresis loop) in yc/ys and ym. The fitter then averages it, and the outlier logic may reject the steep-envelope samples.
kept.proposed: Once per MOX (or per cycle), estimate the delay by cross-correlating |tx|^2 and |rx|^2 over the collected block. Use the FFT through vDSP at 4-8k points. Refine to a fraction of a sample with parabolic interpolation of the correlation peak, or with a Newton step on the phase slope of the cross-spectrum. Smooth the estimate with a slow EMA and feed it to the existing fractional delay. Optionally do a joint delay-and-gain least-squares fit (Gauss-Newton on tau). Show the residual as a diagnostic.
kept.benefit: Removes a manual calibration step and keeps alignment correct across sample-rate changes, firmware or protocol changes, and external feedback paths (couplers, attenuator cables). If the user already set TX delay accurately, the gain for a memoryless model is marginal. Without it, misalignment of even a fraction of a sample at 192 kHz visibly widens the AM/PM scatter and limits correction by several dB. It is also a precondition for proposal 7: memory models are useless without sub-sample alignment.
kept.risk: Correlation can lock onto the wrong peak on strongly periodic signals (two-tone tests). Restrict the search to about ±N samples of the current setting and require a peak-to-sidelobe ratio before accepting an update.
kept.evidence: Envelope cross-correlation with sub-sample refinement is standard in DPD front ends; see Ding, 'Digital Predistortion of Power Amplifiers for Wireless Applications', PhD thesis, Georgia Tech, 2004, ch. 3 (time-delay estimation). Fractional-delay estimation: Jacovitti and Scarano 1993, IEEE Trans. Signal Process., 'Discrete time techniques for time delay estimation'. Line-level: no correlation or alignment code exists in calcc.c (grep), and the delay is set only through SetPSTXDelay.

verdict.reasoning:
The description of the current code is correct. calcc.c:1056-1071 creates rxdelay and txdelay with tdelta=20e-9, which gives a polyphase fractional delay in 20 ns steps. pscc (1882-1888) applies them only while MOX is on and only when a delay is non-zero. SetPSTXDelay (2217-2236) is the only setter. A positive value delays TX and a negative value delays RX. There is no cross-correlation or delay estimation anywhere in the WDSP 2.11 sources, which I checked with grep. In Thetis the control is udPSPhnum: default 150 ns, step 20 ns, tooltip "Compensation delay for the analog PA chain". So a fixed manual delay is the only alignment, as the proposal says.

The benefit is overstated in four places:
(1) "Keeps alignment correct across sample-rate changes" is wrong. SetDelayValue takes seconds and converts them using the delay's own rate, so a rate change does not invalidate the setting.
(2) Coupler and attenuator cables add about 5 ns per metre. That is about 0.001 of a sample at 192 kHz, which is negligible.
(3) Whole-sample alignment between the DAC stream and the feedback DDC is fixed by the FPGA and firmware for a given radio. The manual value only covers the analog PA and LPF group delay, typically 100 to a few hundred ns, or about 0.02 to 0.1 of a sample.
(4) The error from a residual delay tau is about 2*pi*f*tau. For a two-tone test with Δf=1.4 kHz the per-tone error is π·Δf·τ ≈ 4e-4 at 100 ns, about -67 dB. For about 3 kHz of SSB speech at 300 ns it is about -45 to -55 dB. Both are at or below PureSignal's practical correction floor. "Several dB" of lost correction needs an error of roughly 0.3 to 0.5 of a sample (1.5 to 2.6 µs), which normal setups do not reach. External linear amplifiers with long filter chains are the realistic exception.

There is also an implementation gap. The collected samples (putSample, 398-423) are bucketed by amplitude and overwritten in rings, so they are not contiguous in time. Cross-correlating "the collected block" is not possible as written; a separate contiguous TX/RX capture would be needed.

What holds up: the method itself is sound. Envelope cross-correlation with parabolic or phase-slope refinement is standard. The cited references are real and relevant: Ding's 2004 Georgia Tech DPD thesis, and Jacovitti and Scarano, IEEE Trans. Signal Process. 41(2), 1993. The theoretical precision limit (CRLB) at feedback SNR is around 1 ns. The latency cost is negligible because the estimate runs once per cycle off the audio path. It would remove a hidden tuning knob for users with external amplifiers or unusual PA chains, and it would be needed if memory-polynomial models were ever added.

So this is a real but small usability and robustness improvement, not a fix for a measurable defect on typical setups. The search should stay restricted to a window around the current value, gated by peak-to-sidelobe ratio, as the proposal already says.
verdict.corrected_benefit: It would remove the manual "amp delay" setting (default 150 ns, in 20 ns steps) by estimating the analog PA-chain delay automatically, which mainly helps users with external amplifiers or unusual PA and filter chains, where a wrong setting can reach a meaningful fraction of a sample. On typical radios the default residual delay is about 0.03 of a sample at 192 kHz. The resulting AM/PM measurement error is about -50 to -65 dB at speech or two-tone bandwidths, so the gain there is marginal. The setting is already given in seconds and does not depend on the sample rate. Cable lengths are negligible. Implementing it needs a separate contiguous TX/RX capture, because the existing collection is bucketed by amplitude. It is also a prerequisite for any future memory-polynomial model.

refuted.title: Estimate the forward AM/AM and AM/PM conditioned on the noise-free DAC amplitude, then invert (removes indirect-learning bias)
refuted.why:
The description of the current code is accurate. In calcc.c calc() (around lines 1161-1174), x = rx_scale*rx_c, which is the clamped, noisy feedback magnitude. ym = hw_scale*|tx| / (rx_scale*rx_c), and yc/ys are the cos and sin of the tx-rx phase difference. equalize_density bins on a->x (the rx regressor), uses means, and switches to medians in the low bins. This is classic indirect learning: tx is the post-predistortion DAC stream, and the post-inverse is used directly as the predistorter. Sample collection (putSample) already buckets on the noise-free normTX. Only the regressor used for fitting is rx-based. I found no forward-model, direct-learning or ILC path in calcc.c or iqc.c, so WDSP does not already do this.

The cited papers are real and on topic: Zhou and DeBrunner (IEEE TSP 2007), Paaso and Mammela (ISWCS 2008), Chani-Cahuana et al. (TMTT 2016) and Cavers (complex-gain lookup table). But the benefit claimed for this code does not hold up:

(1) The noise-bias mechanism is quantitatively negligible here. With PS feedback noise about 60-70 dB below peak, sigma is about 3e-4 to 1e-3. At the lowest fitted amplitudes (EQ_XMIN 0.02, prefilter 0.04), the relative noise is about 1-3%. The Jensen/ratio bias of averaging |tx|/|rx| scales as (sigma/a)^2, which is about 1e-4 to 1e-3 relative, roughly -60 dB or lower. Regression dilution is just as small, because the noise in x is much smaller than the 0.01 bin width and the inverse curve is nearly flat near 1 at low amplitude. The proposal itself admits the pure-noise bias is marginal.

(2) The main scatter source it cites, PA memory/hysteresis and residual delay, is not estimation bias. It is mismatch from fitting a memoryless model. Inverting E[rx | tx] is also a memoryless compromise, not an 'unbiased' predistorter. Neither ILA nor forward-inversion can correct memory, and memory is what actually limits PureSignal IMD on real HF amplifiers. The DLA-over-ILA results in the literature come mostly from memory-polynomial setups under specific noise and mismatch conditions. They do not show 2-5 dB for a static AM/AM-AM/PM lookup table at 60-70 dB feedback SNR.

(3) The claim that the change would remove the need for the x=0 pin and the prefilter is wrong. The variance of the complex forward-gain estimate rx*conj(tx)/|tx|^2 scales as sigma^2/|tx|^2, so it blows up at small r. Collection also already discards samples below SAMPLE_MIN_X = 0.005. Low-amplitude extrapolation and pinning would still be needed.

(4) Errors below about 0.1 of peak contribute little to the low-order IMD3/IMD5 that dominates amateur SSB/digital splatter specs. So the claimed 2-5 dB on low-order IMD is in the wrong amplitude region and is unsupported.

(5) The cost and risk are large. It changes curve semantics, the display and the correction-file format, and it has to re-create the fold, end-pin and saturation clamp behaviour, where mistakes over-drive peaks.

Net: the proposal is a legitimate alternative architecture, but for this application its benefit is unconfirmed and likely near zero. Refuted under the default-to-refute rule.

refuted.title: Add an optional memory stage: a small generalized memory polynomial on the residual after the static table
refuted.why:
The description of the current code is accurate. In xiqc (iqc.c:99-107), env is computed only from the current I and Q. ym, yc and ys come from get_mag_correction_ema and get_phase_correction_ema, which explicitly ignore prev_y ("(void)prev_y;" in nurbs_spline.c:957-970) and simply interpolate a static curve. So the predistorter is strictly memoryless (AM/AM plus AM/PM). Nothing else in WDSP 2.11 does memory DPD: a search for memory polynomial, Volterra or GMP finds nothing. The citations are real and correctly attributed: Kim and Konstantinou, Electron. Lett. 37(23), 2001; Morgan et al., IEEE TSP 54(10), 2006; Ding et al., IEEE Trans. Commun. 52(1), 2004.

I still refute the proposal as specified, for these reasons.

(1) The memory depth is scaled wrongly for SSB. The PS feedback and correction run at ch.in_rate / dsp_rate, typically 192 kS/s (TXA.c:407-422). A 3 kHz SSB envelope is about 60x oversampled there. M=2..4 taps spans only about 10-20 µs, and over that span |x(n-m)| is almost identical to |x(n)|. The delayed GMP regressors are therefore nearly collinear with the static terms. The least-squares problem is badly conditioned for any signal, not only a steady tone. With ridge regularisation, the only thing it can fit is a small first-derivative term. That term mostly soaks up residual fractional time misalignment between TX and feedback, which is a capture artefact, not PA memory.

(2) The memory mechanisms the proposal names cannot be reached by 20 µs of taps. Electrothermal and supply-sag effects work on millisecond-to-second scales. Bias-network resonances at envelope rates of a few kHz work on hundreds of microseconds. Slow thermal drift is already tracked, roughly, because calcc recalibrates continuously and swaps tables (the SWAP state in xiqc). Fast envelope-rate memory would need sparse, decimated delays or an IIR/low-pass envelope branch (for example a Wiener-Hammerstein or thermal sub-model), not a GMP with M=2..4 at the feedback rate.

(3) The calcc data path does not support it. psCollection (calcc.c:310-372, 411-422) stores isolated TX/RX sample pairs in 16 amplitude buckets of 256 each, ring-indexed per bucket, with no time history. You cannot form x(n-m) from it. A memory stage would need a new contiguous, sub-sample-aligned capture path and a new solver/validation pipeline. That is far more than "a new least-squares stage after the curves pass".

(4) The benefit is speculative even in the proposal's own words: "perhaps 0-6 dB", "may be about zero", "unproven on HF ham amplifiers". For ham use, PS correction is usually limited by feedback SNR and coupler or ADC dynamic range, and voice gives poor excitation diversity. Neither point favours a 20-40 coefficient adaptive model. It also adds a real instability and regression risk to a live transmit path.

Given the default-to-refute rule and no evidence that this configuration helps on HF SSB, I refute it. A narrower idea might be worth measuring: first check two-tone IMD asymmetry versus tone spacing on a real amplifier, then, if memory is confirmed, use a slow envelope-filtered branch. That would be a different proposal.

refuted.title: Keep the fit in double (or use QR) when porting to float32, and simplify to a direct penalised B-spline y(x)
refuted.why:
The description of the current code is mostly accurate. ls_solve_with_cond (nurbs_fit.c:534-591) builds A'A and Atb, factors with cholesky() (505-520), and adds a 1e-8*trace ridge if that fails. The cond_out value is (max/min of the Cholesky diagonal)^2. That estimates cond(A'A), so it is already the squared figure. The 1e8 NF_FIT_BAD_CONDNUM threshold (1355, 1743) therefore applies to cond(A'A), and comparing it with float32's 1/eps of about 1.7e7 is the right comparison. The IRLS loop (1341-1353) calls fit_pass with cond_out=NULL, so those passes are not condition-checked. Its weights are 1/(res+1e-6) applied to the rows, which can widen the spread of A'A by a lot. lowess (extrapolate.c:280-332) and wls_poly (251-278) do accumulate raw moments without centring. PS config is as described: calcc.c sets PS_NF_UNIFORM_KNOTS 1, ADAPTIVE_ITERS 0 and ORDERING_MODE NF_ORDER_BY_X, and parameterise_dispatch (416-429) sets t=x. B-splines reproduce linear functions exactly, so x(t)=t and the curve is in effect y(x). The parametric and fold machinery is therefore largely inert. calcc.c does call nf_fit, then ns_build, then ns_accuracy_check (1282-1635).

Why this is refuted as an improvement to WDSP:
(a) Every routine involved (nurbs_fit.c, extrapolate.c, calcc.c) is written entirely in double. There is no float in the fit path. In Lyra the WDSP C source is built directly (CMakeLists) and is not ported. "Keep calc() and extrapolate in double" is exactly what WDSP already does. The claimed collapse happens only in a float32 port that does not exist and that nobody has proposed, so it is a caveat for porting, not a fix. In double, eps*cond(A'A) is about 2e-16*1e8, roughly 2e-8, which is harmless.
(b) The proposal admits the quality gain is "about the same or marginally better". The extra resampling stages are checked by ns_accuracy_check and add error far below PA predistortion needs, which are about 40-60 dB IMD improvement. What remains is a rewrite for maintainability. It would replace a fitter whose many PS thresholds were tuned against its current behaviour. It would need a new QP or active-set solver and GCV. The benefit to amateur PureSignal operation (SSB, CW and digital linearity) is unquantified and possibly negative until re-tuned. As stated, it is not a demonstrated algorithmic improvement.

The literature is real and relevant in general: Golub and Van Loan sec. 5.3; Eilers and Marx 1996, Stat. Sci. 11(2); Pya and Wood 2015, Stat. Comput. None of it shows a problem in the current double-precision code.

A minor real observation that the proposal did not make its main point: the IRLS refits are not cond-checked and use weights of 1/(r+1e-6). Even in double that could inflate A'A conditioning. It is a small robustness note, not the claimed benefit.

summary: new_window() (lines 52-177) builds one of seven symmetric windows (denominator N-1): rectangular, 4-term Blackman-Harris, Hann, 5-term flat-top, Hamming, Kaiser (with the Abramowitz and Stegun/Numerical Recipes bessi0 approximation) and a 7-term Blackman-Harris in Horner form. Each window is scaled to unity coherent gain, and inv_enb = 1/ENBW is stored. Worker threads (spectra/Cspectra, 603-669 and 837-918) window an overlapped block from a ring buffer and run an FFTW r2c or c2c FFT. eliminate()/Celiminate() (180-281) take |X|^2, drop `clip` bins from each sub-span edge plus fractional fsclipL/H at the span ends (this is how zoom works: bins are thrown away, not re-resolved), and keep the minimum across num_fft LO positions to suppress spurs. stitch() (556-601) joins the sub-spans. detector() (283-462) maps bins to pixels with peak, rosenfell, average, sample or 'rms' when there are more bins than pixels, and interpolates linearly in the power domain when there are more pixels than bins. avenger() (464-554) then applies peak-hold, an exponential IIR on linear power, a boxcar running sum over up to dMAX_AVERAGE=60 frames, or an IIR on dB values, and converts to dB with the table-based mlog10. The calibration term cd[] comes from a cubic spline (build_interpolants/interpolate, 920-1056), and 1-Hz normalisation adds 10log10(N/fs). A separate DetectMaxBin path (705-816) reports a decaying peak over a frequency range for metering.

kept.title: Boxcar averaging (av_mode 2) never clears its running sum, so old frames stay in the display permanently
kept.file_function: analyzer.c:avenger (512-539), SetDisplayNumAverage (1816-1828), SetDisplayAverageMode case 2 (1798-1802), ResetPixelBuffers case 2 (1122-1127)
kept.current: Case 2 keeps a running sum: av_sum[i] += t_pixels[i] - av_buff[out][i]. SetDisplayNumAverage, SetDisplayAverageMode(…,2) and ResetPixelBuffers (case 2 says '//done below') reset only avail_frames, av_in_idx and av_out_idx. None of them zeroes av_sum. SetDisplayNumAverage also does not clamp num against dMAX_AVERAGE (60), but the ring indices wrap at 60.
kept.proposed: (1) Zero av_sum whenever avail_frames/in/out are reset, and clamp num_average to [1, dMAX_AVERAGE]. (2) In LyraDSP, stop subtracting old frames from a running sum. Either keep the accumulator in double, or recompute it from the ring every frame (vDSP_vadd over at most 60x16384 floats, which is trivial), or at least every num_average frames. This removes cancellation drift in the float32 port. Alternatively use Kahan-compensated add/subtract.
kept.benefit: Large and visible. After any change to the average count, the sum of the previous window (S_old) is never subtracted, because the ring entries it came from are overwritten before they are subtracted. The display then shows that frozen spectrum, divided by the frame count, as a permanent pedestal until the mode changes. Switching from mode 3 to mode 2 is worse: av_sum holds dB values around -100 (linear sum, negative), and mlog10 ignores the sign bit (meterlog10.c:547-553), so the trace locks to a meaningless constant. num_average > 60 silently corrupts the window membership. In float32, a running sum that has to cancel a strong carrier (P near 1) after it disappears leaves a residual near 1e-7·P, which is about -70 dB relative to that carrier and can go negative. That puts a fake floor under weak signals where a strong one used to be.
kept.risk: None for correctness. Recomputing the sum costs about 1 M adds per frame at 16k pixels and 60 frames, which is negligible on M-series. Users would see the pedestal disappear.
kept.evidence: Line-level: avenger 519-520/529-530 only add and subtract, and the reset paths at 1799-1801, 1823-1825 and 1136-1138 never touch av_sum. mlog10 masks bits 52-62 only, so sign is ignored. On running-sum error growth: Higham, 'The accuracy of floating point summation', SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 1993; Kahan 1965 compensated summation.

verdict.reasoning:
I read analyzer.c and the description matches the code. In avenger case 2, the fill phase does av_sum += t, and the steady phase does av_sum += t - av_buff[out]. None of the three reset paths touches av_sum when the mode is 2:
- SetDisplayNumAverage (1816-1828) resets only avail_frames, av_in_idx and av_out_idx.
- SetDisplayAverageMode case 2 (1798-1802) does the same.
- ResetPixelBuffers case 2 is an empty '//done below'. It zeroes av_buff and the indices, but av_sum keeps its old contents.

Tracing the path: after a reset, av_sum still holds S_old. The fill phase adds N_new new frames into the ring. From then on, the steady phase subtracts only those new frames, so S_old is never removed, and the display shows (S_old + window)/N_new from then on. If mode 2 is active and the count changes, S_old ≈ N_old·F (F is the old average spectrum). The floor is then lifted by about 10·log10(1 + N_old/N_new), for example +4.8 dB going from 10 to 5 frames, or +12 dB going from 30 to 2. Strong signals from the old window also stay behind as ghost peaks.

How bad a mode switch is depends on the previous mode:
- 3 to 2 is the worst case. av_sum holds dB values around -100 to -160, which swamp the linear powers. mlog10 reads only the exponent and mantissa bits (bits 52 and up, mask 2047), so the sign is ignored, and the trace freezes near a meaningless constant. This is confirmed.
- -1 (peak hold) to 2 leaves a pedestal of peak/N.
- 1 to 2 leaves only a small pedestal, about P/N.
- 0 to 2 is clean, because switching to mode 0 memsets av_sum.

There is no clamp on num_average, while both ring indices wrap at dMAX_AVERAGE (60). With num > 60, the fill phase overwrites slots before they are subtracted, so the sum drifts and can go negative. This only happens if the host passes a value above 60.

Part (2), the float32 running-sum drift, does not apply to WDSP, which keeps av_sum in double: the residual is about 1e-16·P, roughly -160 dB, which is invisible. I also found no LyraDSP or float32 port of this code in the Lyra repo (grep for SetDisplayNumAverage, av_sum and numAverage returned nothing), so that half is a hypothetical design note, not a confirmed defect. Its numbers are sound for a float32 implementation: eps ≈ 6e-8 gives a residual about -70 dB relative to a strong carrier. The Higham (1993) and Kahan (1965) citations are real and relevant.

The fix is trivial and display-only: zero av_sum wherever the case-2 indices are reset, and clamp num to [1, 60]. It has no effect on audio, latency or TX.
verdict.corrected_benefit: This is a real display bug in WDSP 2.11's window averaging (av_mode 2). Changing the average count, switching into mode 2, or calling ResetPixelBuffers leaves the old running sum in av_sum, and it never decays. That leaves a permanent pedestal and ghost peaks, scaled by N_old/N_new. Switching from the log-recursive mode 3 into mode 2 freezes the trace at a constant, because av_sum still holds negative dB values and mlog10 ignores the sign. Switching from mode 0 into mode 2 is unaffected. The fix is to zero av_sum on every reset path and clamp num_average to [1, dMAX_AVERAGE]. That removes the artifacts at no cost, and only the spectrum display is affected. The float32-drift advice only matters if Lyra ports this averager to single precision. No such port exists in the repo today, and WDSP's double accumulator makes drift negligible.

kept.title: Rosenfell detector decides pixel boundaries without det_offset, so pixels are split, merged, or left with last frame's data
kept.current: pix_count = (int)(det_offset + i*pix_per_bin) (332), clamped to num_pixels-1 (333). The 'is the next bin in the same pixel' test uses next_pix_count = (int)((i+1)*pix_per_bin) (335), which has no det_offset and no clamp. det_offset = -pix_per_bin*frac(fsclipL) (1284) is non-zero whenever the span edge is fractional, which is the usual case when dragging or zooming.
kept.proposed: Compute next_pix_count = (int)(det_offset + (i+1)*pix_per_bin) and apply the same clamp. Better, precompute integer bin-boundary indices per pixel once in SetAnalyzer, shared by all detectors: start[p] = ceil((p - det_offset)/pix_per_bin). Every detector then walks [start[p], start[p+1]) with no float re-evaluation. This also makes it easy to centre buckets on the pixel frequencies that interpolate() assumes (f_min + p*(f_max-f_min)/(N-1)). Today the buckets are [p, p+1)/pix_per_bin, which places them up to half a pixel off at the span edges.
kept.benefit: With a fractional edge, the boundary test disagrees with the bin-to-pixel assignment. Some pixels are finalised early: a carrier in the first bins of a pixel is then overwritten by the max/min of the remaining bins and disappears. Other pixels are never finalised, so t_pixels keeps the previous frame's value, because t_pixels is not cleared, and min/max leaks into the neighbouring pixel. Rosenfell is the Thetis default for many users, so this shows up as intermittent dropped peaks or flicker while tuning.
kept.risk: None. The output only becomes what the algorithm intends.
kept.evidence: Line 332 vs 335 in detector(). The other detectors (0, 2, 3, 4) use only pix_count with det_offset, so they are not affected. Rosenfell algorithm as used in Spectrum Lab/Thetis; the odd/even max-min rule is at 352-358.

verdict.reasoning:
I confirmed this in analyzer.c. In detector() case 1 (Rosenfell), line 332 computes pix_count = (int)(det_offset + i*pix_per_bin) with a clamp. Line 335 computes next_pix_count = (int)((i+1)*pix_per_bin), which has no det_offset and no clamp. The other detectors (0, 2, 3, 4) use only the offset form. Line 1284 sets det_offset = -pix_per_bin*frac(fsclipL), so det_offset is in (-pix_per_bin, 0] and is non-zero whenever fsclipL is fractional.

Tracing the mismatch: since d <= 0, floor((i+1)p) >= floor((i+1)p + d), which is the true pixel of bin i+1. So the test can only report a boundary too early. It never misses one. The proposal's second failure mode is wrong: no pixel is left unfinalised, t_pixels does not keep last frame's value, and min/max does not leak into the neighbouring pixel. The only exception is a trivial edge case at the clamped last pixel.

The first failure mode is real and worse than the proposal says. The test finds the boundary about frac bins before the true one. When a bin falls in that gap, which happens with probability about frac at each pixel boundary, the pixel is finalised one bin early. The next bin then finalises on its own and overwrites pixels[pc] with that single bin's value. prev_maxi, used for the odd-pixel rule, is corrupted as well. In those pixels the Rosenfell output reduces to one sample, so a carrier peak elsewhere in the pixel is lost.

I simulated 4096 bins over 1500 pixels. frac(fsclipL) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.9 gave 149, 451, 753 and 1353 pixels written more than once. With the det_offset and clamp fix applied, every case gave 0. With an integer edge (frac = 0) the current code gave 1, the clamp edge case.

The minimal fix is to add det_offset and the clamp at line 335, which matches how the other detectors assign pixels. It is clearly correct and carries no risk. The extra ideas are reasonable refactors but not needed for the fix: precomputed integer bucket boundaries, and re-centring buckets on interpolate()'s pixel frequencies. Re-centring would change what every detector outputs, so it is not 'no risk'. I did not verify the claim that Rosenfell is the Thetis default.
verdict.corrected_benefit: When fsclipL is fractional, about frac(fsclipL)*num_pixels of the pixels currently lose all but their last bin, because the pixel is finalised one bin early and the last bin overwrites it. The same error also corrupts prev_maxi for the odd/even rule. As a result, narrow carriers drop out or the display flickers while you zoom or pan. Adding det_offset and the clamp to next_pix_count at analyzer.c:335 makes Rosenfell group bins exactly as the other detectors do. No pixels are left stale. The bug only causes duplicate writes, not missed ones.

kept.title: Torn frames: stitch() reads result[] and pre_av_out after the next frame's FFT workers have been released
kept.current: Once every sub-span is complete, the last worker clears input_busy for all (ss, LO) (656-658 / 905-907) and then calls stitch(). The sendbuf dispatcher (1066) can immediately queue new FFTs for any buffer with buff_ready set. Those run eliminate() and write result[ss] under EliminateSection only, while stitch() memcpys result[n] into the shared pre_av_out with no lock (567). Two stitch() calls can also overlap, because pre_av_out is written outside ResampleSection.
kept.proposed: Copy result[begin_ss..end_ss] into a per-frame snapshot, or flip a double-buffered result pointer, before clearing input_busy. Then run detection and averaging on the snapshot, and serialise stitch() itself, either with a dedicated lock held around the memcpy and detection or with a single consumer thread. In LyraDSP, a lock-free SPSC handoff of a frame buffer to one 'display' thread is the natural structure.
kept.benefit: Removes occasional frames that mix two FFT epochs. It also removes the num_fft>1 case where new-frame LO0 data, written with spec_flag==0 and so not yet min-eliminated, reaches the display, which lets suppressed spurs flash through. The race opens only when samples are backlogged (max_writeahead > size), so the effect is intermittent. It is a real data race, and ThreadSanitizer will flag it in a Swift/C port.
kept.risk: Negligible: one extra memcpy per frame.
kept.evidence: Ordering at 656-659: InterlockedBitTestAndReset(input_busy) happens before stitch(disp). sendbuf only checks input_busy && buff_ready (1066). The memcpy at 567 is outside every critical section.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the cited code in analyzer.c and it does what the proposal says.

The ordering problem is real. In spectra (lines 652-660) and Cspectra (901-909), the last worker releases StitchSection, clears input_busy for every (ss, LO), and only then calls stitch(disp). The sendbuf dispatcher (lines 1066-1083) checks only that input_busy is clear and buff_ready is set before it queues a new spectra or Cspectra worker. That worker writes result[ss] in eliminate() or Celiminate(), at lines 201-277, while holding only EliminateSection[ss]. Because spec_flag[ss] was reset to 0, the first LO to finish overwrites result[ss] outright instead of taking the minimum. stitch() reads result[n] with a memcpy at line 567 while holding no lock at all. So when num_fft > 1, a new frame's LO0 magnitudes can leak into the old frame before min-elimination has run on them.

buff_ready stays set whenever have_samples is still at least size after subtracting incr (line 1082). That happens whenever the next frame's samples are already buffered: large input blocks, high overlap, or a backlog up to max_writeahead (lines 1617-1624). Nothing in WDSP blocks this; no other path or option serialises stitch against the next frame.

The second race, two stitch() calls overlapping, is also possible. pre_av_out is written before ResampleSection is taken, and detector() reads it inside that section once per pixout. If a whole new frame finishes while an earlier stitch is still detecting a later pixout, the second memcpy overwrites the buffer the first stitch is reading.

How likely it is to show up is a different matter. The dispatcher polls with Sleep(1), which on Windows means 1-15 ms. A new worker then has to window `size` samples and run an FFT of that size before it reaches eliminate. The stitch memcpy takes microseconds. So the tear needs the stitch thread to be preempted or starved between clearing input_busy and finishing the memcpy, or needs very slow detection with many pixouts. In practice that is rare. The result is a cosmetic glitch lasting one frame (for example, a suppressed spur flashing up), with no crash and no effect on audio.

It is still a genuine data race under the C memory model, and ThreadSanitizer would report it in a port. The fix is cheap and safe:
- Copy into pre_av_out (or a snapshot) before clearing input_busy.
- Serialise the consumer side, either with a lock around the memcpy and detection or with a single display thread.

On its own, reordering the memcpy ahead of the input_busy reset fixes the result[] tear. It does not fix two stitch() calls overlapping on pre_av_out; that still needs the serialisation step.

The risk estimate ("one extra memcpy") holds. The fix should not add latency, because the copy replaces the existing stitch memcpy rather than adding a new one.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
This removes a real but rarely triggered data race in WDSP's spectrum analyzer. Today stitch() can copy result[] after the next frame's workers have been released. With num_fft > 1, a new frame's LO0 values can then overwrite min-eliminated bins, so a suppressed spur can flash up for one frame. Two stitch() calls can also overlap on pre_av_out. Triggering it needs the stitch thread to be preempted in a window of a few microseconds while the next frame's samples are already buffered, so users would see it only as an occasional one-frame display glitch.

The main value is for the LyraDSP port. There the fix makes the code correct under the memory model and keeps ThreadSanitizer quiet. Snapshot or memcpy result[] into the frame buffer before clearing input_busy, then hand the buffer to a single display consumer, or hold one lock around the copy and detection. The cost is negligible.

kept.title: DetectMaxBin decays at a rate that depends on level and runs once per FFT, not per frame; replace with a linear-domain release and interpolated peak
kept.current: The decay is applied in dB as dmb_max_dB -= |(1-decay)*dmb_max_dB| (809), so the fall rate is proportional to the absolute dB value. At -100 dB it is about 3.3 dB per call with tau=0.5 s and fps=60, and near 0 dB it is zero. decay is computed from the display frame_rate (745), but the function runs once per Cspectra FFT (870), which happens at fs/incr per second, not at fps. Only the complex path calls it (spectra() never does). It reports the raw maximum bin: no ENBW/cd calibration and no scalloping correction. SetupDetectMaxBin writes the begin/end indices without holding cs_dmb while worker threads read them.
kept.proposed: Hold the peak in linear power: P_hold = max(P_now, P_hold*exp(-T_fft/tau)), with T_fft = incr/fs. That gives a constant dB/s release independent of level and of how often it is called. Report 10log10(scale*cd*P_hold). Refine the maximum with 3-point quadratic interpolation of log-magnitude around the peak bin (Smith and Serra 1987), or a window-specific estimator (Grandke 1983), to remove scalloping loss: about 0.8-1.4 dB worst case for Hann/BH windows, about 0 for flat-top. Take cs_dmb in SetupDetectMaxBin/calc_dmb, and call the function from the real-input path as well.
kept.benefit: Gives the metering feature a calibrated, level-independent ballistic. Today it is effectively an un-held instantaneous maximum whose fall rate depends on the reference level. Interpolation fixes a reading error of up to about 1.4 dB on carriers between bins.
kept.risk: Users will see a slower, smoother meter, which is what was intended. Behaviour changes only if someone tuned tau to compensate for the bug.
kept.evidence: Lines 745, 809 and 870. Release equation: standard peak-program meter ballistics (IEC 60268-10). Smith and Serra, 'PARSHL', ICMC 1987 (quadratic interpolation of the log spectrum). Grandke, IEEE Trans. Instrum. Meas. 1983 (interpolated DFT). Scalloping figures from Harris, Proc. IEEE 1978.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked "/Users/bcrier/Documents/dev/wdsp/wdsp 2.11/Source/analyzer.c" lines 679-830 and the Thetis/Kainos caller in kainos-dev/Project Files/Source/Console/console.cs:52299 and HPSDR/specHPSDR.cs:532,784.

Confirmed:
(1) The release is applied in the dB domain at line 809: dmb_max_dB -= fabs((1-decay)*dmb_max_dB). Each call multiplies the dB value by (2-decay), so the fall is geometric in dB magnitude and the rate depends on the level. The caller passes tau=0.5 and fps=60, which gives 1-decay = 0.0328. That is 3.3 dB per call at -100 dB, about 200 dB/s and speeding up, and almost zero near 0 dB. A linear-power exp(-T/tau) release with tau=0.5 would be about 8.7 dB/s. So the documented "metering time constant" is not what the code does. The held value is in effect the maximum of the last one or two FFTs.
(2) The function is called only from Cspectra (line 870). spectra() calls fftw_execute and never calls DetectMaxBin.
(3) SetupDetectMaxBin and calc_dmb write dmb_begin and dmb_end without cs_dmb, while worker threads read them under the lock. This is a real race. It is mostly harmless because both index sets are valid for the current size.

Overstated:
(a) "Runs at fs/incr, not fps." Thetis sets overlap = max(0, ceil(size - fs/fps)), so incr is about fs/fps and the FFT rate is about fps for typical large FFTs. The rates differ only when size < fs/fps, where the rate becomes fs/size. Deriving T_fft from incr/fs is still more robust, but this half of the bug is minor in practice.
(b) "No ENBW calibration." The window is normalised to coherent gain (inv_coherent_gain, lines 150-170) and scale = 1/N^2. An on-bin carrier therefore already reads correct power. Applying ENBW would be wrong for a peak or carrier reading. Only the frequency-dependent cd hardware calibration is missing.
(c) Scalloping. The figures are real per Harris 1978: about 1.42 dB for Hann and about 0.83 dB for 4-term BH. The default window here is 7-term BH, so worst-case loss is under 1 dB. It only matters for CW or carriers between bins, and Thetis FFTs often have bins of a few Hz.

The references are real and relevant: Smith and Serra PARSHL 1987 (quadratic interpolation of the log-magnitude peak), Grandke 1983 (interpolated DFT), and IEC 60268-10 (PPM ballistics).

Impact is limited. This is an optional "Signal Max FFT Bin" meter, not the receive path. In Thetis, MeterManager bars add their own attack and decay smoothing, which partly hides the WDSP release bug. Anything that consumes GetDetectMaxBin directly (TCI sensors, a new front end) sees the raw, effectively un-held value.
verdict.corrected_benefit: DetectMaxBin's release is a real bug. Applying a multiplicative decay to a dB value makes the fall rate depend on the reference level: about 200 dB/s and speeding up at -100 dBFS, and almost no fall near 0 dBFS. So the tau parameter does not deliver the 0.5 s time constant it documents. Holding the peak in linear power and decaying by exp(-T_fft/tau), with T_fft = incr/fs, gives a constant release in dB/s that matches tau. Also take cs_dmb when writing the indices. Optionally, quadratic log-magnitude peak interpolation removes up to about 0.8 dB of scalloping error (less with the default 7-term BH window) on carriers between bins. The other parts add little. ENBW correction would be wrong for a peak reading because the window is already coherent-gain normalised. Thetis already sets overlap so the FFT rate is about fps. The real-input path is not used for the receive panadapter. Impact is limited to an optional meter, and Thetis's own meter ballistics partly hide it.

kept.title: The 'rms' detector computes sqrt(mean(P^2)) on power bins; true RMS detection is mean power
kept.current: bins[] already holds |X|^2 (eliminate 200/207). Case 4 accumulates psum += bins[i]*bins[i] and outputs sqrt(psum/bcount)*inv_enb, which is the quadratic mean of the powers. Case 2 ('average', 368-392) already outputs mean(P)*inv_enb, which is what swept analyzers call RMS (power) detection.
kept.proposed: Make 'rms' output mean(P), the standard RMS/power detector. To keep two distinct detectors, redefine 'average' as the traditional log/video average: the mean of 10log10(P) over the bucket. Either document its -2.51 dB noise bias, or add +2.51 dB in noise-marker mode.
kept.benefit: For Gaussian noise, P per bin is exponential and E[P^2] = 2E[P]^2, so the current 'rms' reads the noise floor 1.51 dB high relative to true RMS/average. For a carrier occupying 1 of b bins in a pixel it reads P/sqrt(b) instead of P/b, so the carrier-to-noise ratio shown depends on zoom level. The fix is small but corrects calibration whenever more than one bin maps to a pixel. With at most one bin per pixel the result is identical.
kept.risk: Operators who compared 'rms' readings will see about a 1.5 dB shift. Renaming or redefining 'average' changes behaviour and should be opt-in.
kept.evidence: Lines 427/432 vs 378/383. Keysight AN 150 'Spectrum Analysis Basics' and AN 1303 'Spectrum and Signal Analyzer Measurements and Noise' (RMS detector = power average; log average biased -2.51 dB = 10·γ/ln10).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the code path and the description is accurate. eliminate()/Celiminate() (analyzer.c ~200-276) store mag = re^2+im^2 in result[], which means they hold power. stitch() copies result[] into pre_av_out and passes it to detector() as bins (lines 564-586). Case 2 (368-392) outputs mean(P)*inv_enb. Case 4 (417-441) adds up bins[i]*bins[i] and outputs sqrt(psum/bcount)*inv_enb, which is the quadratic mean of the powers. In voltage terms, RMS is sqrt(mean|X|^2), and that is mean(P) in the power domain. So case 4 is not a standard RMS detector. avenger() then converts to dB with 10*log10, so the sqrt does not cancel anywhere. Case 4 only applies when pix_per_bin <= 1. In the interpolation branch, rms and average behave the same.

I simulated independent exponential bins to check the size of the effect. The proposal's flat +1.51 dB figure is only the large-b limit. The real offset against the average detector depends on bins per pixel: b=1 gives 0.0 dB, b=2 gives 0.61, b=4 gives 0.98, b=8 gives 1.22, b=16 gives 1.35 and b=64 gives 1.46 dB. Correlation between neighbouring bins caused by the window would shrink this a little. So the 'rms' noise floor moves with zoom level, which is a real calibration defect, though small. The carrier claim (P/sqrt(b) vs P/b) is correct when the carrier sits in one bin. A windowed carrier spreads over a few bins, but the reading still depends on zoom.

Two nuances. First, the 'average' detector already gives a correctly calibrated power average. Anyone who needs an accurate noise or level reading can use it today (it is the mode used with the normalize-to-1-Hz option), so the practical harm is small. Second, the second half of the proposal, redefining 'average' as a log/video average, is not justified as a bug fix. It changes the behaviour of a detector that is already correct, and log averaging over time already exists as av_mode 3. The cited Keysight notes do exist and are relevant: they describe RMS as power averaging and the log-average bias of -2.51 dB. The fix should be limited to the rms case, for example making rms equal mean(P) or documenting what it computes, and should not touch 'average'. This is a display-only issue with no effect on reception or transmission, so it is low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: The 'rms' detector (case 4) computes sqrt(mean(P^2)) over power bins, which is not a standard RMS/power detector. On noise it reads high compared with the correctly calibrated 'average' detector. The offset depends on how many bins fall in each pixel: about 0.6 dB at 2 bins, 1.0 dB at 4 and 1.35 dB at 16, approaching 1.5 dB. As a result the noise floor and the carrier-to-noise ratio it shows change with zoom. Making case 4 output mean(P), or documenting what it actually computes, removes that inconsistency. The 'average' detector already gives correct readings, so this is a small display-calibration cleanup. Redefining 'average' as a log average is a separate, optional behaviour change and not part of the fix.

kept.title: Zoom by discarding bins and linearly interpolating power: use a chirp-z transform or zoom-FFT for narrow spans
kept.file_function: analyzer.c:detector interpolation branch (444-460); span/zoom set-up in SetAnalyzer (1266-1285); eliminate/Celiminate clipping (180-281)
kept.current: A span narrower than fs comes from clipping fsclipL/H bins off a full-band FFT. When pixels outnumber the remaining bins (pix_per_bin > 1), pixels are linear interpolations in power between adjacent bins (454). That draws each windowed mainlobe as a piecewise-linear 'tent', which looks like straight-line facets on the dB scale, and shows a carrier between bins with scalloping loss and a flat or doubled top. The only way to get finer resolution is a larger FFT of the whole band.
kept.proposed: (a) Display interpolation: when pix_per_bin > 1, evaluate the windowed DTFT at exactly the pixel frequencies across [f_min, f_max] with a chirp-z transform, using Bluestein's algorithm with three FFTs of length L >= N+M-1 in vDSP. For integer oversampling, the cheaper option is to zero-pad the FFT by ceil(pix_per_bin). (b) Resolution: for spans much narrower than fs, use a zoom-FFT. Mix the span centre to DC, decimate by D with a polyphase/CIC+FIR chain (WDSP already has the resampler building blocks), then FFT N points. Same RBW as a D·N-point FFT, but the FFT cost drops by about D·log(DN)/log(N), and RBW can go finer than max_size allows at wide sample rates.
kept.benefit: (a) Correct mainlobe shape and true peak amplitude/frequency at deep zoom. It does not improve RBW or the ability to separate two signals; the gain is display fidelity, clearly visible when zoomed in on CW/FT8 signals. (b) At 1.5 MHz fs with a 10 kHz span, a 1 Hz RBW costs a 16k-point FFT plus decimation instead of a 2M-point FFT. That makes the fine resolution practical on CPU, and keeps FFT sizes where float32 round-off is lowest.
kept.risk: CZT costs roughly 2-3x the current FFT when active, so it is fine on M-series. Zoom-FFT adds a decimation filter whose transition band must sit outside the displayed span: span edges show filter rolloff unless the guard band is clipped, which the existing `clip` mechanism can do. Time resolution is unchanged for the same RBW.
kept.evidence: Rabiner, Schafer and Rader, 'The chirp z-transform algorithm', IEEE Trans. Audio Electroacoust. 1969. Bluestein 1970. Yip, 'Zoom FFT', IEEE Trans. ASSP 1976. Lyons, 'Understanding DSP', 3rd ed., section 13.x (zoom FFT). Current behaviour at line 454: pixels = bins[i-1]*(1-frac) + bins[i]*frac in the linear power domain.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked the current behaviour in analyzer.c and the description is mostly right.
- The FFT length equals the window length (window applied at ~619, no zero-padding anywhere).
- Narrow spans come from clipping fsclipL/fsclipH bins in eliminate/Celiminate (180-281). The fsclip bin counts and pix_per_bin/bin_per_pix are set in SetAnalyzer (~1266-1285).
- When pix_per_bin > 1, detector() ignores det_type and linearly interpolates in linear power between adjacent bins (~454). Only an inv_enb scale is applied.
- Neither zero-padding, CZT nor zoom-FFT exists in the analyzer. Stitching (num_stitch) widens the span, it does not zoom.

Two small inaccuracies:
- Linear-in-power segments plotted in dB are concave curves with kinks at the bins, not straight facets.
- A larger FFT is not the only route to finer resolution. In practice the HPSDR hardware DDC sample-rate choice is already a zoom (mix plus decimate) done before WDSP.
- Scalloping is also partly addressed already: one of the window options (the high-order cosine set at ~158) appears to be a flat-top, which removes amplitude scalloping at the cost of RBW.

Relevance: Lyra runs the RX panadapter analyzer at kAnFftSize = 4096 (src/wdsp_engine.cpp:227) on an HL2-class stream of 48-384 kHz. At 192 kHz that is about 47 Hz per bin. A typical 10-20 kHz zoom over ~1000-2000 pixels gives pix_per_bin of roughly 2-10, so the interpolation branch runs often. With a non-flat-top window, a CW or FT8 carrier between bins shows a flat top and up to ~1.4 dB (Hann) / ~0.8 dB (BH4) low amplitude.

Part (a), recommended form only: zero-pad the FFT by K ≈ ceil(pix_per_bin). This samples the true windowed DTFT at sub-bin spacing, gives correct mainlobe shape, and cuts scalloping to a small fraction of a dB. Time resolution is unchanged, unlike simply raising the FFT size, and the cost is a K-times-larger FFT, trivial on M-series. CZT/Bluestein is real and correct (Rabiner/Schafer/Rader 1969; Bluestein 1970) but overkill here, since zero-padding plus the existing interpolation already gets close enough at the pixel scale.
- Implementation is not trivial: WDSP couples window size to FFT size (fft_in buffers, plans, out_size, scale), and fsclipL/fsclipH are passed in by the caller in bin units. Both WDSP and the caller's clip maths would have to change.
- The gain is cosmetic and for measurement accuracy only. It adds no RBW or selectivity.

Part (b), zoom-FFT, has little value here:
- Yip 1976 and Lyons are real and relevant, but the hardware DDC already decimates.
- Lyra's rates are ≤384 kHz, where a 256k-point double-precision FFT (about 1.5 Hz bins) is cheap on M-series.
- 1 Hz RBW needs about a second of data whatever the method, so the update cost argument is weak. The decimation filter adds group delay and edge rolloff.
- The float32 round-off argument does not apply, because WDSP uses double-precision FFTW.
- The 1.5 MHz / 2M-point scenario does not match this radio.

Verdict: partly valid. Only (a) as zero-padding is worth doing, at low priority.
verdict.corrected_benefit: Decouple the FFT length from the window length and zero-pad by about ceil(pix_per_bin) when the display has more pixels than bins. This matters for Lyra's 4096-point RX analyzer at 96-384 kHz when zoomed to a few kHz to tens of kHz. Peaks then show their real windowed-mainlobe shape instead of power-interpolated kinks and flat tops, scalloping falls from about 0.8-1.4 dB (BH4/Hann) to a small fraction of a dB, and carrier frequency/amplitude readouts improve. There is no change in RBW, selectivity or time resolution, at the cost of a K-times-larger FFT. The fsclip bin maths in WDSP and in the caller must be rescaled. CZT is unnecessary, and zoom-FFT adds little because the radio's DDC already decimates and full-band FFTs at ≤384 kHz are cheap.

kept.title: Scaling inconsistencies: real-input +3 dB, ENBW applied per detector, uncorrected min-of-K and log-average biases, and float32-unsafe constants
kept.file_function: analyzer.c:SetAnalyzer scale (1255-1264); detector inv_enb usage (383, 407, 432, 455); avenger norm (551-553) and case 3 (540-549); eliminate/Celiminate min (201, 208, 255, 270); constants 1.0e-60 (491, 499, 508, 521, 531, 545) and ±1.0e300 (311, 325-327)
kept.current: (a) Real input uses scale = 4/N^2 (1258), so a real cosine of amplitude A reads A^2, its peak squared, while its mean power is A^2/2. Complex input uses 1/N^2, which reads mean power correctly. The DC bin, included when clip=0, is counted twice as well. (b) inv_enb is applied only for average, sample and rms, but norm_oneHz (dB/Hz) is added for every detector, so peak/rosenfell with 'normalize' report a density off by +10log10(ENBW): 1.76 dB for Hann, 3.02 for BH4, 4.20 for BH7, 5.76 for flat-top. (c) Spur elimination keeps min over num_fft LOs. For noise, the minimum of K iid exponential powers has mean μ/K, so the floor reads 10log10(K) dB low. (d) Mode 3 averages dB values, biased -2.51 dB on noise; the comment at 540 acknowledges this but nothing corrects it. (e) The 1e-60 log floor underflows to 0 in float32 (FLT_MIN is about 1.2e-38), and the -1e300 sentinels overflow to -inf.
kept.proposed: Separate 'signal' from 'density' calibration explicitly. (a) Use 2/N^2 for real-input bins 1..N/2-1 and 1/N^2 for DC/Nyquist, or document the convention. (b) Apply inv_enb whenever normalize is on, independent of detector. (c) Multiply the min-eliminated result by K for noise-calibrated displays, or use a median across LOs for K >= 3, which is just as robust against spurs on one LO and has a smaller, known bias. (d) Offer +2.51 dB correction in log-average mode, valid for noise with sample/single-bin detection. (e) In the float32 port use a 1e-30 floor and ±FLT_MAX or ±INFINITY sentinels, and keep cgsum/igsum (window design) and av_sum in double.
kept.benefit: Real and complex input show the same signal at the same level. Noise density and noise-marker readings become correct for every detector, window and LO count. Individual corrections are 1.5-6 dB, constant offsets that cd/calibration may partly absorb today; they matter when the user switches window or detector and the floor jumps. The float32 items prevent -inf pixels and NaN-free-but-wrong log values.
kept.risk: Changing (a)-(c) moves displayed levels, which affects users who calibrated cd against current behaviour. Ship behind a 'calibrated levels' option, or re-run calibration. Median elimination is slightly weaker than min against a spur present on two of three LOs.
kept.evidence: ENBW values computed from new_window coefficients (N=8192): Hann 1.50, BH4 2.005, BH7 2.631, flat-top 3.771 bins. Harris, Proc. IEEE 1978 for ENBW and coherent gain. Order statistics (David and Nagaraja 2003): min of K Exp(μ) is Exp(μ/K). Keysight AN 1303: the 2.51 dB log-average bias. One-sided PSD convention: Heinzel, Rüdiger and Schilling, 'Spectrum and spectral density estimation by the DFT', AEI 2002 (factor 2, not 4, with DC/Nyquist exceptions).

verdict.reasoning:
I checked each item against analyzer.c in WDSP 2.11.

(a) Real-input scale is a convention, not a bug. new_window normalises the window so that sum(w) = N (inv_coherent_gain = N/cgsum). A real cosine of amplitude A then gives |X|^2 = A^2·N^2/4, and the 4/N^2 scale turns that into A^2. A complex exponential of amplitude A gives A^2·N^2, and 1/N^2 turns that into A^2. So a full-scale real sine and a full-scale complex tone both read 0 dB. That is the usual dBFS convention, where a full-scale sine is 0 dBFS (AES17). The claim that real and complex input show the same signal at different levels is therefore misleading: they already agree. Moving to 2/N^2 would make a full-scale sine read -3 dB. The convention does matter for noise density with 'normalize' on real input, which reads 3 dB above the one-sided PSD of Heinzel et al. The DC bin is actually 4x too high (+6 dB), not counted twice. But DC is normally clipped, and real input in WDSP is mostly used for audio displays.

(b) This one is accurate. inv_enb is applied only for detectors 2, 3 and 4 (lines 383-455, and ampl_comp at 448). norm_oneHz is added for every detector at 551-553, and the ENBW values quoted are correct (Hann 1.76 dB, BH4 3.02 dB). The practical value is small, though. A peak or rosenfell detector on noise also picks the maximum of several bins per pixel, a bias that depends on the bins-per-pixel ratio. So a dB/Hz reading from a peak detector is meaningless even with inv_enb applied. The correct fix is to say that density readings need the sample or average detector, which is what bench spectrum analyzers do for noise markers.

(c) This is accurate for num_fft > 1, assuming each LO pass is a separate acquisition with independent noise. The min of K iid Exp(μ) has mean μ/K, so the floor reads 10log10(K) low. Spur elimination with several LOs is rarely enabled; with num_fft = 1 there is no bias. A median needs K >= 3, which triples the acquisitions.

(d) This is accurate and well known (the 2.51 dB log-average bias). The code comment says mode 3 is cosmetic. An optional +2.51 dB correction for noise is harmless but minor.

(e) This is inaccurate for the current code. The detector arrays, the sentinels and the mlog10 argument are all double. Only the final log value is cast to float (dOUTREAL), and -600 dB fits easily in float. The 1e-60 floor and ±1e300 sentinels never pass through float32. This item applies only to a hypothetical float32 port, which is the porter's job, not a WDSP defect.

Overall, some sub-claims are real but small (b, c when K > 1, d). (a) misreads a deliberate dBFS convention, and (e) is not a bug in WDSP. Changing (a) through (c) would also shift levels that users have already calibrated against.
verdict.corrected_benefit:
Small consistency gains in narrow cases:
- Applying inv_enb when 'normalize' (dB/Hz) is on with a peak or rosenfell detector removes a window-dependent offset of 1.8 to 5.8 dB. Peak-detector density stays biased by the max-of-bins-per-pixel effect, so the better fix is to document, or enforce, the sample or average detector for density readings.
- With spur elimination using num_fft = K > 1, the noise floor reads 10log10(K) dB low. A documented correction, or a median when K >= 3, would fix that. It has no effect at K = 1.
- Log-average mode (av_mode 3) could offer an optional +2.51 dB noise correction.
- Real-input noise density with 'normalize' reads 3 dB above the one-sided PSD, and the DC bin reads 6 dB high. Signal levels are already consistent between real and complex input under the full-scale-sine = 0 dBFS convention, so they should not be changed.
- The float32 points apply only to a port that computes the log argument in float, not to WDSP as it stands.

kept.title: Calibration spline: wrong system for 3 points, out-of-bounds read for fewer than 3, unbounded cubic extrapolation; use clamped PCHIP
kept.current: build_interpolants sets the end condition S0=S1 and S(n-1)=S(n-2). For n==3 the single interior row takes the 'i==1' branch, with dmain = 3dx0+2dx1 (1003), so it misses the dx1 term that S2=S1 contributes. The correct value is 3dx0+3dx1, which makes S1 too large. For n<3 the function returns -1 (988), but SetCalibration ignores this and still sets n_freqs=k (1595). With n_freqs==1, interpolate takes k = n-2 = -1 for f > freqs[0] (940) and reads ac*[-1]. n_points > dMAX_N (100) overflows the stack array y[dMAX_N] and freqs. Outside the calibration range the end cubic is extrapolated without limit (937-940), and the result is squared (969), so it can blow up.
kept.proposed: Validate n (1 gives a constant, 2 gives linear, cap at dMAX_N) and return or propagate errors. Build the curve with a shape-preserving monotone cubic (PCHIP, Fritsch and Carlson 1980), or at least with natural/not-a-knot conditions solved correctly for n=3. Hold the end values, or extrapolate linearly in dB, outside [freqs[0], freqs[n-1]].
kept.benefit: Prevents crashes and garbage from short or oversize calibration tables. PCHIP avoids the overshoot between sparse calibration points that a cubic spline produces near steep filter edges, which would otherwise appear as ripple of a few tenths of a dB on the panadapter floor. The effect is small in normal use, but these are real faults.
kept.risk: PCHIP is slightly less smooth (C1 instead of C2) and gives slightly different values between points. That is fine for amplitude calibration.
kept.evidence: Lines 988/1595 (error ignored), 940 (k = n-2), 1000-1004 (n==3 branch), 1580/1590 (fixed-size y with an unchecked n_points). Fritsch and Carlson, 'Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation', SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 1980.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked analyzer.c in WDSP 2.11, and the defect claims mostly hold.

(1) The n==3 system. The end conditions S0=S1 and S(n-1)=S(n-2) make the first interior row (3dx0+2dx1)S1 + dx1*S2 = d1 and the last interior row dx(n-3)*S(n-3) + (2dx(n-3)+3dx(n-2))*S(n-2) = d(n-2). When n=3 both conditions fall on the same row, which should read (3dx0+3dx1)S1 = d1. The code takes the i==1 branch at line 1000 and uses dmain = 3dx0+2dx1, and back-substitution gives S1 = v/b. So |S1| comes out too large. The curve still passes through every point, because ac0 and ac1 force the knots. But the slope no longer matches at x1.

(2) build_interpolants returns -1 when n<3, or when there are duplicate or too-close frequencies (line 988 and the dx check). SetCalibration ignores the return value and still writes n_freqs=k (line 1595). With n=1 and f > freqs[0], interpolate sets k = n-2 = -1 and reads ac*[-1], which is a heap out-of-bounds read. With n=0, freqs[-1] is read. With n=2, the stale or zero coefficients are used.

(3) n_points is never checked against dMAX_N=100. The stack array y[dMAX_N][dMAX_M] and the heap array freqs[set] (malloc'd as dMAX_N) overflow once there are more than 100 distinct points.

(4) Extrapolation: one detail is wrong. Because S0=S1 and S(n-1)=S(n-2), ac3 is exactly 0 on the two end segments. So the extrapolation outside the range is quadratic, not cubic. It is still unbounded, and line 969 squares it.

The practical impact is close to nil, which undercuts the claimed benefit. interpolate() runs only when fmin or fmax is non-zero (line 1245). Otherwise cd[] stays at 1.0. Thetis (specHPSDR.cs) passes span_min_freq and span_max_freq of 0.0 by default and only declares SetCalibration as an extern, never calling it. Lyra (wdsp_engine.cpp) passes calset 0 and fmin/fmax 0.0, 0.0, and never resolves SetCalibration at all. So no known client runs this path. The claim of 'ripple of a few tenths of a dB on the panadapter floor' is speculative and does not happen in practice.

Fritsch and Carlson (1980) is a real and relevant paper, and PCHIP is a reasonable choice for sparse amplitude-calibration points. But the overshoot benefit is unproven, and the difference is purely a matter of taste for a path nobody uses. The hardening part (check n, cap at dMAX_N, propagate the error, clamp extrapolation) is a valid fix for latent bugs that a future API user could hit. The algorithm swap is not justified on any measured benefit.
